Source: American College of Radiology · https://acsearch.acr.org/docs/69483/narrative/

Topic: Recognizing neurologic red flags in low back pain
Prompt: A different adult with back pain develops new urinary retention, saddle sensory loss and bilateral leg weakness. Which urgent imaging test is indicated?
Answer: Lumbar spine MRI for suspected cauda equina compression.
Reason: New bladder and sacral neurologic deficits change the imaging pathway.
Source: American College of Radiology · https://acsearch.acr.org/docs/69483/narrative/

Topic: Preventing contracture and detecting blunt muscle injury
Prompt: How does a contracture differ from weakness when an examiner moves the limb for the patient?
Answer: A contracture limits passive range of motion.
Reason: Shortened soft tissues or joint changes impose a mechanical limit.
Source: Oxford Health NHS Foundation Trust · https://www.oxfordhealth.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2023/06/1.6.2-contracture-prevention-advice-sheet.pdf

Topic: Preventing contracture and detecting blunt muscle injury
Prompt: A bedbound patient consistently rests with both knees flexed. What general rehabilitation measure helps prevent a fixed knee flexion contracture?
Answer: Regular position changes and individualized range-of-motion work, including extension as tolerated.
Reason: Prolonged positioning in a shortened range promotes loss of passive movement.
Source: Oxford Health NHS Foundation Trust · https://www.oxfordhealth.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2023/06/1.6.2-contracture-prevention-advice-sheet.pdf

Topic: Preventing contracture and detecting blunt muscle injury
Prompt: After a transtibial amputation, a patient continuously rests with a pillow behind the knee. What problem can this create for later prosthetic walking?
Answer: A knee flexion contracture.
Reason: Sustained flexion shortens the available extension range and can impair prosthetic alignment.
Source: VA/DoD lower limb amputation guideline · https://www.healthquality.va.gov/guidelines/Rehab/amp/LLA-CPG_2024-Guideline_final_20250110.pdf

Topic: Preventing contracture and detecting blunt muscle injury
Prompt: Blunt impact causes painful swelling and discoloration of a muscle despite intact overlying skin. What produces the bruising?
Answer: Blood leaking from injured vessels into the soft tissue.
Reason: This is a contusion rather than a skin laceration.
Source: Royal Children’s Hospital Melbourne · https://www.rch.org.au/trauma-service/manual/musculoskeletal-injury/

Topic: Managing open and high-energy musculoskeletal injuries
Prompt: After immediate life threats from an explosion have been addressed, a survivor has an open tibial fracture. Which time-sensitive drug treatment is indicated while surgical care is arranged?
Answer: Prompt IV antibiotic prophylaxis for an open fracture.
Reason: Contamination and exposed tissues increase infection risk. Give antibiotics without waiting for operative debridement.
Source: NICE · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng37/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Managing open and high-energy musculoskeletal injuries
Prompt: A displaced limb fracture is being splinted. Why repeat and document distal neurovascular findings immediately afterward?
Answer: To detect a new deficit or change in perfusion after alignment or splinting.
Reason: Documenting a baseline and repeat exam guides urgent reassessment.
Source: NICE · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng37/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Selecting hip imaging during infancy
Prompt: Why can ultrasound show a young infant's femoral head more completely than plain radiography?
Answer: Much of the femoral head remains cartilaginous.
Reason: Ultrasound depicts unossified structures and can assess motion and coverage.
Source: ACR and RSNA · https://www.radiologyinfo.org/en/info/acs-dysplasia-hip-child

Topic: Selecting hip imaging during infancy
Prompt: Why does the preferred initial imaging test for suspected developmental hip dysplasia change as an infant gets older?
Answer: Progressive femoral head ossification improves radiographic assessment.
Reason: Age and the physical examination guide modality selection.
Source: ACR and RSNA · https://www.radiologyinfo.org/en/info/acs-dysplasia-hip-child

Topic: Selecting hip imaging during infancy
Prompt: A 7-week-old infant born breech has a normal exam but is being imaged because of the risk factor. What initial imaging is appropriate?
Answer: Hip ultrasound.
Reason: It assesses the largely cartilaginous infant hip at this age.
Source: ACR and RSNA · https://www.radiologyinfo.org/en/info/acs-dysplasia-hip-child

Topic: Selecting hip imaging during infancy
Prompt: A 9-month-old has asymmetric hip abduction and suspected developmental dysplasia. Which initial imaging study is generally preferred?
Answer: An AP pelvic radiograph.
Reason: Ossification at this age permits useful assessment of bony alignment and acetabular development.
Source: ACR and RSNA · https://www.radiologyinfo.org/en/info/acs-dysplasia-hip-child

Topic: Selecting hip imaging during infancy
Prompt: The parents of a healthy breech newborn with a normal hip exam ask why planned screening ultrasound is scheduled in several weeks instead of on day one. What limitation of immediate ultrasound matters?
Answer: Physiologic neonatal laxity and immaturity can produce transient abnormal findings.
Reason: Timing differs if examination suggests frank instability, which needs prompt specialist assessment.
Source: ACR and RSNA · https://www.radiologyinfo.org/en/info/acs-dysplasia-hip-child

Topic: Evaluating a child with a skeletal dysplasia
Prompt: An infant with achondroplasia develops central apneas, brisk reflexes and clonus. What structural complication needs prompt specialist assessment?
Answer: Foramen magnum narrowing with cervicomedullary compression.
Reason: The neurologic and respiratory changes can reflect brainstem or upper cord compression.
Source: GeneReviews · https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1152/

Topic: Recognizing limb development and alignment patterns
Prompt: In phocomelia, which parts of a limb can be markedly shortened or absent despite a more distal hand or foot being present?
Answer: The intervening long-bone segments.
Reason: This limb reduction pattern can occur after certain teratogenic exposures, including thalidomide.
Source: FDA prescribing information · https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2026/020785s074lbl.pdf

Topic: Recognizing limb development and alignment patterns
Prompt: A nonambulatory child with spinal muscular atrophy develops asymmetric loss of hip abduction and difficulty sitting. Which hip alignment complication warrants assessment?
Answer: Hip subluxation or dislocation.
Reason: Neuromuscular weakness can compromise containment of the femoral head.
Source: POSNA · https://posna.org/physician-education/study-guide/spinal-muscular-atrophy

Topic: Recognizing limb development and alignment patterns
Prompt: When a standing child's knees touch but the ankles remain apart, what is the alignment called?
Answer: Genu valgum (knock-knees).
Reason: Genu varum produces the opposite pattern, with the knees separated when the ankles are together.
Source: POSNA · https://posna.org/physician-education/study-guide/genu-valgum

Topic: Recognizing limb development and alignment patterns
Prompt: A healthy 4-year-old has mild symmetric knock-knees, normal stature, no pain and a normal gait. What is the most likely explanation?
Answer: Physiologic genu valgum.
Reason: Symmetric valgus can be normal at preschool age and usually decreases with growth.
Source: POSNA · https://posna.org/physician-education/study-guide/genu-valgum

Topic: Recognizing limb development and alignment patterns
Prompt: A 9-year-old develops progressively worsening unilateral valgus after a physeal injury. Is routine reassurance for physiologic knock-knees sufficient?
Answer: No. Evaluate for pathologic asymmetric growth and refer to pediatric orthopedics.
Reason: Age, progression, asymmetry and prior growth plate injury change the assessment.
Source: POSNA · https://posna.org/physician-education/study-guide/genu-valgum

Topic: Recognizing limb development and alignment patterns
Prompt: In clubfoot, what is meant by equinus at the ankle?
Answer: Persistent plantar flexion with limited dorsiflexion.
Reason: Equinus is one component of the clubfoot deformity.
Source: POSNA · https://posna.org/physician-education/study-guide/clubfoot

Topic: Recognizing limb development and alignment patterns
Prompt: A newborn has a rigid foot held in equinus with hindfoot varus and forefoot adduction that cannot be passively corrected. What condition fits?
Answer: Congenital talipes equinovarus (clubfoot).
Reason: A fixed, multicomponent deformity differs from a flexible positional foot.
Source: POSNA · https://posna.org/physician-education/study-guide/clubfoot

Topic: Recognizing limb development and alignment patterns
Prompt: A baby's clubfoot has been corrected by Ponseti casting and tenotomy as needed. What is the purpose of the prescribed foot abduction brace?
Answer: To maintain correction and reduce relapse during growth.
Reason: A corrected appearance at the end of casting does not remove the need for maintenance.
Source: POSNA · https://posna.org/physician-education/study-guide/clubfoot

Topic: Recognizing heritable bone and muscle disease
Prompt: A child has recurrent low-trauma fractures and a family history of brittle bones, but the sclerae are white. Does this finding alone exclude osteogenesis imperfecta?
Answer: No.
Reason: Scleral color varies by OI phenotype. Evaluate the entire clinical, radiographic and family pattern.
Source: GeneReviews · https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1295/

Topic: Recognizing heritable bone and muscle disease
Prompt: During the simulated constant-workload bicycle test, heart rate falls as symptoms ease despite continued exercise. What clinical phenomenon does this illustrate?
Answer: Second wind in McArdle disease.
Reason: Greater availability of circulating fuels improves exercise tolerance after the initial difficulty.
Source: GeneReviews · https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1344/

Topic: Recognizing heritable bone and muscle disease
Prompt: A patient with McArdle disease has severe exertional muscle pain and cola-colored urine after sprinting. What acute organ complication should be evaluated along with muscle injury?
Answer: Acute kidney injury from rhabdomyolysis.
Reason: Myoglobin release can damage renal tubules and warrants prompt evaluation.
Source: GeneReviews · https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1344/

Topic: Recognizing heritable bone and muscle disease
Prompt: Why are skeletal muscle and other high-energy tissues often affected in mitochondrial respiratory-chain disorders?
Answer: They depend heavily on oxidative phosphorylation for ATP.
Reason: Impaired ATP production can manifest as exercise intolerance, weakness or multisystem disease.
Source: GeneReviews · https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1224/

Topic: Recognizing heritable bone and muscle disease
Prompt: An adult has exercise intolerance, ptosis and external ophthalmoplegia. Muscle biopsy shows ragged-red fibers. Which disease category fits best?
Answer: A mitochondrial myopathy.
Reason: The constellation suggests abnormal mitochondrial function and accumulation in muscle.
Source: GeneReviews · https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1224/

Topic: Recognizing anesthetic-triggered malignant hyperthermia
Prompt: In classic RYR1-related malignant hyperthermia, triggering anesthesia causes excessive release of which ion into skeletal muscle cytosol?
Answer: Calcium.
Reason: Uncontrolled calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum drives contraction and hypermetabolism.
Source: GeneReviews · https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1146/

Topic: Recognizing anesthetic-triggered malignant hyperthermia
Prompt: Why can end-tidal CO₂ rise rapidly during malignant hyperthermia even at unchanged or increased minute ventilation?
Answer: Hypermetabolic skeletal muscle produces excess CO₂.
Reason: The carbon dioxide rise can precede marked hyperthermia.
Source: GeneReviews · https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1146/

Topic: Recognizing anesthetic-triggered malignant hyperthermia
Prompt: During volatile anesthesia the ventilator settings are unchanged, rigidity develops, and the monitor shows these trends. Which crisis should be treated immediately?
Answer: Malignant hyperthermia.
Reason: Excess CO₂ production and tachycardia with rigidity can appear before a large temperature rise.
Source: Malignant Hyperthermia Association of the United States · https://www.mhaus.org/healthcare-professionals/managing-a-crisis/

Topic: Recognizing anesthetic-triggered malignant hyperthermia
Prompt: A patient receiving sevoflurane develops generalized rigidity and rapidly rising end-tidal CO₂ despite increased ventilation. Core temperature is 37.4°C. Should treatment for suspected malignant hyperthermia wait for fever?
Answer: No. Act immediately.
Reason: Hyperthermia can be a late sign.
Source: Malignant Hyperthermia Association of the United States · https://www.mhaus.org/healthcare-professionals/managing-a-crisis/

Topic: Recognizing anesthetic-triggered malignant hyperthermia
Prompt: The anesthetic trigger has been stopped and the team is hyperventilating with 100% oxygen for suspected malignant hyperthermia. Which specific drug should be given promptly?
Answer: IV dantrolene.
Reason: Dantrolene reduces pathologic calcium release in skeletal muscle.
Source: Malignant Hyperthermia Association of the United States · https://www.mhaus.org/healthcare-professionals/managing-a-crisis/

Topic: Recognizing anesthetic-triggered malignant hyperthermia
Prompt: Rigidity and excessive end-tidal CO₂ persist after the first IV dantrolene dose during an MH crisis. What should the team do about dantrolene?
Answer: Give further IV doses according to the MH crisis protocol while reassessing the response.
Reason: Treatment is titrated to control of hypermetabolism, alongside supportive care.
Source: Malignant Hyperthermia Association of the United States · https://www.mhaus.org/healthcare-professionals/managing-a-crisis/

Topic: Recognizing anesthetic-triggered malignant hyperthermia
Prompt: Besides potent volatile anesthetics, which depolarizing neuromuscular blocker can trigger malignant hyperthermia?
Answer: Succinylcholine.
Reason: A trigger-free plan avoids both classes in susceptible patients.
Source: Malignant Hyperthermia Association of the United States · https://www.mhaus.org/healthcare-professionals/be-prepared/safe-and-unsafe-anesthetics/

Topic: Recognizing anesthetic-triggered malignant hyperthermia
Prompt: A patient with known MH susceptibility needs elective surgery. Which plan is appropriate: sevoflurane maintenance or a trigger-free IV anesthetic with a prepared machine?
Answer: A trigger-free IV anesthetic with a properly prepared machine.
Reason: Potent volatile agents and succinylcholine are triggers.
Source: Malignant Hyperthermia Association of the United States · https://www.mhaus.org/healthcare-professionals/be-prepared/safe-and-unsafe-anesthetics/

Topic: Recognizing anesthetic-triggered malignant hyperthermia
Prompt: A person with confirmed MH susceptibility needs a dental procedure using lidocaine alone. Must lidocaine be avoided solely because of MH susceptibility?
Answer: No. Local anesthetics are considered safe for MH-susceptible patients.
Reason: The trigger list includes potent volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine.
Source: Malignant Hyperthermia Association of the United States · https://www.mhaus.org/healthcare-professionals/be-prepared/safe-and-unsafe-anesthetics/

Topic: Distinguishing drug-associated muscle disorders
Prompt: A patient on prolonged systemic prednisone has slowly progressive painless hip-girdle weakness, a normal CK and no rash. Which drug complication fits?
Answer: Glucocorticoid myopathy.
Reason: The chronic form often causes proximal weakness with little muscle enzyme elevation.
Source: DailyMed · https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=41ade439-59f2-dfd1-e063-6294a90aca0f&type=display

Topic: Distinguishing drug-associated muscle disorders
Prompt: A patient with likely chronic glucocorticoid myopathy still needs anti-inflammatory therapy. What medication strategy should be discussed with the treating team?
Answer: Reduce glucocorticoid exposure safely if feasible and consider a steroid-sparing plan.
Reason: Tapering must account for the underlying disease and adrenal suppression.
Source: DailyMed · https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=41ade439-59f2-dfd1-e063-6294a90aca0f&type=display

Topic: Distinguishing drug-associated muscle disorders
Prompt: An adult taking a statin reports mild muscle aching. CK is normal. Does a normal CK exclude statin-associated myalgia?
Answer: No.
Reason: Symptoms can occur without biochemical evidence of muscle necrosis. Assess timing and alternate causes.
Source: American College of Cardiology · https://tools.acc.org/StatinIntolerance/index.html

Topic: Distinguishing drug-associated muscle disorders
Prompt: Mild muscle symptoms resolved after a statin was stopped, and reversible contributors have been addressed. What can help identify a tolerable lipid-lowering regimen?
Answer: A supervised trial of a lower dose or a different statin when appropriate.
Reason: Recurrence and tolerability guide long-term management in patients without severe injury.
Source: American College of Cardiology · https://tools.acc.org/StatinIntolerance/index.html

Topic: Distinguishing drug-associated muscle disorders
Prompt: After cocaine intoxication with prolonged agitation and hyperthermia, a patient develops dark urine and very high CK. What complication explains the laboratory findings?
Answer: Rhabdomyolysis.
Reason: Intense activity, heat and ischemia can contribute to skeletal muscle injury.
Source: AAST clinical consensus · https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8804685/

Topic: Distinguishing drug-associated muscle disorders
Prompt: An adult with HIV develops progressive proximal weakness and muscle pain during prolonged treatment with zidovudine. What medication adverse effect warrants evaluation?
Answer: Zidovudine-associated myopathy.
Reason: Prolonged use can be associated with symptomatic muscle injury. HIV itself and other drugs can also cause weakness.
Source: NIH · https://clinicalinfo.hiv.gov/en/drugs/zidovudine/patient

Topic: Recognizing muscle injury and its renal complications
Prompt: Which heme protein released during extensive skeletal muscle injury can darken urine and injure renal tubules?
Answer: Myoglobin.
Reason: Severe muscle breakdown can also release potassium and raise CK.
Source: AAST clinical consensus · https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8804685/

Topic: Recognizing muscle injury and its renal complications
Prompt: After prolonged immobilization, a patient has thigh pain, markedly elevated CK and urine dipstick positive for blood with almost no red cells on microscopy. Which pigment fits?
Answer: Myoglobin.
Reason: The heme-sensitive dipstick can detect muscle pigment even in the absence of urinary red cells.
Source: AAST clinical consensus · https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8804685/

Topic: Recognizing muscle injury and its renal complications
Prompt: A patient with extensive rhabdomyolysis develops peaked T waves. Which electrolyte disturbance is an immediate concern?
Answer: Hyperkalemia.
Reason: Damaged muscle releases potassium and can cause lethal dysrhythmia.
Source: AAST clinical consensus · https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8804685/

Topic: Recognizing muscle injury and its renal complications
Prompt: A patient with rhabdomyolysis is receiving isotonic IV fluids but remains anuric despite escalating rates. Why should fluids not be increased indefinitely?
Answer: Fluid can accumulate and cause life-threatening volume overload.
Reason: Reassess the cause of anuria and indications for renal support rather than escalating without renal clearance.
Source: AAST clinical consensus · https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8804685/

Topic: Distinguishing spinal imaging findings from symptomatic compression
Prompt: What does radiculopathy localize dysfunction to?
Answer: A spinal nerve root.
Reason: A root lesion can produce a myotomal weakness, dermatomal sensory loss or altered reflex.
Source: American College of Radiology · https://acsearch.acr.org/docs/69483/narrative/

Topic: Distinguishing spinal imaging findings from symptomatic compression
Prompt: Lumbar MRI shows a posterolateral L4–L5 herniated disc compressing the traversing root. Which weakness supports L5 involvement?
Answer: Weak great-toe extension.
Reason: The usual posterolateral L4–L5 lesion affects the traversing L5 root.
Source: American College of Radiology · https://acsearch.acr.org/docs/69483/narrative/

Topic: Distinguishing spinal imaging findings from symptomatic compression
Prompt: A pain-free adult has a degenerative lumbar disc bulge reported incidentally. What should determine whether future symptoms are attributed to that finding?
Answer: Concordance between the clinical distribution, examination and imaging.
Reason: Degenerative changes can occur in people without symptoms.
Source: American College of Radiology · https://acsearch.acr.org/docs/69483/narrative/

Topic: Distinguishing spinal imaging findings from symptomatic compression
Prompt: In degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis, what has moved relative to its neighbor?
Answer: One vertebral body has translated relative to the adjacent vertebra.
Reason: This is distinct from a displaced intervertebral disc fragment.
Source: American College of Radiology · https://acsearch.acr.org/docs/69483/narrative/

Topic: Identifying mechanically weakened bone
Prompt: What makes a fracture pathologic?
Answer: It occurs through bone weakened by an underlying lesion or disease.
Reason: The force can be too small to fracture otherwise healthy bone.
Source: POSNA · https://posna.org/blogs/resident-review/december-2017/benign-bone-tumors

Topic: Identifying mechanically weakened bone
Prompt: A child fractures the proximal humerus during a minor fall. A large simple bone cyst occupies the fracture site. How should the fracture be classified?
Answer: A pathologic fracture through a bone cyst.
Reason: The focal lesion substantially weakens the bone.
Source: POSNA · https://posna.org/blogs/resident-review/december-2017/benign-bone-tumors

Topic: Recognizing periarticular degeneration and soft-tissue changes
Prompt: Which tissue contracts in Dupuytren disease?
Answer: The palmar fascia.
Reason: Fibrous cords shorten and draw the fingers into flexion.
Source: American Society for Surgery of the Hand · https://www.assh.org/handcare/servlet/servlet.FileDownload?file=00P0a00000ocYEaEAM

Topic: Recognizing periarticular degeneration and soft-tissue changes
Prompt: An adult has a palmar cord to the ring finger, a painless fixed flexion deformity and difficulty laying the palm flat on a table. Which disorder fits?
Answer: Dupuytren contracture.
Reason: The palpable fascial cord helps distinguish it from a flexor tendon problem.
Source: American Society for Surgery of the Hand · https://www.assh.org/handcare/servlet/servlet.FileDownload?file=00P0a00000ocYEaEAM

Topic: Recognizing periarticular degeneration and soft-tissue changes
Prompt: What tissue is softened or damaged in chondromalacia patellae?
Answer: Articular cartilage on the undersurface of the patella.
Reason: Patellofemoral pain alone does not establish cartilage damage.
Source: Hospital for Special Surgery · https://www.hss.edu/health-library/conditions-and-treatments/list/patellofemoral-disorders

Topic: Recognizing periarticular degeneration and soft-tissue changes
Prompt: Several weeks after a deep thigh contusion, an athlete develops a firm intramuscular mass with peripheral ossification on radiographs. Which post-traumatic process fits?
Answer: Myositis ossificans (heterotopic ossification).
Reason: Bone forms in soft tissue after injury, producing a zonal pattern as it matures.
Source: Lacout et al., imaging series · https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/pmid/22623814/

Topic: Recognizing periarticular degeneration and soft-tissue changes
Prompt: An uninjured limb loses muscle bulk after weeks in a cast with little use. Which cellular change is responsible?
Answer: Reduced size of existing skeletal muscle fibers (disuse atrophy).
Reason: Reduced loading leads to loss of contractile protein and cross-sectional area.
Source: NASA bed rest study · https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7688251/

Topic: Recognizing periarticular and tendon-sheath disorders
Prompt: Pressure on a taut band in the trapezius reproduces a patient's usual distant shoulder ache despite a normal shoulder joint examination. What is the likely source?
Answer: A myofascial trigger point.
Reason: Focal muscle tenderness can produce a characteristic referred pain pattern.
Source: Royal Orthopaedic Hospital · https://roh.nhs.uk/services-information/pain-management/trigger-point

Topic: Investigating a painful joint effusion
Prompt: A hot native knee has inflammatory synovial fluid with 28,000 leukocytes/µL. Can the count alone exclude bacterial arthritis?
Answer: No.
Reason: A lower leukocyte count reduces probability but does not exclude infection. Culture is still important when suspicion persists.
Source: European Bone and Joint Infection Society · https://jbji.copernicus.org/articles/8/29/2023/index.html

Topic: Investigating a painful joint effusion
Prompt: A febrile patient with a hot native knee has urate crystals in the aspirate. What microbiologic study is still required when septic arthritis is suspected?
Answer: Synovial fluid culture.
Reason: A crystal flare and bacterial infection can coexist.
Source: European Bone and Joint Infection Society · https://jbji.copernicus.org/articles/8/29/2023/index.html

Topic: Recognizing deep musculoskeletal infection
Prompt: A biopsy shows pus within skeletal muscle fibers, while the neighboring joint is uninvolved. What is the anatomic diagnosis?
Answer: Pyomyositis.
Reason: The collection is intramuscular, distinguishing it from septic arthritis or a superficial abscess.
Source: IDSA · https://www.idsociety.org/practice-guideline/skin-and-soft-tissue-infections/

Topic: Recognizing deep musculoskeletal infection
Prompt: MRI shows a discrete intramuscular abscess in a stable febrile patient, without rapidly spreading fascial necrosis. Which source-control target should be addressed?
Answer: The intramuscular abscess should be drained.
Reason: Localized pus and extensive fascial necrosis require different source-control plans.
Source: IDSA · https://www.idsociety.org/practice-guideline/skin-and-soft-tissue-infections/

Topic: Recognizing deep musculoskeletal infection
Prompt: A patient with a dry, demarcated ischemic toe has no drainage or systemic infection. Which underlying problem should the vascular team assess to guide limb management?
Answer: Whether blood flow can be restored to viable tissue.
Reason: Perfusion assessment helps determine revascularization and the extent of tissue loss.
Source: NHS · https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/gangrene/

Topic: Sequencing evaluation of vertebral infection
Prompt: Why can destruction of the anterior portions of adjacent vertebral bodies in spinal TB produce an angular kyphosis?
Answer: The vertebral bodies collapse anteriorly into a wedge.
Reason: Loss of anterior column height bends the spine forward.
Source: IDSA · https://www.idsociety.org/practice-guideline/vertebral-osteomyelitis/

Topic: Sequencing evaluation of vertebral infection
Prompt: A patient has a chronic destructive vertebral lesion, a large paraspinal collection and epidemiologic risk for tuberculosis. Which microbiologic evaluation should be added to routine studies on a diagnostic biopsy?
Answer: Mycobacterial testing, including culture, of the involved tissue.
Reason: Routine bacterial testing alone is insufficient when tuberculous spondylitis is suspected.
Source: IDSA · https://www.idsociety.org/practice-guideline/vertebral-osteomyelitis/

Topic: Localizing proximal weakness and inflammatory myopathy
Prompt: A patient has proximal weakness and Gottron papules. Biopsy shows small fibers concentrated at the outer margins of fascicles. What is this distribution called?
Answer: Perifascicular atrophy.
Reason: The characteristic pattern involves fibers at fascicle edges.
Source: EULAR/ACR inflammatory myopathy classification study · https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5846474/

Topic: Localizing proximal weakness and inflammatory myopathy
Prompt: A muscle biopsy from a patient with symmetric proximal weakness shows CD8-positive cells surrounding and invading individual nonnecrotic fibers. Which connective-tissue compartment is inflamed?
Answer: The endomysium.
Reason: This helps differentiate the pattern from perifascicular injury in dermatomyositis.
Source: EULAR/ACR inflammatory myopathy classification study · https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5846474/

Topic: Localizing proximal weakness and inflammatory myopathy
Prompt: A patient labeled as having polymyositis has years of slowly progressive asymmetric quadriceps and finger-flexor weakness despite glucocorticoids. What diagnosis merits reconsideration?

Topic: Distinguishing water-soluble vitamin functions

Topic: Distinguishing water-soluble vitamin functions

Topic: Distinguishing water-soluble vitamin functions

Prompt: A patient with persistent glossitis despite restored riboflavin intake develops impaired position sense and macrocytosis. Which coexisting deficiency should now be evaluated promptly?

Topic: Recognizing thiamine deficiency and treating emergencies

Topic: Recognizing thiamine deficiency and treating emergencies

Topic: Recognizing thiamine deficiency and treating emergencies

Answer: No. It remained 1 cm.
Reason: Both arms increased by the same amount. The readings do not show increasing asymmetry at this site.
Source: Lymphedema (PDQ®) - NCI · https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/treatment/side-effects/lymphedema/lymphedema-hp-pdq

Topic: Reading a symptom and activity diary
Prompt: What two time intervals are most useful when asking about post-exertional malaise?
Answer: The time from exertion to worsening and the duration of recovery.
Reason: Ask about effects on ordinary function as well as symptom intensity.
Source: Recommendations · Myalgic encephalomyelitis (or encephalopathy)/chronic fatigue syndrome: diagnosis and management  · Guidance · NICE · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng206/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Reading a symptom and activity diary
Prompt: After a routine activity the patient benefits from a brief rest, and this diary shows recovery by evening. Does the record document a delayed multi-day flare?
Answer: No. Symptoms returned to baseline that day.
Reason: This diary alone does not establish or exclude a broader fatigue disorder.
Source: Recommendations · Myalgic encephalomyelitis (or encephalopathy)/chronic fatigue syndrome: diagnosis and management  · Guidance · NICE · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng206/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Reading a symptom and activity diary
Prompt: In the second diary, when is the largest deterioration relative to the same activity?
Answer: The following day.
Reason: Symptoms remain above baseline through the next day as well, supporting a delayed post-exertional pattern. A diagnosis requires the broader history.
Source: Recommendations · Myalgic encephalomyelitis (or encephalopathy)/chronic fatigue syndrome: diagnosis and management  · Guidance · NICE · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng206/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Evaluating injury and immediate safety in childhood
Prompt: Why does a child's actual motor development matter when evaluating a bruise?
Answer: It affects whether the reported accidental mechanism is developmentally plausible.
Reason: Assess the child, history and relevant medical conditions together.
Source: The Evaluation of Suspected Child Physical Abuse · https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article-lookup/doi/10.1542/peds.2015-0356

Topic: Evaluating injury and immediate safety in childhood
Prompt: A healthy toddler who walks independently has a small shin bruise after a witnessed stumble onto the shin. Does this history and finding alone establish physical abuse?
Answer: No. The account fits the child's abilities and the observed event.
Reason: Other concerning history or exam findings would warrant assessment.
Source: The Evaluation of Suspected Child Physical Abuse · https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article-lookup/doi/10.1542/peds.2015-0356

Topic: Evaluating injury and immediate safety in childhood
Prompt: A young infant who cannot yet roll or cruise has an unexplained bruise. What is its clinical significance?
Answer: It warrants prompt medical and safeguarding assessment.
Reason: Unexpected bruising in a nonmobile infant can be an early sign of injury. Also consider bleeding disorders.
Source: The Evaluation of Suspected Child Physical Abuse · https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article-lookup/doi/10.1542/peds.2015-0356

Topic: Evaluating injury and immediate safety in childhood
Prompt: What is the purpose of a skeletal survey in a young child with suspected physical abuse?
Answer: To identify clinically unsuspected skeletal injuries.
Reason: Use an age-appropriate standardized series interpreted by clinicians experienced in pediatric imaging.
Source: ACR Appropriateness Criteria · Suspected Physical Abuse—Child · https://acsearch.acr.org/docs/69443/Narrative/

Topic: Evaluating injury and immediate safety in childhood
Prompt: A clinically stable 9-month-old has an unexplained fracture and concern for physical abuse. Which imaging study assesses for additional occult fractures?
Answer: A complete skeletal survey.
Reason: The absence of tenderness elsewhere does not rule out other injuries.
Source: ACR Appropriateness Criteria · Suspected Physical Abuse—Child · https://acsearch.acr.org/docs/69443/Narrative/

Topic: Evaluating injury and immediate safety in childhood
Prompt: An infant with suspected abusive head trauma develops a seizure and reduced consciousness. What takes priority over completion of routine skeletal imaging?
Answer: Emergency stabilization and urgent evaluation for intracranial injury.
Reason: Treat airway, breathing, circulation and the seizure, and arrange appropriate urgent neuroimaging.
Source: Abusive Head Trauma in Infants and Children: Technical Report · https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/doi/10.1542/peds.2024-070457/201049

Topic: Evaluating injury and immediate safety in childhood
Prompt: Why should an initial negative skeletal survey not end a safeguarding evaluation when clinical concern remains high?
Answer: Some fractures may be occult initially, and the clinical concern extends beyond the bones.
Reason: Consult the child protection team and arrange follow-up imaging when indicated.
Source: ACR Appropriateness Criteria · Suspected Physical Abuse—Child · https://acsearch.acr.org/docs/69443/Narrative/

Topic: Evaluating injury and immediate safety in childhood
Prompt: A child under two is clinically stable in a verified safe placement. The first skeletal survey was negative, but suspicion of physical abuse remains high. What imaging follow-up is generally appropriate?
Answer: A follow-up skeletal survey in about two weeks, coordinated with the child protection team.
Reason: Healing can make previously occult fractures visible.
Source: ACR Appropriateness Criteria · Suspected Physical Abuse—Child · https://acsearch.acr.org/docs/69443/Narrative/

Topic: Evaluating injury and immediate safety in childhood
Prompt: Another medically stable child may be in immediate danger at the planned discharge destination. Can a future imaging appointment substitute for a safe disposition?
Answer: No. Coordinate immediate protective assessment and a safe discharge or admission plan.
Reason: Follow reporting duties in the applicable jurisdiction and document the safety concern.
Source: The Evaluation of Suspected Child Physical Abuse · https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article-lookup/doi/10.1542/peds.2015-0356

Topic: Protecting a child during evaluation of reported illness
Prompt: In factitious disorder imposed on another, to whom is the psychiatric diagnosis assigned?
Answer: The individual who falsifies or induces illness in another person.
Reason: The dependent patient is the person at risk of harm.
Source: Caregiver-Fabricated Illness in a Child: A Manifestation of Child Maltreatment · https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article-lookup/doi/10.1542/peds.2013-2045

Topic: Protecting a child during evaluation of reported illness
Prompt: A caregiver is independently shown to have deliberately misrepresented a child's illness while presenting the child as sick, with no apparent external reward. Which diagnosis describes the caregiver's behavior?
Answer: Factitious disorder imposed on another.
Reason: Assess the child for harm and continuing risk.
Source: Caregiver-Fabricated Illness in a Child: A Manifestation of Child Maltreatment · https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article-lookup/doi/10.1542/peds.2013-2045

Topic: Protecting a child during evaluation of reported illness
Prompt: Several clinicians have yet to explain a child's episodic symptoms. The caregiver is anxious and no falsification has been established. Does diagnostic uncertainty establish factitious disorder imposed on another?
Answer: No. Continue clinically appropriate evaluation and assess safety according to the evidence.
Reason: A negative workup and an anxious caregiver do not demonstrate deception.
Source: Caregiver-Fabricated Illness in a Child: A Manifestation of Child Maltreatment · https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article-lookup/doi/10.1542/peds.2013-2045

Topic: Protecting a child during evaluation of reported illness
Prompt: Why identify the original observer of a symptom in a complex pediatric history?
Answer: Repeated documentation may all derive from the same report.
Reason: Separate who observed what from the medical interpretation.
Source: Caregiver-Fabricated Illness in a Child: A Manifestation of Child Maltreatment · https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article-lookup/doi/10.1542/peds.2013-2045

Topic: Protecting a child during evaluation of reported illness
Prompt: A child is admitted for episodic illness. The record excerpts shown describe yesterday’s event. How many independent firsthand accounts of that event do they contain?
Answer: One, from the caregiver.
Reason: The later notes repeat the same account. This alone does not establish whether the event occurred.
Source: Caregiver-Fabricated Illness in a Child: A Manifestation of Child Maltreatment · https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article-lookup/doi/10.1542/peds.2013-2045

Topic: Protecting a child during evaluation of reported illness
Prompt: Which entry in this pediatric chart supplies a new firsthand observation that warrants its own clinical evaluation?
Answer: The 10 a.m. bedside nursing entry.
Reason: The nurse personally witnessed a new episode. Keep its findings distinct from the earlier home report.
Source: Caregiver-Fabricated Illness in a Child: A Manifestation of Child Maltreatment · https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article-lookup/doi/10.1542/peds.2013-2045

Topic: Protecting a child during evaluation of reported illness
Prompt: What clinical goal takes priority when caregiver-fabricated illness is suspected?
Answer: Protect the dependent patient from further harm while meeting genuine medical needs.
Reason: Coordinate care and safeguarding using documented observations.
Source: Caregiver-Fabricated Illness in a Child: A Manifestation of Child Maltreatment · https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article-lookup/doi/10.1542/peds.2013-2045

Topic: Protecting a child during evaluation of reported illness
Prompt: A stable child has had multiple unnecessary procedures. The family requests repetition of an invasive test without a new indication. What should the care team do?
Answer: Defer the unindicated procedure and coordinate a single multidisciplinary assessment and safety plan.
Reason: Review the longitudinal record and seek child protection expertise.
Source: Caregiver-Fabricated Illness in a Child: A Manifestation of Child Maltreatment · https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article-lookup/doi/10.1542/peds.2013-2045

Topic: Protecting a child during evaluation of reported illness
Prompt: During the same evaluation the child develops new hypoxemia directly observed by staff. What now takes priority?
Answer: Immediate medical assessment and stabilization of the hypoxemia.
Reason: Safeguarding concerns can coexist with independent or acute illness.
Source: Caregiver-Fabricated Illness in a Child: A Manifestation of Child Maltreatment · https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article-lookup/doi/10.1542/peds.2013-2045

Topic: Recognizing partner violence and providing survivor-centered care
Prompt: Two partners discuss contraception, disagree initially, and each remains free to decline sex or a method without repercussions. Does disagreement alone establish reproductive coercion?
Answer: No. Assess whether choices are voluntary and free of pressure or interference.
Reason: Ask privately if there is concern.
Source: Reproductive and Sexual Coercion · ACOG · https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2013/02/reproductive-and-sexual-coercion

Topic: Recognizing partner violence and providing survivor-centered care
Prompt: Why should an accompanying partner not serve as interpreter for a confidential IPV assessment?
Answer: The patient may be unable to disclose safely or freely.
Reason: Arrange privacy and an independent professional interpreter when needed.
Source: Health care for women subjected to intimate partner violence or sexual violence: a clinical handbook · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-RHR-14.26/

Topic: Recognizing partner violence and providing survivor-centered care
Prompt: At a routine visit a patient can speak privately and needs a language interpreter. How should an IPV assessment be conducted?
Answer: Use an independent professional interpreter and nonjudgmental, confidential inquiry, explaining confidentiality limits.
Reason: Invite disclosure and assess immediate needs when relevant.
Source: Health care for women subjected to intimate partner violence or sexual violence: a clinical handbook · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-RHR-14.26/

Topic: Recognizing partner violence and providing survivor-centered care
Prompt: The partner insists on answering and will not leave. Is it appropriate to ask detailed IPV screening questions in front of the partner?
Answer: No. Arrange a safe opportunity for private communication.
Reason: Avoid a confrontation or disclosure in a setting that could increase risk.
Source: Health care for women subjected to intimate partner violence or sexual violence: a clinical handbook · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-RHR-14.26/

Topic: Recognizing partner violence and providing survivor-centered care
Prompt: Which question should come early after an adult discloses partner violence?
Answer: Whether the patient is safe now and has urgent medical or safety needs.
Reason: Listen, validate and discuss options without pressuring the patient.
Source: Health care for women subjected to intimate partner violence or sexual violence: a clinical handbook · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-RHR-14.26/

Topic: Recognizing partner violence and providing survivor-centered care
Prompt: An adult with capacity has no urgent injuries, reports a safe place to stay and wants an advocate's help without making immediate relationship decisions. What should the clinician offer?
Answer: A patient-directed safety plan, advocacy connection and a safe way to follow up.
Reason: Discuss confidentiality and applicable reporting requirements.
Source: Health care for women subjected to intimate partner violence or sexual violence: a clinical handbook · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-RHR-14.26/

Topic: Recognizing partner violence and providing survivor-centered care
Prompt: A patient discloses an immediate threat at the proposed discharge destination and has nowhere safe to go. What changes in the plan?
Answer: Address immediate safety before discharge with the patient and appropriate emergency or advocacy services.
Reason: Coordinate available protection and explain any legally required actions.
Source: Health care for women subjected to intimate partner violence or sexual violence: a clinical handbook · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-RHR-14.26/

Topic: Evaluating and responding to elder mistreatment
Prompt: What makes financial exploitation different from a voluntary financial gift by an older adult?
Answer: Unauthorized or improper use of the person's resources, often involving coercion or deception.
Reason: Age or generosity alone does not establish incapacity or abuse.
Source: Elder Abuse · National Institute on Aging · https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/elder-abuse/elder-abuse

Topic: Evaluating and responding to elder mistreatment
Prompt: An older adult understands a proposed gift, describes its effect on finances and chooses it freely without pressure. Does an adult child's disagreement establish exploitation?
Answer: No. Respect the decision and assess further if there are specific concerns.
Reason: Consider capacity for this decision and the circumstances.
Source: Elder Abuse · National Institute on Aging · https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/elder-abuse/elder-abuse

Topic: Evaluating and responding to elder mistreatment
Prompt: An older patient reports that a relative repeatedly takes money without permission, leaving the patient unable to buy prescriptions. What type of mistreatment warrants evaluation?
Answer: Financial exploitation.
Reason: Interview privately and address medication access and safety.
Source: Elder Abuse · National Institute on Aging · https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/elder-abuse/elder-abuse

Topic: Evaluating and responding to elder mistreatment
Prompt: Why interview an older patient privately when dependence on a caregiver and mistreatment are concerns?
Answer: Privacy can reveal the patient's preferences, unmet needs and fears without interference.
Reason: Offer communication aids or a qualified interpreter as needed.
Source: Elder Abuse · National Institute on Aging · https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/elder-abuse/elder-abuse

Topic: Evaluating and responding to elder mistreatment
Prompt: An older adult cannot shop after a new mobility limitation. The patient and a willing caregiver both ask for help obtaining food. What should the initial assessment clarify?
Answer: Which needs are unmet, why and what practical assistance is available.
Reason: A care gap requires support; it does not by itself establish intentional abuse.
Source: Elder Abuse · National Institute on Aging · https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/elder-abuse/elder-abuse

Topic: Evaluating and responding to elder mistreatment
Prompt: A dependent older adult privately reports a caregiver routinely withholds prescribed medicines and food despite having them available. What concern needs a prompt safety assessment?
Answer: Caregiver neglect or abuse.
Reason: Evaluate the health consequences and arrange appropriate protective and social services.
Source: Elder Abuse · National Institute on Aging · https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/elder-abuse/elder-abuse

Topic: Evaluating and responding to elder mistreatment
Prompt: What should guide a safeguarding plan besides the type of suspected elder mistreatment?
Answer: Immediate danger, medical needs, decision-making capacity, patient preferences and local reporting duties.
Reason: Include adult protective services or local equivalents as appropriate.
Source: What If I Suspect Abuse, Neglect, or Exploitation? · ACL Administration for Community Living · https://acl.gov/programs/protection-and-advocacy-systems/what-if-i-suspect-abuse-neglect-or-exploitation

Topic: Evaluating and responding to elder mistreatment
Prompt: A medically stable older adult with capacity wants help with exploitation and can stay safely with a trusted person tonight. What response respects that choice?
Answer: Discuss options, connect the patient with protective or advocacy services and agree on safe follow-up.
Reason: Explain reporting obligations and document the patient's own account.
Source: What If I Suspect Abuse, Neglect, or Exploitation? · ACL Administration for Community Living · https://acl.gov/programs/protection-and-advocacy-systems/what-if-i-suspect-abuse-neglect-or-exploitation

Topic: Evaluating and responding to elder mistreatment
Prompt: An older adult with acute injuries and delirium cannot participate reliably in planning and would be returned immediately to an unsafe setting. What should be prioritized?
Answer: Emergency medical care and a safe disposition with the safeguarding team.
Reason: Assess and treat the delirium, assess capacity and coordinate protective action.
Source: What If I Suspect Abuse, Neglect, or Exploitation? · ACL Administration for Community Living · https://acl.gov/programs/protection-and-advocacy-systems/what-if-i-suspect-abuse-neglect-or-exploitation

Topic: Trauma-informed care after sexual assault
Prompt: What is the consent principle for a medical forensic examination of a conscious adult with capacity?
Answer: Explain and seek consent for each component, with the option to decline or stop.
Reason: Provide indicated medical care and discuss choices in a trauma-informed manner.
Source: U.S. Department of Justice · A National Protocol for Sexual Assault Medical Forensic Examinations, Adults/Adolescents, Third Edition · https://www.justice.gov/ovw/media/1367191/dl

Topic: Trauma-informed care after sexual assault
Prompt: An adult consents to examination of a painful wrist after sexual assault. Does that automatically authorize collection of forensic samples?
Answer: No. Seek separate informed consent for evidence collection.
Reason: Consent to medical care is specific to the care agreed to.
Source: U.S. Department of Justice · A National Protocol for Sexual Assault Medical Forensic Examinations, Adults/Adolescents, Third Edition · https://www.justice.gov/ovw/media/1367191/dl

Topic: Trauma-informed care after sexual assault
Prompt: An adult who initially agreed to forensic photography asks to stop before it is complete. What should the examiner do?
Answer: Stop and clarify which other care, if any, the patient wants to continue.
Reason: Previously given consent can be withdrawn.
Source: U.S. Department of Justice · A National Protocol for Sexual Assault Medical Forensic Examinations, Adults/Adolescents, Third Edition · https://www.justice.gov/ovw/media/1367191/dl

Topic: Trauma-informed care after sexual assault
Prompt: What should be assessed first when someone presents after a recent sexual assault?
Answer: Immediate safety and urgent medical needs.
Reason: Offer access to specialized trauma-informed services and discuss options with the patient.
Source: U.S. Department of Justice · A National Protocol for Sexual Assault Medical Forensic Examinations, Adults/Adolescents, Third Edition · https://www.justice.gov/ovw/media/1367191/dl

Topic: Trauma-informed care after sexual assault
Prompt: An adult with significant bleeding and signs of shock presents after an assault. What takes priority over forensic evidence collection?
Answer: Emergency stabilization and treatment of injury.
Reason: Coordinate further care and consent once medically feasible.
Source: U.S. Department of Justice · A National Protocol for Sexual Assault Medical Forensic Examinations, Adults/Adolescents, Third Edition · https://www.justice.gov/ovw/media/1367191/dl

Topic: Trauma-informed care after sexual assault
Prompt: A medically stable patient with pregnancy potential presents the morning after an assault involving pregnancy risk. What time-sensitive preventive option should be offered?
Answer: Emergency contraception.
Reason: Discuss pregnancy testing and follow-up as well as STI prevention and examination options.
Source: Sexual Assault and Abuse and STIs - STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/sexual-assault-adults.htm

Topic: Trauma-informed care after sexual assault
Prompt: When should indicated HIV nonoccupational postexposure prophylaxis be started after a substantial-risk exposure?
Answer: As soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours.
Reason: Obtain appropriate baseline testing without delaying the first dose when indicated.
Source: Antiretroviral Postexposure Prophylaxis After Sexual, Injection Drug Use, or Other Nonoccupational Exposure to HIV — CDC Recommendations, United States, 2025 · https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/74/rr/rr7401a1.htm

Topic: Trauma-informed care after sexual assault
Prompt: An adult presents 18 hours after a substantial-risk assault exposure to a person with HIV without sustained viral suppression. What HIV prevention should be offered promptly?
Answer: A 28-day course of HIV nPEP, with baseline tests and follow-up.
Reason: Discuss adherence and tolerability. Do not delay indicated treatment while awaiting routine lab results.
Source: Antiretroviral Postexposure Prophylaxis After Sexual, Injection Drug Use, or Other Nonoccupational Exposure to HIV — CDC Recommendations, United States, 2025 · https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/74/rr/rr7401a1.htm

Topic: Trauma-informed care after sexual assault
Prompt: Another survivor first presents ten days after the only exposure. What HIV-related care should be offered now?
Answer: HIV testing, counseling, follow-up testing and assessment for ongoing prevention such as PrEP if indicated.
Reason: Ten days is beyond the recommended nPEP initiation window. Other medical and support needs still merit care.
Source: Antiretroviral Postexposure Prophylaxis After Sexual, Injection Drug Use, or Other Nonoccupational Exposure to HIV — CDC Recommendations, United States, 2025 · https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/74/rr/rr7401a1.htm

Topic: Prioritizing and reassessing multisystem trauma
Prompt: What is the purpose of a structured primary survey in multisystem trauma?
Answer: Identify and treat immediately life-threatening problems as they are found.
Reason: Catastrophic external hemorrhage, airway, breathing and circulation warrant rapid assessment.
Source: NICE NG39 · Major trauma assessment and initial management · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng39/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Prioritizing and reassessing multisystem trauma
Prompt: After a collision, an adult has gurgling respirations, pooled blood in the mouth and falling oxygen saturation. Which immediate physiologic threat is apparent?
Answer: Failure to maintain a patent, protected airway.
Reason: Call for airway support and clear the airway while other injuries are assessed.
Source: NICE NG39 · Major trauma assessment and initial management · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng39/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Prioritizing and reassessing multisystem trauma
Prompt: A second patient after a collision is speaking clearly with equal breath sounds, but has major ongoing external bleeding, confusion and hypotension. What threat requires immediate control?
Answer: Hemorrhage causing inadequate circulation.
Reason: Control bleeding and resuscitate while continuing the trauma survey.
Source: NICE NG39 · Major trauma assessment and initial management · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng39/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Prioritizing and reassessing multisystem trauma
Prompt: Why does an initially improved blood pressure fail to establish that traumatic bleeding is controlled?
Answer: A transient response to resuscitation can precede recurrent hypoperfusion.
Reason: Reassess circulation, bleeding, mental status and other injuries serially.
Source: NICE NG39 · Major trauma assessment and initial management · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng39/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Prioritizing and reassessing multisystem trauma
Prompt: After initial resuscitation an adult with suspected multiple injuries has the sustained observations shown, no peritonitis and no current need for immediate intervention. Which strategy can now define internal injuries?
Answer: Trauma-protocol CT with ongoing monitoring when appropriate.
Reason: A sustained response can make diagnostic imaging feasible; reassess if stability changes.
Source: NICE NG39 · Major trauma assessment and initial management · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng39/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Prioritizing and reassessing multisystem trauma
Prompt: An adult with blunt abdominal trauma has free intraperitoneal fluid and the serial observations shown, with new diffuse tenderness and deteriorating perfusion despite resuscitation. What takes precedence over scheduled CT?
Answer: Immediate trauma-team hemorrhage control and resuscitation.
Reason: The initial blood pressure improvement was transient.
Source: NICE NG39 · Major trauma assessment and initial management · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng39/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Reassessing patients after blast exposure
Prompt: Why can an intact skin examination be falsely reassuring in a symptomatic blast-exposed patient?
Answer: Internal pulmonary or other organ injury may occur without a visible external wound.
Reason: Use symptoms, examination and physiologic monitoring to direct evaluation.
Source: Blast Injuries: Fact Sheets for Professionals · https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/21571/cdc_21571_DS1.pdf

Topic: Reassessing patients after blast exposure
Prompt: An alert patient has an isolated traumatic tympanic membrane perforation after a blast, normal oxygenation and no chest findings. Does the ear finding alone diagnose blast lung injury?
Answer: No. Evaluate the chest and observe or investigate according to the clinical course.
Reason: Ear findings alone cannot establish the pulmonary diagnosis.
Source: Blast Injuries: Fact Sheets for Professionals · https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/21571/cdc_21571_DS1.pdf

Topic: Reassessing patients after blast exposure
Prompt: A patient has intact eardrums but develops dyspnea, hypoxemia and new bilateral lung opacities after a blast. Does a normal ear exam exclude blast lung injury?
Answer: No. Evaluate and support the pulmonary injury.
Reason: Assess for other thoracic injuries as part of the trauma evaluation.
Source: Blast Injuries: Fact Sheets for Professionals · https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/21571/cdc_21571_DS1.pdf

Topic: Reassessing patients after blast exposure
Prompt: Why obtain serial examinations in a patient at risk after blast exposure?
Answer: Some important injuries become clinically apparent only after an interval.
Reason: Reassess respiration, circulation, abdominal findings and neurologic status according to the presentation.
Source: Blast Injuries: Fact Sheets for Professionals · https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/21571/cdc_21571_DS1.pdf

Topic: Reassessing patients after blast exposure
Prompt: An adult under observation develops new tachypnea, hemoptysis and falling SpO₂ after an initially reassuring lung examination. Which evaluation takes priority?
Answer: Immediate reassessment of oxygenation, ventilation and thoracic injury.
Reason: Provide support while evaluating for blast lung or other chest injury.
Source: Blast Injuries: Fact Sheets for Professionals · https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/21571/cdc_21571_DS1.pdf

Topic: Reassessing patients after blast exposure
Prompt: Another patient maintains normal breathing but develops increasing abdominal tenderness and guarding several hours later. Which occult complication requires urgent surgical assessment?
Answer: Bowel injury, including possible perforation.
Reason: A reassuring first abdominal exam does not exclude a delayed presentation.
Source: Blast Injuries: Fact Sheets for Professionals · https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/21571/cdc_21571_DS1.pdf

Topic: Reassessing patients after blast exposure
Prompt: What determines whether a suspected traumatic tension pneumothorax requires treatment before imaging?
Answer: Hemodynamic instability or severe respiratory compromise with compatible findings.
Reason: Rapid clinical assessment guides emergency treatment.
Source: NICE NG39 · Major trauma assessment and initial management · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng39/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Reassessing patients after blast exposure
Prompt: An adult has isolated hearing loss after blast exposure, a perforated eardrum and stable serial respiratory and abdominal assessments. What follow-up should address the persistent deficit?
Answer: Otologic and hearing evaluation, with return precautions for evolving symptoms.
Reason: Arrange specialist or audiology assessment as clinically appropriate.
Source: Blast Injuries: Fact Sheets for Professionals · https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/21571/cdc_21571_DS1.pdf

Topic: Reassessing patients after blast exposure
Prompt: A monitored survivor develops severe dyspnea, hypotension and markedly reduced breath sounds on one side. Tension pneumothorax is suspected. Should chest radiography delay emergency treatment?
Answer: No. Arrange immediate decompression by the trauma team.
Reason: The severe respiratory and circulatory findings make this a clinical emergency.
Source: NICE NG39 · Major trauma assessment and initial management · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng39/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Assessing reactions to insect stings
Prompt: What distinguishes a large local sting reaction from a systemic allergic reaction?
Answer: The local response remains contiguous with the sting site, while systemic manifestations occur beyond it.
Reason: Assess airway, breathing and circulation whenever systemic symptoms are reported.
Source: Stinging insect hypersensitivity · https://www.aaaai.org/Aaaai/media/Media-Library-PDFs/Allergist%20Resources/Statements%20and%20Practice%20Parameters/Stinging-insect-hypersensitivity-2016.pdf

Topic: Assessing reactions to insect stings
Prompt: A patient has extensive swelling of the hand and forearm after a bee sting on one finger, without symptoms elsewhere. What type of reaction does this pattern suggest?
Answer: A large local reaction.
Reason: Marked local swelling alone is not systemic anaphylaxis.
Source: Stinging insect hypersensitivity · https://www.aaaai.org/Aaaai/media/Media-Library-PDFs/Allergist%20Resources/Statements%20and%20Practice%20Parameters/Stinging-insect-hypersensitivity-2016.pdf

Topic: Assessing reactions to insect stings
Prompt: After a wasp sting, another patient develops wheezing and hypotension without visible hives. What systemic reaction must be recognized?
Answer: Anaphylaxis.
Reason: A dangerous systemic reaction can occur without skin findings.
Source: World Allergy Organization Anaphylaxis Guidance 2020 · https://doi.org/10.1016/j.waojou.2020.100472

Topic: Assessing reactions to insect stings
Prompt: Which drug is first-line for sting-induced anaphylaxis?
Answer: Intramuscular epinephrine.
Reason: Give it promptly in the anterolateral thigh and activate emergency care.
Source: World Allergy Organization Anaphylaxis Guidance 2020 · https://doi.org/10.1016/j.waojou.2020.100472

Topic: Assessing reactions to insect stings
Prompt: A patient with a sting has mild focal pain and itching, normal breathing and stable vitals. What type of initial care is appropriate?

Topic: CARS · Humanities · Keeping a promptbook
Prompt:
At the first reading of a comedy, the director found a pause marked in the promptbook after a character announced that the house had been sold. A penciled note in the margin said “six seconds.” The production that supplied this book had been admired for the peculiar chill that passed through the room at precisely this moment. Our director set a watch on the rehearsal table. The actors waited six seconds. Nothing in particular happened.

The note had been written by a stage manager, who occupied a seat from which the room could be heard unusually well. She kept a record because the actor who spoke next had a habit of swallowing the first word of his line. At one performance the audience laughed at the announcement. The laugh grew, faltered as people understood who would lose their home, and went out in scattered coughs. Six seconds passed before the room was quiet enough for a softly spoken reply. The record was an accurate measurement of that evening. The difficulty arose when an accurate measurement was promoted to an instruction.

A sympathetic reader might replace “six seconds” with “wait for quiet.” That would work on an evening when the audience laughed. Yet on another evening silence fell at once. An actor who answered immediately made the reply sound like a practical objection to the sale. An actor who allowed the silence to sit for a moment made the same words sound like an acknowledgment of grief. Quiet supplied an opportunity to speak, but it did not choose between those meanings.

It is tempting to conclude that nothing worth preserving can be written down. The company's understudy offers a reason for resisting that conclusion. She had never seen the celebrated performance. The stage manager's note made her ask why anyone would count the interval at all. In answering, her colleagues recalled that the announcement had once been played as a joke and the reply had interrupted the laughter. That earlier failure was useful to her. Having heard what the actors had once overlooked, she could listen for it herself. A record may do its best work by provoking a question that its maker had no occasion to put on paper.

I would keep the number in a new promptbook, accompanied by the reason it had been measured. I would also keep the director's unsuccessful rehearsal with the watch. It shows a future company how easily a description can acquire authority when it sits beside an actor's line. Such a book will sometimes disappoint a reader looking for a way to recover the experience of one remarkable night. But a company does not need to reproduce the six seconds in order to inherit something from that night. It can inherit the responsibility for deciding what the coming reply will sound like to the people actually in the room.

What was the stage manager originally using the six-second interval to document?
Choices:
How long it took for the audience to understand the sale
When the next line could be heard clearly at one performance
The duration the director thought necessary to suggest grief
The interval the actor normally preferred between lines
Answer: When the next line could be heard clearly at one performance
Reason: She was concerned that the first word was getting lost. The recorded interval ended when that evening’s audience was quiet enough to hear it.
Source: Original passage and item · AAMC CARS framework · https://students-residents.aamc.org/whats-mcat-exam/critical-analysis-and-reasoning-skills-section-overview

The laugh grew, faltered as people understood who would lose their home, and went out in scattered coughs. Six seconds passed before the room was quiet enough for a softly spoken reply. The record was an accurate measurement of that evening. The difficulty arose when an accurate measurement was promoted to an instruction.

It is tempting to conclude that nothing worth preserving can be written down. The company's understudy offers a reason for resisting that conclusion. She had never seen the celebrated performance. In answering, her colleagues recalled that the announcement had once been played as a joke and the reply had interrupted the laughter. That earlier failure was useful to her. Having heard what the actors had once overlooked, she could listen for it herself. A record may do its best work by provoking a question that its maker had no occasion to put on paper.

It shows a future company how easily a description can acquire authority when it sits beside an actor's line. Such a book will sometimes disappoint a reader looking for a way to recover the experience of one remarkable night. But a company does not need to reproduce the six seconds in order to inherit something from that night. It can inherit the responsibility for deciding what the coming reply will sound like to the people actually in the room.

It makes her a better judge of the precise length of the original silence.
It implies that the other actors misremembered the earlier interruption.
It establishes that the note communicated the original staging without explanation.
It shows that the note could help someone who could not imitate the performance from memory.
Answer: It shows that the note could help someone who could not imitate the performance from memory.

Topic: CARS · Humanities · Rereading a clue
Prompt:
Halfway through a short detective story, a landlady tells her visitor that the tenant upstairs has finally gone home. The sentence costs a translator an afternoon. In the language of the story the landlady uses a form of address that suggests a previous acquaintance with her visitor. It would be an odd form to use with a stranger, although a woman of her age might use it with someone considerably younger. The visitor's age has yet to be mentioned. Two pages later, when we learn that the visitor is her son, the landlady's speech sounds quite ordinary. A reader who happened to notice it on the first encounter may enjoy having noticed it. A reader who passed it by can later find it waiting on the page.

The translator's language supplies no corresponding distinction in its pronouns. One solution is to let the landlady call her visitor “dear.” But imagine the visitor addressed that way in a story full of brisk professional exchanges. What had been an unobtrusive irregularity might become the only conspicuously intimate word on the page. Another solution is to omit the distinction. The disclosure of the visitor's identity would still surprise, yet on returning to the scene a reader would find nothing there to reconsider. Both solutions preserve what the landlady tells the visitor about the tenant. They offer rather different terms on which a reader may come to know the landlady.

A third translator lets the landlady interrupt the visitor before he has quite finished explaining why he came. Several other conversations in the story have made a point of observing formal courtesies. Breaking that rhythm here gives a reader a small reason to suspect familiarity. An impatient landlady has ample reason to interrupt a stranger, too. The device borrows no particular word from the original. Its defense is that it permits two readings before the disclosure and makes one of them especially satisfying afterward.

It would be a mistake to turn this defense into a general license to put interruptions wherever a translator has lost a nuance. Suppose the landlady's unfailing courtesy, even under provocation, is what later persuades a witness to trust her. An interruption could then repair a local difficulty at the expense of a more distant part of the story. Before deciding how much ingenuity a sentence will bear, one has to ask what else the proposed solution obliges the book to say.

Nor would a survey showing equal numbers of surprised readers settle the matter. Two readers can be equally astonished by a revelation, yet only one may feel invited to turn back a page. If I could ask those readers a second question, I would ask what they hoped to find when they turned back. A translation owes something to that return journey. A clue that everyone sees at once, and a clue that nobody could possibly have seen, each affords the reader rather little occasion to make it.

What feature of the landlady’s original form of address matters most to the author?
Choices:
It creates a clue whose importance can change on rereading.
It tells the visitor more about the missing tenant than the narrator knows.
It identifies the visitor’s age more reliably than his relationship.
It marks a level of intimacy that a first-time reader must recognize.
Answer: It creates a clue whose importance can change on rereading.
Reason: The address initially admits more than one explanation. After the family relationship is disclosed, a reader can recover the clue.
Source: Original passage and item · AAMC CARS framework · https://students-residents.aamc.org/prepare-mcat-exam/whats-mcat-exam-pdf-outline

Topic: CARS · Social science · The night watch
Prompt:
The cooperative that shared a kiln among the potters of a coastal town had no official night watch. Somebody nevertheless had to stay with a firing until the kiln could safely be left. A potter might volunteer because a neighbor had covered for her last winter, because his own pots occupied most of the shelves, or because the other potters had small children. Asked who owed whom a night, members would usually name several considerations and then admit that the considerations did not point in quite the same direction. An economist visiting the workshop described the result as a system of exchange without accounts. That was close enough to win nods from the members and imprecise enough to conceal their most interesting disagreement.

When the cooperative doubled in size, a treasurer proposed that one night on watch earn one credit. Anyone who had used up her credits would take the next available shift. The proposal appealed especially to newcomers. An established potter could decline a night with a two-word reference to a sick aunt. A newcomer with an equally sick relative might have to tell a long and embarrassing story before the request seemed reasonable. A credit in the book would entitle either to say no without giving an account of her household. It would be easy to mistake the old members' discretion for a courtesy that the new members enjoyed equally.

After a season of bookkeeping, however, two experienced members objected that the accounts omitted the work of instructing novices. Teaching someone to load the kiln might save the cooperative many spoiled firings, yet no credit was issued for it. The treasurer offered to add a column for instruction. This reply pleased the member who did most of the teaching. It failed to satisfy the other, who had never taught a novice. Her complaint was that the new arrangement settled in advance which acts the members could invoke when deciding a shift. Before the ledger, she said, a contribution that nobody had thought important on Monday could be recognized as decisive on Friday. With another column there would merely be two things the cooperative had already thought of on Monday.

The distinction is easy to miss if we ask members only whether they consider the distribution of nights fair. Both critics might give the same low rating, and the newcomer, glad of her credit, a high one. If the credit for teaching were introduced, a rise in the average rating could be perfectly genuine without answering the second critic. Her concern would be better tested by watching what happens the first time a member offers a reason for changing shifts that the ledger has no place to record.

Nothing in this account requires the cooperative to abandon credits. A member who can politely decline without describing an ill relative has gained something that a richer communal discussion would not supply. The choice worth investigating is whether a posted balance must settle every case, or whether a member may occasionally reopen a case without being forced to reopen the door to her private life.

What feature of the ledger concerns the critic who has never taught a novice?
Choices:
It places too little monetary value on the skilled work of teaching.
It makes the grounds for changing shifts depend on categories chosen in advance.
It gives newcomers more opportunities to decline a shift than established members.
It leaves the cooperative unable to determine how many shifts a member has worked.
Answer: It makes the grounds for changing shifts depend on categories chosen in advance.
Reason: Her objection concerns which reasons can be considered, including contributions that acquire significance only later.

Topic: CARS · Social sciences · Counting library requests
Prompt:
Every spring our library association prints a league table of the most requested books. The figures are exact enough. A borrower enters a title on a slip, hands it to the clerk, and the clerk records one request. Last year a trustee proposed that the association buy next year's books in proportion to the totals on those slips. A branch serving keen readers of gardening books would acquire more gardening books. A branch whose readers cared little for gardening would be spared them. The proposal sounded like a modest way of letting readers themselves write the purchase order.

I spent a morning beside the returns counter at two branches. At the first, the clerk knew that three copies of a popular garden manual had recently arrived. She pointed people toward a shelf so close to the counter that she could see the green covers from her chair. At the second branch a reader looking for that manual was told that the only copy had gone missing. He filled in a slip. By noon the first branch had put the manual into six hands and registered no requests for it. The second had registered four requests and put the book into no hands at all.

The trustee had made a reasonable inference from a different sort of record. If people unable to borrow a book invariably filled in a slip, four slips would indeed mark four occasions on which another copy might have helped. She had quietly extended that inference to a comparison of readers' interests across branches. Yet the success that a well-stocked branch enjoyed in meeting an interest also gave that interest a way to disappear from the list. One could buy exactly in proportion to the figures and, a year later, congratulate oneself on having reduced the recorded enthusiasm for precisely the books the new copies were serving.

There is a more uncomfortable complication. At a third branch the slips sit behind the counter. The clerk gladly provides one to anyone who asks. A reader first has to know that the little transaction is possible, then care enough to conduct it in front of three people waiting to borrow books. Moving the slips out onto a table might increase requests while leaving both the collection and the readers' wishes unchanged. That rise would be an achievement for the new arrangement. It would be a curious reason to charge the branch with a sudden failure to stock its shelves.

I would keep the figures. On a particular afternoon four unsuccessful searches for the same manual give a librarian a fine reason to telephone another branch. When deciding how to spend next year's money, I would ask the successful readers a question too. The slip was designed to help someone who had gone away empty-handed. Its designers deserve credit for recording a disappointment so that someone could act on it. They never arranged to count every occasion for delight.
