Choices:
The meaning of a request count depends on how books and request slips are made available.
Clerks cannot reliably remember which titles borrowers have requested.
The association should give branches equal budgets regardless of their readers.
Purchases should follow the number of visitors rather than any record of reading.
Answer: The meaning of a request count depends on how books and request slips are made available.
Reason: The two branch comparisons show how both supply and ease of reporting affect what gets counted.

Topic: CARS · Humanities · Sitting for a portrait
Prompt:
For the first hour of sitting for my portrait, I tried to hold a pleasant expression that I imagined I wore whenever I opened the door to a friend. The painter let me keep it until the effort began to show. Then she asked me to describe the walk to her studio. I have no great gift for describing streets, and presently I stopped trying to look pleasant and began trying to remember where the road bent. She put down the little brush with which she had been drawing my mouth and picked up a larger one.

When my sister saw the finished portrait, she objected that the eyebrows were wrong. Mine were quite level, she said, whereas the painter had made one higher. I fetched a photograph taken the week before. There they were, two short horizontal strokes looking as if they had been ruled. The painter fetched three pages of drawings. On the first my eyebrows were level, on the second the left one had gone up, and on the third it was coming down again. My sister laughed. She had often seen me make that movement when I was trying to fish a name out of my memory. She could recognize the gesture while disputing the accuracy of the particular face in which the painter had set it down.

It is tempting to give the painter an easy victory here. Say that the camera copies surfaces while the painter sees a person, and the case is closed. But the photograph had caught me leaning forward, shoulders lifted a little, listening to a question. That posture was familiar to my sister too. Nothing in the instrument had prevented it from recording a revealing moment. And there are perfectly competent painters whose subjects seem all to have spent the sitting waiting for the same train. A distinction between tools cannot explain why one image reminds us of its sitter and another merely of the instructions the sitter was trying to obey.

What the drawings supplied was evidence about a choice. An eyebrow that went up once when I sneezed might be accurately drawn as high. My sister would have needed a different story to find the sneeze convincing as a likeness. The return of a movement at the edge of an effort to remember gave the painter a reason for selecting it. A reason need not compel agreement. My colleague, who has mostly seen me listening in meetings, might reasonably have chosen the photograph.

I would be sorry if the gallery hung the three drawings alongside the portrait as a sort of proof. They changed my sister's mind by reminding her of times she had already seen me. A stranger could inspect every mark and still have no experience against which to recognize the gesture. The drawings can show that a painter noticed a recurring movement. Recognizing the person in that movement is a further event, and it takes place as much in front of the canvas as on it.

Which statement most closely captures the author's account of a convincing likeness?
Choices:
A portrait is convincing when it records the greatest number of facial details.
A convincing likeness can emerge when a chosen feature meets a viewer's experience of the sitter.
Agreement among longtime acquaintances is a necessary test of a successful portrait.
A viewer must see the preparatory material before recognizing the sitter.
Answer: A convincing likeness can emerge when a chosen feature meets a viewer's experience of the sitter.
Reason: The painter selects a recurring gesture and the sister connects it to her own memory.

Prompt: A pathology report says the specimen was insufficient. A patient reading the portal asks, “So it’s benign?” What should the clinician explain?
Answer: There was too little tissue for a reliable conclusion, and the team needs to discuss further evaluation.
Reason: An inadequate specimen does not provide a negative diagnosis.
Source: NICE CG138 · Patient experience in adult services · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg138/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Explaining diagnostic uncertainty and arranging reassessment
Prompt: Symptoms persist after an initially reassuring evaluation. The patient says, “You said everything was fine.” How should the clinician explain the reason for reassessment?
Answer: Explain which serious causes seemed unlikely then and why persistent symptoms now warrant another look.
Reason: A change in the clinical course can change the assessment.
Source: NICE CG138 · Patient experience in adult services · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg138/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Explaining diagnostic uncertainty and arranging reassessment
Prompt: What makes a follow-up plan for a pending diagnostic result actionable?
Answer: A named responsible clinician, a timeframe and a way to reach the patient.
Reason: A vague instruction to check the portal leaves responsibility unclear.
Source: NICE CG138 · Patient experience in adult services · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg138/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Explaining diagnostic uncertainty and arranging reassessment
Prompt: A patient will leave the hospital before pathology returns. The community clinician has not agreed to track the result. Who should ensure follow-up is assigned?
Answer: The discharging team should retain responsibility until it confirms an explicit handoff.
Reason: Document the owner, the expected timing and what the patient should do if no one calls.
Source: AHRQ · TeamSTEPPS Pocket Guide, handoff and check-back · https://www.ahrq.gov/sites/default/files/wysiwyg/teamstepps-program/teamstepps-pocket-guide.pdf

Topic: Explaining diagnostic uncertainty and arranging reassessment
Prompt: A receiving clinician has explicitly accepted follow-up, but the patient's recorded phone is disconnected. What still needs to be resolved before relying on the plan?
Answer: Agree on a reliable contact method with the patient and pass it to the responsible clinician.
Reason: An identified owner still needs a workable way to communicate the result.
Source: AHRQ · TeamSTEPPS Pocket Guide, handoff and check-back · https://www.ahrq.gov/sites/default/files/wysiwyg/teamstepps-program/teamstepps-pocket-guide.pdf

Topic: Matching recommendations to a patient's priorities
Prompt: When several treatments are medically reasonable, what should the clinician clarify before recommending one?
Answer: Which benefits, harms and burdens matter most to this patient.
Reason: The same outcome estimates can support different choices.
Source: NICE NG197 · Shared decision making, risk communication and decision aids · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng197/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Matching recommendations to a patient's priorities
Prompt: Two reasonable treatments offer comparable cancer control. A musician has already said preserving fine finger movement is their chief concern. What should the clinician compare next?
Answer: How each option is likely to affect hand function.
Reason: Use the stated priority to make the comparison relevant.
Source: NICE NG197 · Shared decision making, risk communication and decision aids · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng197/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Matching recommendations to a patient's priorities
Prompt: What should a clinician ask when a patient is unsure how to participate in a preference-sensitive decision?
Answer: How much information and what role the patient wants in deciding.
Reason: A patient may welcome a clear recommendation and still retain authority.
Source: NICE NG197 · Shared decision making, risk communication and decision aids · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng197/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Matching recommendations to a patient's priorities
Prompt: A capable patient understands the options but asks, “What would you recommend, knowing that I want to remain independent?” What should the clinician provide?
Answer: A recommendation tied to that goal, then invite the patient's response.
Reason: Giving a reasoned recommendation can support shared decision-making.
Source: NICE NG197 · Shared decision making, risk communication and decision aids · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng197/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Matching recommendations to a patient's priorities
Prompt: A stable patient considering elective treatment says, “I need a day to discuss these trade-offs with my partner.” What is an appropriate response when delay is safe?
Answer: Agree on time to deliberate and a specific follow-up to revisit the choice.
Reason: The request expresses a preference about the decision process.
Source: NICE NG197 · Shared decision making, risk communication and decision aids · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng197/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Responding to fear, silence and anger in a clinical encounter
Prompt: What should the clinician do with an emotional cue before moving on to technical details?
Answer: Acknowledge it and give the patient room to respond.
Reason: The patient's response helps determine when they are ready for information.
Source: NICE CG138 · Patient experience in adult services · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg138/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Responding to fear, silence and anger in a clinical encounter
Prompt: How can a clinician name an apparent emotion without presuming to know exactly how the patient feels?
Answer: Offer a tentative reflection and invite correction.
Reason: For example, “You seem worried. Have I understood that correctly?”
Source: NICE CG138 · Patient experience in adult services · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg138/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Responding to fear, silence and anger in a clinical encounter
Prompt: After hearing a diagnosis, a patient says, “I can't tell my family.” What could the clinician ask before offering advice about disclosure?
Answer: “What worries you most about telling them?”
Reason: The concern could involve burden, conflict, safety or something else.
Source: NICE CG138 · Patient experience in adult services · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg138/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Responding to fear, silence and anger in a clinical encounter
Prompt: A clinician says, “You sound afraid of the operation.” The patient replies, “It's losing my job that scares me.” What is the best next response?
Answer: Acknowledge the financial worry and explore what support would help.
Reason: Use the patient's correction to redirect the conversation.
Source: NICE CG138 · Patient experience in adult services · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg138/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Responding to fear, silence and anger in a clinical encounter
Prompt: What can the clinician ask after acknowledging emotion to see whether to resume a difficult discussion?
Answer: “Would you like a little time, or would you like to hear more now?”
Reason: Give the patient control over the pace.
Source: NICE CG138 · Patient experience in adult services · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg138/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Responding to fear, silence and anger in a clinical encounter
Prompt: After receiving bad news, a patient is silently crying and has stopped taking in information. What should the clinician do before describing the treatment schedule?
Answer: Pause, stay present and check when the patient wants to continue.
Reason: Additional details are unlikely to be useful in that moment.
Source: NICE CG138 · Patient experience in adult services · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg138/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Responding to fear, silence and anger in a clinical encounter
Prompt: A tearful patient says, “Please keep going. I need to know what the biopsy showed.” What response respects that preference?
Answer: Give the requested information in small, clear portions and check in as you go.
Reason: Visible distress alone does not mean the patient wants information withheld.
Source: NICE CG138 · Patient experience in adult services · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg138/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Eliciting reasons for change and making a feasible plan
Prompt: What is the clinician listening for when eliciting change talk?
Answer: The patient's own reasons, desire, ability, need or commitment to change.
Reason: These statements can guide a collaborative next step.
Source: SAMHSA TIP 35 · Enhancing motivation for change · https://library.samhsa.gov/sites/default/files/tip-35-pep19-02-01-003.pdf

Topic: Eliciting reasons for change and making a feasible plan
Prompt: A patient says, “I'd like to cut down so I can be there for my kids.” Which part of the statement should the clinician reflect?
Answer: The patient's wish to be present for their children.
Reason: Reflecting the personally meaningful reason can invite elaboration.
Source: SAMHSA TIP 35 · Enhancing motivation for change · https://library.samhsa.gov/sites/default/files/tip-35-pep19-02-01-003.pdf

Topic: Eliciting reasons for change and making a feasible plan
Prompt: A patient says, “Drinking helps me unwind, and I'm not ready to change.” What response can keep the conversation open?
Answer: Acknowledge the perceived benefit and ask permission to explore the patient's perspective.
Reason: Arguing for immediate action can obscure the ambivalence.
Source: SAMHSA TIP 35 · Enhancing motivation for change · https://library.samhsa.gov/sites/default/files/tip-35-pep19-02-01-003.pdf

Topic: Eliciting reasons for change and making a feasible plan
Prompt: What separate judgments do importance and confidence ratings capture?
Answer: How much the change matters and how able the person feels to make it.
Reason: Someone can value a change highly while doubting they can carry it out.
Source: SAMHSA TIP 35 · Enhancing motivation for change · https://library.samhsa.gov/sites/default/files/tip-35-pep19-02-01-003.pdf

Topic: Eliciting reasons for change and making a feasible plan
Prompt: A patient rates stopping tobacco 9/10 in importance but 2/10 in confidence. Which question is most relevant next?
Answer: “What would make trying this feel a little more doable?”
Reason: Explore supports and manageable steps.
Source: SAMHSA TIP 35 · Enhancing motivation for change · https://library.samhsa.gov/sites/default/files/tip-35-pep19-02-01-003.pdf

Topic: Eliciting reasons for change and making a feasible plan
Prompt: A patient feels fully capable of stopping but rates its importance 2/10. What question explores motivation without prescribing a goal?
Answer: “What, if anything, might make a change worthwhile for you?”
Reason: Low importance is a different barrier from low confidence.
Source: SAMHSA TIP 35 · Enhancing motivation for change · https://library.samhsa.gov/sites/default/files/tip-35-pep19-02-01-003.pdf

Topic: Eliciting reasons for change and making a feasible plan
Prompt: What makes a collaboratively selected behavior goal specific enough to review at follow-up?
Answer: An observable action with an agreed time or frequency.
Reason: Ask the patient what feels achievable and how they would recognize success.
Source: SAMHSA TIP 35 · Enhancing motivation for change · https://library.samhsa.gov/sites/default/files/tip-35-pep19-02-01-003.pdf

Topic: Eliciting reasons for change and making a feasible plan
Prompt: A patient intended to walk after dinner but reports that the only nearby route is unsafe after dark. What should the clinician explore?
Answer: A feasible alternative time or location that the patient would choose.
Reason: Adjust the plan to the environment.
Source: SAMHSA TIP 35 · Enhancing motivation for change · https://library.samhsa.gov/sites/default/files/tip-35-pep19-02-01-003.pdf

Topic: Eliciting reasons for change and making a feasible plan
Prompt: A patient has access to the original activity but now says it was the clinician's goal, not theirs. What should happen before setting another target?
Answer: Revisit the patient's own priorities and readiness.
Reason: Changing the schedule alone cannot resolve a goal the patient never endorsed.
Source: SAMHSA TIP 35 · Enhancing motivation for change · https://library.samhsa.gov/sites/default/files/tip-35-pep19-02-01-003.pdf

Topic: Verifying that instructions can be understood and carried out
Prompt: When checking discharge readiness, what should follow a correct verbal description of a treatment requiring manual skill?
Answer: Ask the patient to demonstrate the task with the equipment they will use.
Reason: Knowledge of the steps and ability to perform them can differ.
Source: AHRQ · Use the teach-back method · https://www.ahrq.gov/health-literacy/improve/precautions/tool5.html

Topic: Presenting benefits and harms over the same interval
Prompt: What quantities should a discussion include when treatment lowers one risk but raises another?
Answer: Absolute changes in both outcomes over the same time horizon.
Reason: The patient can then judge how much each outcome matters.
Source: NICE NG197 · Shared decision making, risk communication and decision aids · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng197/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Presenting benefits and harms over the same interval
Prompt: Use the one-year decision aid. Among 1,000 similar people, how many events of each kind would change with treatment?
Answer: 20 fewer strokes and 5 more major bleeds.
Reason: Subtract event counts within each row of the comparison.
Source: NICE NG197 · Shared decision making, risk communication and decision aids · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng197/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Presenting benefits and harms over the same interval
Prompt: The lower-risk group's one-year decision aid is shown. How many strokes would be prevented per 1,000 people treated?
Answer: 5 fewer strokes per 1,000.
Reason: Stroke falls from 10 to 5 per 1,000 while the increase in major bleeding remains 5 per 1,000.
Source: NICE NG197 · Shared decision making, risk communication and decision aids · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng197/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Preserving the patient's voice in interpreted encounters
Prompt: Through a qualified interpreter, a patient gives a long account of their symptoms. To whom should the clinician direct the next question?
Answer: Address the patient directly in the first person.
Reason: Allow enough time for accurate interpretation.
Source: US Department of Justice · ADA requirements for effective communication · https://www.ada.gov/resources/effective-communication/

Topic: Preserving the patient's voice in interpreted encounters
Prompt: A capable adult using a qualified interpreter asks to discuss medications without their visiting relatives. How should the room arrangement change?
Answer: Offer a private discussion with the patient and interpreter.
Reason: Interpretation supports direct communication while preserving privacy.
Source: HHS Office for Civil Rights · Language access and effective communication · https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/ocr-dcl-section-1557-language-access.pdf

Topic: Preserving the patient's voice in interpreted encounters
Prompt: When selecting a communication aid for a Deaf patient, what features of the encounter matter?
Answer: The patient's usual communication method and the nature, length and complexity of the exchange.
Reason: A method adequate for a short logistical exchange may be inadequate for consent.
Source: US Department of Justice · ADA requirements for effective communication · https://www.ada.gov/resources/effective-communication/

Topic: Preserving the patient's voice in interpreted encounters
Prompt: During an elective interpreted consent visit, the patient repeatedly says the interpreter cannot be understood because the audio cuts out. What should happen before consent is obtained?
Answer: Restore effective interpretation or arrange another qualified interpreter and repeat the affected discussion.
Reason: Merely booking an interpreter does not establish understanding.
Source: HHS Office for Civil Rights · Language access and effective communication · https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/ocr-dcl-section-1557-language-access.pdf

Topic: Keeping the patient's values central in surrogate discussions
Prompt: A proxy says, “I would want surgery, but my father repeatedly told me he would decline it in exactly this situation.” Whose preference should guide substituted judgment?
Answer: The father's preference.
Reason: The proxy represents the patient's values.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Decisions for adult patients who lack capacity · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/decisions-adult-patients-who-lack-capacity

Topic: Keeping the patient's values central in surrogate discussions
Prompt: An incapacitated adult never expressed a relevant preference, and nobody can reasonably infer one. Which standard should guide a surrogate's choice?
Answer: The patient's best interests.
Reason: Consider likely benefits, burdens and quality of life as experienced by the patient.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Decisions for adult patients who lack capacity · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/decisions-adult-patients-who-lack-capacity

Topic: Checking the scope and continuing validity of permission
Prompt: A patient signs consent for a left-sided elective procedure. The team also wants to perform an unrelated elective procedure on the right. What further decision is needed?
Answer: Specific informed authorization for the additional procedure.
Reason: The original permission has a defined scope.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Checking the scope and continuing validity of permission
Prompt: What makes authorization for an elective procedure voluntary?
Answer: The patient can choose freely, including declining or withdrawing consent.
Reason: A completed form does not override a subsequent capable refusal.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Explaining consequences that matter to the person deciding
Prompt: What is the purpose of explaining benefits and burdens before seeking treatment authorization?
Answer: To let the patient weigh the likely consequences in light of their own goals.
Reason: Discuss the nature and purpose of the intervention and reasonable alternatives.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Explaining consequences that matter to the person deciding
Prompt: A proceduralist describes the chance of symptom relief but omits a serious recognized complication relevant to the decision. What part of the consent discussion is missing?
Answer: Disclosure of the material risk and its consequences.
Reason: The chance of benefit alone cannot support an informed comparison.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Explaining consequences that matter to the person deciding
Prompt: A professional singer asks about a low-frequency risk of persistent voice change. Why does this merit specific discussion?
Answer: It could materially affect an outcome the patient especially values.
Reason: Clinical importance depends partly on the patient's circumstances.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Explaining consequences that matter to the person deciding
Prompt: When explaining that an intervention benefits some patients, what distinction prevents a misleading promise?
Answer: Separate the estimated likelihood of benefit from certainty about an individual result.
Reason: Explain relevant uncertainty in accessible language.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Explaining consequences that matter to the person deciding
Prompt: A patient says, “You said eight out of ten improve, so I will improve.” What clarification should the clinician give?
Answer: About eight of ten similar patients improved; the outcome for this patient remains uncertain.
Reason: An estimate for a group cannot guarantee an individual's result.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Explaining consequences that matter to the person deciding
Prompt: A patient understands the probability of symptom relief but asks whether the relief usually lasts weeks or years. What information is still needed?
Answer: The expected duration of benefit and uncertainty about it.
Reason: Probability of an initial response does not answer a durability question.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Explaining consequences that matter to the person deciding
Prompt: When should previously discussed treatment risks be revisited before an elective procedure?
Answer: When new information materially changes the expected benefit or harm.
Reason: A decision should reflect the patient's current circumstances.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Explaining consequences that matter to the person deciding
Prompt: After consent, a new illness materially raises the estimated anesthesia risk of tomorrow's elective operation. What should the team do before proceeding?
Answer: Explain the changed risk and alternatives, then revisit the patient's decision.
Reason: Prior consent did not include the new risk estimate.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Explaining consequences that matter to the person deciding
Prompt: A patient awaiting an elective procedure believes the quoted 2% complication risk meant two cases in ten. The estimate itself is unchanged. What needs correction?
Answer: Clarify that 2% means about two in 100 and check understanding before proceeding.
Reason: This is a misunderstanding of the denominator, even though clinical risk is unchanged.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Comparing a proposed intervention with observation or deferral
Prompt: What comparison is missing if a patient hears only about the recommended intervention?
Answer: Reasonable alternatives, including forgoing treatment and its likely consequences.
Reason: The patient needs a reference point for the proposed benefit and harm.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Comparing a proposed intervention with observation or deferral
Prompt: A stable patient asks what happens if they choose monitoring for a condition that can safely be observed. What should the clinician explain?
Answer: The expected course with observation and what change would prompt reassessment.
Reason: Observation can be an active option with a follow-up plan.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Comparing a proposed intervention with observation or deferral
Prompt: A patient with a time-sensitive condition asks whether waiting is an option. What should the clinician disclose about waiting?
Answer: The risks of delay, including loss of benefit if a treatment window closes.
Reason: Respecting choice includes explaining time-sensitive consequences.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Comparing a proposed intervention with observation or deferral
Prompt: When active surveillance is offered alongside treatment, what practical requirement should be made explicit?
Answer: What monitoring is needed and when a change would prompt treatment.
Reason: Surveillance involves continued assessment.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Comparing a proposed intervention with observation or deferral
Prompt: A patient prefers surveillance but thinks this means no further visits or tests. What is the most important misconception to correct?
Answer: Explain the required follow-up and the findings that would trigger reconsideration.
Reason: The choice should reflect what the strategy actually involves.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Comparing a proposed intervention with observation or deferral
Prompt: A patient understands surveillance but cannot travel for the required visits. What should the team explore before finalizing that choice?
Answer: Whether monitoring can be made accessible or another reasonable option would fit better.
Reason: Feasibility changes the choice even if the biological risks are unchanged.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Comparing a proposed intervention with observation or deferral
Prompt: What should a clinician clarify after a capable patient declines one proposed intervention?
Answer: Which other forms of care the patient would still accept.
Reason: Refusal can be specific to one intervention.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Comparing a proposed intervention with observation or deferral
Prompt: A patient declines elective surgery but wants help managing pain. What care should remain available?
Answer: Discuss and offer appropriate symptom treatment and follow-up.
Reason: Declining surgery does not end the therapeutic relationship.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Comparing a proposed intervention with observation or deferral
Prompt: A patient who once declined surgery now asks to reconsider after symptoms worsen. What should the clinician do?
Answer: Reassess current options and revisit the informed decision with the patient.
Reason: A prior capable refusal does not permanently bind a capable patient who changes their mind.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Consent and interpretation when a placebo is proposed
Prompt: What makes a substance a placebo for the specific condition being treated?
Answer: It has no expected specific pharmacologic effect on that condition.
Reason: Context and expectations can still affect the patient's experience.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Use of placebo in clinical practice · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/use-placebo-clinical-practice

Topic: Consent and interpretation when a placebo is proposed
Prompt: A patient who agreed to a placebo reports less pain after taking it. Does that response show the original pain was fabricated?
Answer: No. Symptom improvement does not establish deception.
Reason: A placebo response cannot separate genuine from feigned pain.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Use of placebo in clinical practice · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/use-placebo-clinical-practice

Topic: Consent and interpretation when a placebo is proposed
Prompt: A patient reports no relief after an agreed placebo. Does this prove the symptom has a specific organic cause?
Answer: No. Lack of a placebo response does not determine etiology.
Reason: Investigate according to the clinical history and findings.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Use of placebo in clinical practice · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/use-placebo-clinical-practice

Topic: Consent and interpretation when a placebo is proposed
Prompt: For placebo use compatible with good clinical care, what does the AMA say the patient must generally agree to?
Answer: The possibility of receiving a placebo.
Reason: Consent need not specify exactly when a placebo will be used.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Use of placebo in clinical practice · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/use-placebo-clinical-practice

Topic: Consent and interpretation when a placebo is proposed
Prompt: An informed patient explicitly agrees that an appropriate trial may include placebo at an unspecified point. Is the undisclosed timing alone a violation of that agreement?
Answer: No. The timing can remain unspecified within the patient's agreed plan.
Reason: The possible use of placebo was discussed.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Use of placebo in clinical practice · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/use-placebo-clinical-practice

Topic: Consent and interpretation when a placebo is proposed
Prompt: A patient declines the physician's proposal to include a placebo in symptom treatment. What should the physician do?
Answer: Respect the refusal and discuss other appropriate measures.
Reason: Avoid covert substitution.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Use of placebo in clinical practice · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/use-placebo-clinical-practice

Topic: Consent and interpretation when a placebo is proposed
Prompt: A patient originally agreed to possible placebo use but now withdraws that permission while still requesting treatment. What changes?
Answer: Stop placebo use and revise the care plan with the patient.
Reason: The previous agreement does not authorize continued use after withdrawal.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Use of placebo in clinical practice · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/use-placebo-clinical-practice

Topic: Managing financial interests in clinical recommendations
Prompt: A physician earns more if patients choose a facility she partly owns. Which feature creates a conflict even when the test is indicated?
Answer: The physician's financial interest in the destination of the referral.
Reason: A sound indication does not remove the competing interest.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Physician self-referral · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/physician-self-referral

Topic: Managing financial interests in clinical recommendations
Prompt: A physician with no stake in a facility recommends it because it is the only center offering a needed service. Does this fact alone show a financial self-referral conflict?
Answer: No financial interest is identified in this scenario.
Reason: Evaluate the actual relationship and alternatives.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Physician self-referral · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/physician-self-referral

Topic: Managing financial interests in clinical recommendations
Prompt: What information helps a patient evaluate a referral to a clinician-owned facility?
Answer: The clinician's interest and reasonable alternative providers when available.
Reason: This supports an informed choice about where to receive a needed service.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Physician self-referral · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/physician-self-referral

Topic: Managing financial interests in clinical recommendations
Prompt: After hearing the ownership disclosure, a patient requests a medically appropriate independent imaging center. What should the referring physician do?
Answer: Facilitate the patient's informed choice of provider.
Reason: Disclosure is meaningful only if the patient can act on it.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Physician self-referral · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/physician-self-referral

Topic: Managing financial interests in clinical recommendations
Prompt: Which judgment should precede a discussion of where a patient will receive a profitable service?
Answer: Whether the service is medically appropriate for this patient.
Reason: A financial benefit must not drive the indication.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Physician self-referral · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/physician-self-referral

Topic: Managing financial interests in clinical recommendations
Prompt: A test is clinically indicated and a physician-owned site is a reasonable option. What does the patient need before selecting it?
Answer: Disclosure of the interest and a fair discussion of reasonable alternatives.
Reason: The patient can then choose where to obtain appropriate care.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Physician self-referral · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/physician-self-referral

Topic: Including children in treatment decisions at their developmental level
Prompt: A ten-year-old understands an elective procedure when it is explained simply, but nobody has spoken to them. What should the clinician seek in addition to parental permission?
Answer: The child's developmentally appropriate assent.
Reason: Speak directly to the child and invite questions.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Pediatric decision making · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/pediatric-decision-making

Topic: Including children in treatment decisions at their developmental level

Answer: An agreed goal and a defined point to reassess benefit with the patient or surrogate.
Reason: Clarify options if the goal is unmet.

Topic: Reassessing life support against the patient's goals
Prompt: At the planned review an ICU patient's recovery is promising, but a new reversible complication obscures the agreed endpoint. What should the team discuss before extending the trial?
Answer: Whether a specific extension still fits the patient's goals and what the new endpoint will be.
Reason: Avoid an open-ended extension by inertia.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/withholding-or-withdrawing-life-sustaining-treatment

Topic: Reassessing life support against the patient's goals
Prompt: When a life-support trial is reassessed, what should be compared?
Answer: The patient's observed course against the agreed clinical goal and values.
Reason: Interpret both response and burden.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/withholding-or-withdrawing-life-sustaining-treatment

Topic: Reassessing life support against the patient's goals
Prompt: The record shows a completed trial of ventilation. Given the patient's goal and current course, what should the team discuss at the review?
Answer: A plan to wean support as clinically appropriate in keeping with the original goal.
Reason: Arrival of the review date alone is not a reason to stop beneficial treatment abruptly.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/withholding-or-withdrawing-life-sustaining-treatment

Topic: Interpreting an advance directive in the patient's current situation
Prompt: An adult writes, “If I cannot decide and my illness is irreversible, I decline prolonged ventilation.” What kind of direction is this?
Answer: A conditional statement of treatment preferences.
Reason: Clarify whether its conditions apply when the decision arises.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Advance directives · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/advance-directives

Topic: Interpreting an advance directive in the patient's current situation
Prompt: A signed document names a sister as health-care agent but says nothing about ventilation. What does that document establish about ventilation itself?
Answer: No specific ventilation preference; it identifies the designated decision maker.
Reason: The agent may need to use other evidence of the patient's wishes.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Advance directives · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/advance-directives

Topic: Interpreting an advance directive in the patient's current situation
Prompt: Before applying a treatment limit from an advance directive, what should the clinician verify?
Answer: The patient's current capacity and whether the directive's stated conditions match the situation.
Reason: An available document still requires interpretation in context.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Advance directives · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/advance-directives

Topic: Interpreting an advance directive in the patient's current situation
Prompt: An adult lacks decision capacity, has the irreversible condition specified in a valid directive, and the proposed treatment is precisely what the directive declines. What should guide the decision?
Answer: Follow the applicable preference and discuss implementation with the surrogate and team.
Reason: Avoid substituting an unrelated default treatment plan.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Advance directives · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/advance-directives

Topic: Interpreting an advance directive in the patient's current situation
Prompt: Which condition determines whether the team should seek a current decision directly from the patient before relying on an old directive?
Answer: Current decision-making capacity for this choice.
Reason: Ask the patient and reassess capacity when it may have changed.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Advance directives · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/advance-directives

Topic: Interpreting an advance directive in the patient's current situation
Prompt: After a capable patient changes their resuscitation preference, the bedside orders still reflect the older directive. What needs to be done now?
Answer: Reconcile the orders and handoff with the current decision and document it clearly.
Reason: Sharing an updated preference prevents the old plan from directing an emergency response.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Advance directives · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/advance-directives

Topic: Identifying the agent and clarifying the proxy's role
Prompt: An adult names their daughter as health care agent in case they lose capacity. The adult is capable and wants to decide today. Who gives authorization?
Answer: The patient.
Reason: The designation supports future decisions when needed.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Decisions for adult patients who lack capacity · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/decisions-adult-patients-who-lack-capacity

Topic: Identifying the agent and clarifying the proxy's role
Prompt: An incapacitated patient named a health care agent but left no instructions about the present choice. Which role should the clinician explain to that agent?
Answer: Help choose on the patient's behalf using known wishes or, if unavailable, the patient's interests.
Reason: Naming an agent need not specify every future treatment.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Decisions for adult patients who lack capacity · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/decisions-adult-patients-who-lack-capacity

Topic: Identifying the agent and clarifying the proxy's role
Prompt: Several relatives disagree about who should speak. A valid, applicable designation names an available agent. What should the team verify before relying on the loudest relative?
Answer: The designation and the named agent's authority for this decision.
Reason: Family participation and legal decision authority are distinct.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Decisions for adult patients who lack capacity · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/decisions-adult-patients-who-lack-capacity

Topic: Identifying the agent and clarifying the proxy's role
Prompt: An incapacitated patient needs a nonurgent decision. The named agent cannot be reached, and the directive lists an alternate. What should the clinician check next?
Answer: Whether the alternate may act under the document and applicable law, and how to reach them.
Reason: Follow the authorized process and continue efforts to establish the patient's wishes.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Decisions for adult patients who lack capacity · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/decisions-adult-patients-who-lack-capacity

Topic: Separating profound coma, confounders and death by neurologic criteria
Prompt: A deeply comatose patient has a clear pupillary light reflex. What does that establish about a proposed neurologic determination of death?
Answer: Brainstem function remains, so criteria are not met.
Reason: A severe impairment of consciousness alone is insufficient.
Source: AAN, AAP, CNS and SCCM · Pediatric and adult death by neurologic criteria consensus guideline · https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.0000000000207740

Topic: Separating profound coma, confounders and death by neurologic criteria
Prompt: A ventilated patient shows genuine spontaneous respiratory effort. How does that change assessment for death by neurologic criteria?
Answer: Spontaneous breathing is incompatible with the required apnea.
Reason: Confirm that detected breaths are genuine and interpret the examination under the guideline.
Source: AAN, AAP, CNS and SCCM · Pediatric and adult death by neurologic criteria consensus guideline · https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.0000000000207740

Topic: Separating profound coma, confounders and death by neurologic criteria
Prompt: What must be established about the cause of coma before evaluating for death by neurologic criteria?
Answer: A known catastrophic, permanent brain injury capable of explaining the findings.
Reason: Prerequisites and confounders must also be addressed.
Source: AAN, AAP, CNS and SCCM · Pediatric and adult death by neurologic criteria consensus guideline · https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.0000000000207740

Topic: Separating profound coma, confounders and death by neurologic criteria
Prompt: After cardiac arrest, a patient remains markedly hypothermic and unresponsive. Why must determination wait for the guideline's temperature and observation prerequisites?
Answer: Hypothermia can suppress neurologic function and alter drug clearance.
Reason: Absent responses under these conditions are not sufficient.
Source: AAN, AAP, CNS and SCCM · Pediatric and adult death by neurologic criteria consensus guideline · https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.0000000000207740

Topic: Separating profound coma, confounders and death by neurologic criteria
Prompt: What distinction should the team make when describing a neurologic death evaluation that is still incomplete?
Answer: The patient has devastating injury, but death has not yet been determined.
Reason: Explain what remains to be evaluated without predicting the result as certain.
Source: AAN, AAP, CNS and SCCM · Pediatric and adult death by neurologic criteria consensus guideline · https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.0000000000207740

Topic: Separating profound coma, confounders and death by neurologic criteria
Prompt: The neurologic examination is inconclusive because sedative effects have not been excluded. A relative asks if the patient is already dead. What should the clinician say?
Answer: Death has not been established; explain the confounder and the reassessment plan.
Reason: Use language that accurately reflects the stage of evaluation.
Source: AAN, AAP, CNS and SCCM · Pediatric and adult death by neurologic criteria consensus guideline · https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.0000000000207740

Topic: Distinguishing death determination, pronouncement and certification
Prompt: What is death pronouncement?
Answer: An authorized clinician's determination and documentation that the patient has died under applicable criteria.
Reason: Follow jurisdictional requirements and institutional procedures.
Source: Palliative Care Network of Wisconsin · Death pronouncement in the hospital · https://www.mypcnow.org/fast-fact/death-pronouncement-in-the-hospital/

Topic: Distinguishing death determination, pronouncement and certification
Prompt: An authorized clinician examines a patient after an expected death and completes the hospital's determination process. A relative asks when the cause investigation will be finished. Which fact can be communicated now?
Answer: That the patient has died.
Reason: Determining the cause and, when needed, notifying the medical examiner are separate tasks.
Source: Palliative Care Network of Wisconsin · Death pronouncement in the hospital · https://www.mypcnow.org/fast-fact/death-pronouncement-in-the-hospital/

Topic: Distinguishing death determination, pronouncement and certification
Prompt: A death certificate lists “cardiac arrest” with no disease or injury leading to it. What additional information should the certifier seek?
Answer: The causal disease or injury and the chain of events leading to death.
Reason: Cardiac arrest alone describes a mechanism common to many deaths.
Source: CDC NCHS · Physician’s handbook on medical certification of death · https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvss/handbook/2023-physicians-mcod-handbook.pdf

Topic: Distinguishing death determination, pronouncement and certification
Prompt: What should the authorized clinician confirm before recording the pronouncement of an expected inpatient death?
Answer: Patient identity and the required examination findings under local protocol.
Reason: Review the clinical circumstances and resuscitation plan.
Source: Palliative Care Network of Wisconsin · Death pronouncement in the hospital · https://www.mypcnow.org/fast-fact/death-pronouncement-in-the-hospital/

Topic: Distinguishing death determination, pronouncement and certification
Prompt: A monitor loses its signal in a patient without a known treatment limit. What is the first clinical action?
Answer: Assess the patient immediately and initiate the appropriate emergency response if indicated.
Reason: Loss of a monitor signal is not a death determination.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · What happened on telemetry? · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/web-mm/what-happened-telemetry

Topic: Distinguishing death determination, pronouncement and certification
Prompt: During an expected comfort-focused death, staff report that breathing has stopped. What should the clinician do before telling the family that death is confirmed?
Answer: Personally complete the applicable determination and document the observed findings.
Reason: A report prompts assessment; it does not by itself complete pronouncement.
Source: Palliative Care Network of Wisconsin · Death pronouncement in the hospital · https://www.mypcnow.org/fast-fact/death-pronouncement-in-the-hospital/

Topic: Distinguishing death determination, pronouncement and certification
Prompt: What time distinction matters when death was unwitnessed?
Answer: Distinguish when death was pronounced from the actual or presumed time of death.
Reason: Use the certificate's instructions and local process for unknown or presumed times.
Source: CDC NCHS · Physician’s handbook on medical certification of death · https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvss/handbook/2023-physicians-mcod-handbook.pdf

Topic: Distinguishing death determination, pronouncement and certification
Prompt: Review the record of an unwitnessed inpatient death. Which time belongs in the field for verified pronouncement?
Reason: The observations do not establish the exact moment death occurred.
Source: CDC NCHS · Physician’s handbook on medical certification of death · https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvss/handbook/2023-physicians-mcod-handbook.pdf

Topic: Distinguishing death determination, pronouncement and certification
Prompt: Relatives of a patient who died unexpectedly ask for the cause before any cause has been established. What should the clinician communicate?
Answer: Confirm the death, acknowledge that the cause is uncertain and explain the next required review and contact.
Reason: Avoid offering speculation as an established cause.
Source: Palliative Care Network of Wisconsin · Death pronouncement in the hospital · https://www.mypcnow.org/fast-fact/death-pronouncement-in-the-hospital/

Topic: Protecting independent end-of-life decisions during donation discussions
Prompt: A family is considering withdrawal of ventilation for a dying patient. The team learns the patient might be eligible for organ donation. What should govern the withdrawal decision?
Answer: The patient's goals and the clinically relevant benefits and burdens of treatment.
Reason: Potential benefit to organ recipients must not determine the decision.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Organ donation after cardiac death · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/organ-donation-after-cardiac-death

Topic: Protecting independent end-of-life decisions during donation discussions
Prompt: A patient would have wanted continued life-sustaining treatment in the present circumstances. Does a prior wish to donate organs supply a reason to withdraw support now?
Answer: No. Respect the patient's treatment goals.
Reason: A wish to donate after death is distinct from authorization to bring about withdrawal.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Organ donation after cardiac death · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/organ-donation-after-cardiac-death

Topic: Protecting independent end-of-life decisions during donation discussions
Prompt: Why separate the clinicians determining death from the recovery team?
Answer: To keep death determination independent of the interests of potential recipients.
Reason: Use the same applicable criteria whether or not donation is possible.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Organ donation after cardiac death · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/organ-donation-after-cardiac-death

Topic: Protecting independent end-of-life decisions during donation discussions
Prompt: A possible organ donor does not meet the required criteria for determination of death. The recovery team is worried about timing. What should the treating team do?
Answer: Continue appropriate patient care and follow the determination protocol without shortening it.
Reason: Time pressure cannot change the standard for determining death.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Organ donation after cardiac death · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/organ-donation-after-cardiac-death

Topic: Protecting independent end-of-life decisions during donation discussions
Prompt: What aspect of care must remain a priority when a patient may donate after circulatory death?
Answer: The dying patient's comfort and treatment preferences.
Reason: Coordinate roles with the designated donation service.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Organ donation after cardiac death · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/organ-donation-after-cardiac-death

Topic: Protecting independent end-of-life decisions during donation discussions
Prompt: During a planned comfort-focused withdrawal, staff wonder about delaying relief of dyspnea to preserve organ function. What should the treating team prioritize?
Answer: Prompt, proportionate relief of the patient's breathlessness.
Reason: The obligation to the patient continues regardless of donation plans.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Organ donation after cardiac death · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/organ-donation-after-cardiac-death

Topic: Distinguishing palliative needs from Medicare hospice eligibility
Prompt: What distinguishes Medicare hospice eligibility from a general need for palliative care?
Answer: Hospice requires certification of qualifying terminal prognosis and a hospice election.
Reason: Palliative symptom support can be appropriate earlier in illness.
Source: CMS · Medicare hospice benefit · https://www.cms.gov/medicare/payment/fee-for-service-providers/hospice

Topic: Distinguishing palliative needs from Medicare hospice eligibility
Prompt: An adult with cancer and an estimated prognosis of years needs help controlling symptoms during treatment. Which service can be considered without meeting a six-month prognosis criterion?
Answer: Palliative care.
Reason: Symptoms and goals can justify palliative involvement earlier.
Source: NCI · Palliative care in cancer · https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/advanced-cancer/care-choices/palliative-care-fact-sheet

Topic: Distinguishing palliative needs from Medicare hospice eligibility
Prompt: A hospice-eligible adult asks whether enrolling means no treatment for symptoms. What is the core purpose of the hospice plan?
Answer: Comfort-oriented care, including symptom management and patient and family support.
Reason: The election changes how care related to the terminal illness is organized and covered.
Source: CMS · Medicare hospice benefit · https://www.cms.gov/medicare/payment/fee-for-service-providers/hospice

Topic: Distinguishing palliative needs from Medicare hospice eligibility
Prompt: A physician judges that an adult Medicare beneficiary with advanced cancer is likely to live four months if the illness follows its normal course, but cannot predict the precise date of death. Does this uncertainty alone preclude hospice certification?
Answer: No. Certification is based on the prognosis in the normal course of the illness.
Reason: Eligibility also requires the other benefit conditions and a valid election.
Source: CMS · Medicare hospice benefit · https://www.cms.gov/medicare/payment/fee-for-service-providers/hospice

Topic: Distinguishing palliative needs from Medicare hospice eligibility
Prompt: A patient with disabling symptoms has an expected survival of several years in the normal course of illness. Which part of initial Medicare hospice eligibility has not been established?
Answer: The required terminal prognosis.
Reason: Consider appropriate palliative support for current needs.
Source: CMS · Medicare hospice benefit · https://www.cms.gov/medicare/payment/fee-for-service-providers/hospice

Topic: Distinguishing palliative needs from Medicare hospice eligibility
Prompt: What allows Medicare hospice care to continue into a later benefit period?
Answer: Continued eligibility with the required recertification.
Reason: Follow applicable documentation and face-to-face requirements.
Source: CMS · Medicare hospice benefit · https://www.cms.gov/medicare/payment/fee-for-service-providers/hospice

Topic: Matching end-of-life symptom treatment to the cause of distress
Prompt: What patient preference should be elicited when symptom relief might also cause drowsiness?
Answer: How the patient weighs relief against remaining alert.
Reason: Reassess benefits and unwanted effects together.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Matching end-of-life symptom treatment to the cause of distress
Prompt: A dying patient says, “I need my pain treated but want to be awake when my son comes.” What should guide the plan?
Answer: Agree on a symptom target and titrate treatment while monitoring alertness.
Reason: These goals call for tailoring the plan with the patient.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Matching end-of-life symptom treatment to the cause of distress
Prompt: Pain is now well controlled, but a patient is too drowsy for a conversation they value. What aspect of treatment warrants reassessment?
Answer: Medication burden and unwanted sedation, along with other causes of drowsiness.
Reason: A low pain score alone does not establish that the patient's goals are met.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Matching end-of-life symptom treatment to the cause of distress
Prompt: In a dying adult with breathlessness, what should be assessed before choosing symptom treatment?
Answer: Potential reversible causes, symptoms, oxygenation and the patient's goals.
Reason: Offer suitable nonpharmacologic and pharmacologic measures.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Matching end-of-life symptom treatment to the cause of distress
Prompt: A dying patient is breathless but has no clinical evidence of symptomatic hypoxemia. Should oxygen routinely be started simply because breathlessness is present?
Answer: No. Offer measures targeted to the distress and likely cause.
Reason: Positioning, airflow and appropriate medication may help.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Matching end-of-life symptom treatment to the cause of distress
Prompt: A dying patient has distressing dyspnea with documented hypoxemia. Which supportive treatment is now reasonable to offer and reassess for benefit?
Answer: Supplemental oxygen.
Reason: The purpose is relief of distress in a patient with symptomatic hypoxemia.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Matching end-of-life symptom treatment to the cause of distress
Prompt: What makes a symptom refractory when considering palliative sedation?
Answer: Appropriate symptom-specific treatments have failed or cannot provide relief within an acceptable time or burden.
Reason: Use specialist input, informed decision-making and proportionate care.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Sedation to unconsciousness in end-of-life care · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/sedation-unconsciousness-end-life-care

Topic: Matching end-of-life symptom treatment to the cause of distress
Prompt: A dying patient with severe discomfort becomes restless and is found to have a painful distended bladder. What should the team address before escalating sedating medication?
Answer: Treat the likely urinary retention in keeping with the patient's goals.
Reason: A reversible source of distress can mimic refractory agitation.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Matching end-of-life symptom treatment to the cause of distress
Prompt: An imminently dying patient has intolerable physical symptoms despite appropriate specialist-directed treatment and requests further relief. What option may now be discussed with informed consent and a monitoring plan?
Answer: Proportionate palliative sedation, with sedation to unconsciousness considered only as a last resort.
Reason: The intent is relief of otherwise refractory suffering.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Sedation to unconsciousness in end-of-life care · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/sedation-unconsciousness-end-life-care

Topic: Giving relatives a clear update consistent with patient preferences
Prompt: What should be clarified with a capable dying patient before detailed information is shared with relatives?
Answer: What information the patient wants shared and with whom.
Reason: Ask about preferred involvement and revisit if wishes change.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Giving relatives a clear update consistent with patient preferences
Prompt: A capable patient asks for their sister to join a prognosis discussion but wants the details explained in plain language. How should the team proceed?
Answer: Invite the sister with permission and explain the findings to the patient in accessible terms.
Reason: Family involvement should support the patient's preferred discussion.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Giving relatives a clear update consistent with patient preferences
Prompt: A relative asks for a guaranteed date of death when the clinical course is uncertain. What response is appropriate if the patient permits discussion?
Answer: Give the best supported estimate or range, acknowledge uncertainty and offer updates.
Reason: False precision can mislead families making plans.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Giving relatives a clear update consistent with patient preferences
Prompt: What should the clinician ask when a relative says comfort-focused care means “nothing will be done”?
Answer: “What are you worried will happen if we change the focus of treatment?”
Reason: Find the concern before explaining what care will continue.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Giving relatives a clear update consistent with patient preferences
Prompt: A family agrees to comfort-focused care but fears no one will come if the patient becomes frightened at night. What should the team explain?
Answer: Who is available, how to reach them and what help they can provide overnight.
Reason: Give a practical response to the specific concern about abandonment.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Giving relatives a clear update consistent with patient preferences
Prompt: Before giving a family another update about a dying patient, what question helps identify their current need?
Answer: “What have you understood so far, and what would you most like to know now?”
Reason: Different relatives may have heard or understood different information.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Giving relatives a clear update consistent with patient preferences
Prompt: With the patient's permission, a family asks what physical changes they may see as death approaches. What should the clinician explain?
Answer: Likely changes in breathing, alertness or intake and whom to call for distress.
Reason: Tailor the level of detail to what the family wants.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Giving relatives a clear update consistent with patient preferences
Prompt: A patient thought to be dying stabilizes unexpectedly. Relatives are still organizing around an earlier prediction of death that night. What communication is needed?
Answer: Explain the change, acknowledge the new uncertainty and agree on when the team will reassess.
Reason: Continue symptom care and support as the prognosis is revisited.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Exploring and responding to existential distress near death
Prompt: A dying patient says, “I don't want to be alone this evening.” What question helps identify the support they would value?
Answer: “Is there someone you would like us to contact or arrange to stay with you?”
Reason: Begin with the patient's own preference.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Exploring and responding to existential distress near death
Prompt: A dying patient asks for a particular faith ritual. What should the clinician ask before choosing whom to call?
Answer: Whom the patient would like involved and what is important about the ritual.
Reason: Arrange the requested support when feasible and desired.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Exploring and responding to existential distress near death
Prompt: What open question can uncover existential concerns in a patient approaching death?
Answer: “What is weighing on you most right now?”
Reason: Invite the patient's own language without assuming a religious framework.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Exploring and responding to existential distress near death
Prompt: A patient says prayer has become important and asks to see a chaplain. What is an appropriate response?
Answer: Arrange the requested spiritual support and ask about any particular preferences.
Reason: Include the patient in selecting support.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Exploring and responding to existential distress near death
Prompt: A patient says life feels unfinished but declines religious support and wants help talking to a sibling. What should the team offer?
Answer: Help arranging the conversation, with social-work or counseling support if desired.
Reason: Respect the patient's preferred approach to meaning and relationships.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Exploring and responding to existential distress near death
Prompt: What should be assessed when a dying patient reports severe distress despite a low pain score?
Answer: Psychological, social, spiritual and other physical contributors to distress.
Reason: A low score in one domain does not identify the cause.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Exploring and responding to existential distress near death
Prompt: A previously lonely patient now reports severe focal pain and grimaces with repositioning. What should the team reassess before assuming distress remains primarily existential?
Answer: The new physical pain and its cause, alongside ongoing emotional needs.
Reason: Changed evidence should change the symptom plan.
Source: NICE NG31 · Care of dying adults in the last days of life · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng31/chapter/recommendations

Topic: Recognizing whether a service has the capacity to deliver care
Prompt: What does a structure measure describe?
Answer: A resource or organizational feature available to deliver care.
Reason: Examples include staffing and equipment.
Source: AHRQ · Types of health care quality measures · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/types.html

Topic: Recognizing whether a service has the capacity to deliver care
Prompt: A second ward counts the patients whose medicines were actually reviewed by a pharmacist. How should that measure be classified?
Answer: A process measure.
Reason: It measures the action delivered rather than the presence of a pharmacist.
Source: AHRQ · Types of health care quality measures · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/types.html

Topic: Recognizing whether a service has the capacity to deliver care
Prompt: Which data would establish whether an emergency service has the equipment required for a new pathway?
Answer: An inventory of functioning required equipment available to the service.

Topic: Recognizing whether a service has the capacity to deliver care

Topic: Recognizing whether a service has the capacity to deliver care
Prompt: All wards own a machine, but only daytime staff can unlock the storage room. Which capacity measure would better capture overnight readiness?
Answer: The proportion of ward-night shifts with access to a functioning machine.
Reason: An inventory of purchases misses availability at the time of need.

Topic: Recognizing whether a service has the capacity to deliver care
Prompt: What additional measure tests the next link after a hospital hires discharge pharmacists?
Answer: The proportion of eligible discharges that receive a pharmacist review.

Topic: Recognizing whether a service has the capacity to deliver care
Prompt: Pharmacist staffing improves, but the same fraction of eligible patients gets a discharge review. Which link in the proposed improvement remains unproven?
