Reason: Investigate workflow before attributing outcome changes to more reviews.
Source: AHRQ · Types of health care quality measures · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/types.html

Topic: Recognizing whether a service has the capacity to deliver care
Prompt: Overall staffing meets the new target, but night discharges rarely get reviewed. What structure should be examined more closely?
Answer: Staffing and access to the review service by shift.
Reason: An aggregate resource count can conceal gaps when care is delivered.
Source: AHRQ · Types of health care quality measures · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/types.html

Topic: Measuring whether eligible patients received a specified action
Prompt: What is the numerator of a measure asking whether eligible patients received a particular care process?
Answer: Eligible patients or care opportunities in which the specified action occurred.
Reason: Define the observation period and action precisely.
Source: AHRQ · Types of health care quality measures · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/types.html

Topic: Measuring whether eligible patients received a specified action
Prompt: A hospital changes the measure from discharge medication reviews completed to the number of patients injured by discharge medication errors. What type of measure is the latter?
Answer: A patient outcome measure.
Reason: It tracks harm after care.
Source: AHRQ · Types of health care quality measures · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/types.html

Topic: Measuring whether eligible patients received a specified action
Prompt: What determines which patients belong in a measure's denominator?
Answer: The specified population, period and inclusion and exclusion criteria.
Reason: Apply the definition consistently.
Source: AHRQ · Types of health care quality measures · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/types.html

Topic: Measuring whether eligible patients received a specified action
Prompt: A service offered a recommended review to 72 of 80 eligible discharges. What was its offer rate?
Reason: Divide 72 by 80, the eligible denominator.
Source: AHRQ · Types of health care quality measures · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/types.html

Topic: Measuring whether eligible patients received a specified action
Prompt: A second service also offered 72 reviews to 80 eligible patients. It reports 72% using all 100 discharges, including 20 exclusions. What caused the apparent difference?
Answer: It used the wrong denominator.
Reason: Adherence among eligible discharges was 90% at both services.
Source: AHRQ · Types of health care quality measures · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/types.html

Topic: Measuring whether eligible patients received a specified action
Prompt: A team wants to measure whether patients actually complete a follow-up call. Why is a placed call order an inadequate numerator?
Answer: It records intent rather than a completed conversation.
Reason: Choose evidence aligned with the intended action.
Source: AHRQ · Types of health care quality measures · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/types.html

Topic: Measuring whether eligible patients received a specified action
Prompt: A report counts 96 signed call orders as 96 completed conversations. The call log confirms 61 completed conversations. Which count belongs in a completed-contact numerator?
Reason: Orders can be useful for another metric but do not establish contact.
Source: AHRQ · Types of health care quality measures · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/types.html

Topic: Measuring whether eligible patients received a specified action
Prompt: A clinic changes its objective to a documented outreach attempt regardless of whether the patient answers. What should change in the numerator?
Answer: Count eligible patients with a documented attempt, including unanswered attempts.
Reason: State the revised definition before comparing performance.
Source: AHRQ · Types of health care quality measures · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/types.html

Topic: Interpreting harm and recovery as patient outcomes
Prompt: What aspect of care does an outcome measure capture?
Answer: A change in a patient's health, function or experience of harm.
Reason: A process measure records what care was delivered.
Source: AHRQ · Types of health care quality measures · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/types.html

Topic: Interpreting harm and recovery as patient outcomes
Prompt: A ward tracks new pressure injuries developing during admission. Which type of quality measure is the injury rate?
Answer: An outcome measure.
Reason: The injuries are events experienced by patients.
Source: AHRQ · Types of health care quality measures · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/types.html

Topic: Interpreting harm and recovery as patient outcomes
Prompt: The ward instead records the fraction of patients examined for pressure injury on arrival. Which type of measure is that?
Answer: A process measure.
Reason: A completed assessment is an action, not an injury outcome.
Source: AHRQ · Types of health care quality measures · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/types.html

Topic: Interpreting harm and recovery as patient outcomes
Prompt: What distinguishes a measure of medication-related harm from a measure of reporting activity?
Answer: It counts verified injuries in a defined population and period.
Reason: The number of forms filed also depends on reporting behavior.
Source: AHRQ · Types of health care quality measures · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/types.html

Topic: Interpreting harm and recovery as patient outcomes
Prompt: A reporting campaign doubles incident forms. Can that count alone show that more patients suffered medication injury?
Answer: No. Check verified harm using comparable ascertainment and denominators.
Reason: Staff may simply be reporting more consistently.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Measurement of patient safety · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/measurement-patient-safety

Topic: Interpreting harm and recovery as patient outcomes
Prompt: What patient characteristic can make crude comparisons of mortality across hospitals misleading?
Answer: Differences in baseline illness severity or other prognostic factors.
Reason: Use appropriate case-mix assessment and comparable definitions.
Source: AHRQ · Types of health care quality measures · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/types.html

Topic: Interpreting harm and recovery as patient outcomes
Prompt: Hospital A treats many critically ill transfers and has higher crude mortality than B. What should be addressed before attributing the gap to quality?
Answer: Differences in predicted risk and case mix.
Reason: Even after adjustment, residual confounding may remain.
Source: AHRQ · Types of health care quality measures · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/types.html

Topic: Interpreting harm and recovery as patient outcomes
Prompt: A hospital begins active follow-up for complications after discharge while another counts only inpatient events. What must be harmonized before comparing complication rates?
Answer: The outcome window and detection method.
Reason: Risk adjustment alone cannot repair inconsistent ascertainment.
Source: AHRQ · Types of health care quality measures · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/types.html

Topic: Looking for unintended effects of improvement work
Prompt: What question does a balancing measure answer?
Answer: Whether changing one aspect of the system caused problems elsewhere.
Reason: Choose a plausible unintended consequence of the specific change.
Source: IHI · Establishing measures · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/establishing-measures

Topic: Looking for unintended effects of improvement work
Prompt: A new double-check aims to reduce medication errors. What time-based balancing measure would test a plausible downside?
Answer: Time to delivery of urgent doses.
Reason: The new checks may reduce error while delaying treatment.
Source: IHI · Establishing measures · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/establishing-measures

Topic: Looking for unintended effects of improvement work
Prompt: A discharge initiative targets shorter hospital stays. Which return-to-care outcome could provide a balancing measure?
Answer: Unplanned readmissions within a defined interval.
Reason: A shorter stay may shift burden to the period after discharge.
Source: IHI · Establishing measures · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/establishing-measures

Topic: Looking for unintended effects of improvement work
Prompt: What should a team compare when evaluating a prototype meant to speed discharge?
Answer: The target measure together with a plausible balancing measure.
Reason: Assess both using consistent definitions and intervals.
Source: IHI · Establishing measures · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/establishing-measures

Topic: Looking for unintended effects of improvement work
Prompt: The pilot record shows faster discharge but more urgent return visits among the same eligible population. What potential trade-off should the team investigate?
Answer: Whether quicker discharge has increased unplanned returns.
Reason: The comparison flags a concern; investigate other explanations before concluding causation.
Source: IHI · Establishing measures · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/establishing-measures

Topic: Looking for unintended effects of improvement work
Prompt: The second pilot has the same improvement in discharge time. What does its return-visit record show?
Answer: No observed increase in the return-visit rate during these periods.
Reason: Keep monitoring and assess uncertainty; the short pilot cannot guarantee absence of harm.
Source: IHI · Establishing measures · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/establishing-measures

Topic: Distinguishing consistent completion from a favorable average
Prompt: What does all-or-none reliability measure for a required bundle?
Answer: The fraction of eligible cases receiving every required component.
Reason: Count the cases, not the average of component percentages.
Source: IHI · Four steps for developing reliable processes · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/four-steps-developing-reliable-processes

Topic: Distinguishing consistent completion from a favorable average
Prompt: A patient receives three of four required handoff elements. Does this handoff count as complete on an all-or-none measure?
Answer: No. It is incomplete for that case.
Reason: The completed components can still be tracked separately.
Source: IHI · Four steps for developing reliable processes · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/four-steps-developing-reliable-processes

Topic: Distinguishing consistent completion from a favorable average
Prompt: Each of two required steps is documented for 90% of patients. Can the exact percentage receiving both be calculated from these marginal rates alone?
Answer: No. You need their overlap at the patient level.
Reason: The missed steps could occur in the same or different patients.
Source: IHI · Four steps for developing reliable processes · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/four-steps-developing-reliable-processes

Topic: Distinguishing consistent completion from a favorable average
Prompt: What information should be obtained before calculating the fraction who received a complete two-step bundle?
Answer: Whether each eligible case received both steps.
Reason: Aggregated counts for each step lose the joint information.
Source: IHI · Four steps for developing reliable processes · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/four-steps-developing-reliable-processes

Topic: Distinguishing consistent completion from a favorable average
Prompt: Read the case-level pilot sheet. What fraction received the full two-step bundle?
Answer: Three of four, or 75%.
Reason: The same patient missed both steps.
Source: IHI · Four steps for developing reliable processes · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/four-steps-developing-reliable-processes

Topic: Distinguishing consistent completion from a favorable average
Prompt: In the second pilot, three of four received each individual step. What fraction received both?
Answer: Two of four, or 50%.
Reason: The two failures occurred in different patients.
Source: IHI · Four steps for developing reliable processes · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/four-steps-developing-reliable-processes

Topic: Distinguishing consistent completion from a favorable average
Prompt: What does a recovery step do in a reliability plan?
Answer: Detect a prior failure in time to correct it before harm.
Reason: Design for both reliable initial performance and timely detection.
Source: IHI · Four steps for developing reliable processes · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/four-steps-developing-reliable-processes

Topic: Distinguishing consistent completion from a favorable average
Prompt: A discharge step is routinely omitted because ownership is undefined. Which redesign directly targets that failure?
Answer: Assign the step to a named role at a defined point in the workflow.
Reason: Education alone leaves the ownership gap unresolved.
Source: IHI · Four steps for developing reliable processes · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/four-steps-developing-reliable-processes

Topic: Distinguishing consistent completion from a favorable average
Prompt: The owner is clear, but occasional omissions reach patients without anyone noticing. Which change would add a recovery step?
Answer: Check for outstanding tasks before discharge and route exceptions to someone able to resolve them.
Reason: The check acts on missed work before the transition.
Source: IHI · Four steps for developing reliable processes · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/four-steps-developing-reliable-processes

Topic: Using predictions and small tests to decide what to change next
Prompt: A team tries one new discharge prompt and records whether the patient can explain the plan. Which PDSA phase includes carrying out this first test?
Answer: Do.

Topic: Using predictions and small tests to decide what to change next
Prompt: The patient understood less than the team predicted. Which phase compares the observation with the prediction?
Answer: Study.
Reason: Use the difference to learn before deciding what to change.
Source: IHI · Plan-Do-Study-Act worksheet · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/plan-do-study-act-pdsa-worksheet

Topic: Using predictions and small tests to decide what to change next
Prompt: What implementation detail should be recorded during a small test when the result may be hard to interpret?
Answer: Whether the change was delivered as planned and under what conditions.
Reason: A null result can reflect an untested change.
Source: IHI · Plan-Do-Study-Act worksheet · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/plan-do-study-act-pdsa-worksheet

Topic: Using predictions and small tests to decide what to change next
Prompt: A nurse never received the new prompt because the template was unavailable. Patient understanding did not improve. What conclusion is premature?
Answer: That the prompt itself is ineffective when used.
Reason: Repair the delivery problem and test again.
Source: IHI · Plan-Do-Study-Act worksheet · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/plan-do-study-act-pdsa-worksheet

Topic: Using predictions and small tests to decide what to change next
Prompt: What question should the Act phase answer after a small test?
Answer: Whether to adopt, adapt or abandon the change for the next cycle.
Reason: Use the results and the conditions under which they occurred.
Source: IHI · Plan-Do-Study-Act worksheet · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/plan-do-study-act-pdsa-worksheet

Topic: Using predictions and small tests to decide what to change next
Prompt: A revised discharge process works on nights and days on one unit. Before hospital-wide implementation, how could the team test generalizability?
Answer: Try it in additional representative settings or patient groups and keep measuring performance.
Reason: Spread can expose conditions the original unit did not face.
Source: IHI · Plan-Do-Study-Act worksheet · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/plan-do-study-act-pdsa-worksheet

Topic: Recognizing time order, a baseline median and a sustained shift

Answer: The reference median and the applicable consecutive-point rule.

Topic: Recognizing time order, a baseline median and a sustained shift

Answer: It meets the shift rule and warrants investigation of what changed.

Topic: Recognizing time order, a baseline median and a sustained shift
Prompt: A second service has one exceptionally fast week, followed by alternating values about the same baseline median. Does the single fast week establish a sustained shift by the six-point rule?
Answer: No. There are not six consecutive points on one side.
Reason: Check the unusual week without claiming a sustained change.
Source: IHI · Run-chart rules reference sheet · https://www.ihi.org/sites/default/files/lms/legacy/education/IHIOpenSchool/Courses/Documents/11_RunChartRulesReferenceSheet.pdf

Topic: Distinguishing process limits from targets and patient reference ranges

Answer: Possible special-cause variation.

Topic: Distinguishing process limits from targets and patient reference ranges
Prompt: Every week is within the process limits, yet waits consistently exceed the clinic's target. What does the chart imply about meeting the target?

Topic: Distinguishing process limits from targets and patient reference ranges

Answer: The relevant upper or lower control limit.
Reason: Crossing the mean alone is insufficient.

Topic: Distinguishing process limits from targets and patient reference ranges
Prompt: What decision does a special-cause signal support before broad process redesign?
Answer: Investigate what was different in the signaled period.

Topic: Separating unwarranted variation from appropriate individualization

Topic: Separating unwarranted variation from appropriate individualization
Prompt: Two equally eligible patients want the same beneficial service. Only patients seen on Tuesday are offered it because of a scheduling custom. What does this suggest?

Topic: Separating unwarranted variation from appropriate individualization
Prompt: Two patients with the same diagnosis receive different medicines because one has a serious contraindication. How should that difference be interpreted?
Answer: It can be appropriate individualization.

Topic: Separating unwarranted variation from appropriate individualization
Prompt: One clinic counts contraindicated patients as missed treatments while another excludes them as specified. What should be done before interpreting their adherence difference?
Answer: Recalculate both with the same eligible denominator.

Topic: Separating unwarranted variation from appropriate individualization
Prompt: After applying the same exclusions, one shift still omits a required check far more often. What should be investigated next?
Answer: The local workflow and barriers on that shift.
Reason: A persistent difference merits investigation before assuming individual negligence.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Separating unwarranted variation from appropriate individualization
Prompt: Which process feature helps a standardized pathway remain usable for atypical patients?
Answer: An explicit route to document an appropriate exception and choose an alternative.
Reason: Review exception patterns to improve the pathway.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Separating unwarranted variation from appropriate individualization
Prompt: A team finds the same routine check performed four different ways with no clinical reason for variation. What initial design change is reasonable?
Answer: Agree on a standard, evidence-informed method and pilot it with the users.
Reason: Measure performance and unintended consequences.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Separating unwarranted variation from appropriate individualization
Prompt: A default medication on a pathway is contraindicated for one patient. What should the team do with the pathway in this case?
Answer: Use and document the appropriate exception, then ensure a safe alternative plan.
Reason: A high compliance target cannot justify an unsafe default.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Using checklists to surface unresolved concerns

Answer: To share relevant information and identify unresolved discrepancies before harm.

Topic: Using checklists to surface unresolved concerns

Source: WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241598590

Topic: Using checklists to surface unresolved concerns
Prompt: At the time-out the team discovers a side discrepancy and postpones incision. Did the checklist process fail merely because it delayed starting?
Answer: No. Detecting the discrepancy before incision is an intended function.
Reason: Resolve the concern before proceeding.

Topic: Using checklists to surface unresolved concerns
Prompt: What comparison separates a missing checklist safeguard from a skipped one?
Answer: Compare the written checklist with observation of how it was actually used.
Reason: The remedies address different causes.
Source: WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241598590

Topic: Using checklists to surface unresolved concerns
Prompt: A team faithfully completes the full checklist, but the local high-risk step identified in repeated incidents is absent. What needs review?
Answer: The checklist's content and fit to the local workflow.
Reason: Pilot a change based on the identified hazard.
Source: WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241598590

Topic: Using checklists to surface unresolved concerns
Prompt: The required check is present in the checklist, but auditors see staff prefill it before the information arrives. What needs review?
Answer: How and when the team executes the check.
Reason: Adding the same words a second time is unlikely to fix the workflow.
Source: WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241598590

Topic: Using checklists to surface unresolved concerns
Prompt: What observation helps validate a reported 100% checklist completion rate?
Answer: Direct observation of whether the checks occur at the intended time with the relevant team.
Reason: Paper completion and meaningful execution can diverge.
Source: WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241598590

Topic: Using checklists to surface unresolved concerns
Prompt: A surgical checklist pilot finds introductions and hazard discussion occur in only half of directly observed cases despite signed forms. Which behavior should the next test target?
Answer: The team's actual participation in the discussion.

Source: WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241598590

Topic: Using checklists to surface unresolved concerns

Answer: Whether discrepancies are detected and resolved and whether targeted harms or delays change.

Topic: Defining the eligible denominator and unit of analysis

Topic: Defining the eligible denominator and unit of analysis
Prompt: What should be documented before a performance measure is tracked over time?
Answer: Its numerator, denominator, exclusions, interval and data source.
Reason: These specifications make repeated measurements comparable.

Topic: Defining the eligible denominator and unit of analysis
Prompt: A policy expands eligibility for screening to a new age group midyear. How could the clinic compare delivery over time without hiding that change?

Topic: Applying published measure specifications before comparing clinicians

Answer: Exactly what is measured, including the eligible population and how performance is counted.

Topic: Applying published measure specifications before comparing clinicians

Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Applying published measure specifications before comparing clinicians
Prompt: A clinician feels a patient was atypical, but the patient meets eligibility and no published exclusion or exception applies. May the reviewer quietly remove that patient to improve the score?
Answer: No. Apply the specification consistently and flag any limitation separately.
Reason: Discretionary exclusions undermine comparability.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Applying published measure specifications before comparing clinicians
Prompt: What should accompany a clinician's count of patients meeting a process measure?
Answer: The number of eligible patients and the measure period.
Reason: Include exclusions as defined by the specification.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Applying published measure specifications before comparing clinicians
Prompt: Review the two clinicians' reports. Which clinician had the higher proportion meeting the process measure?
Answer: Clinician B, at 90%.
Reason: A delivered the service to 48 of 60 (80%); B delivered it to 27 of 30 (90%).
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Applying published measure specifications before comparing clinicians
Prompt: A clinician meets a measure for 4 of 4 eligible patients. What important limitation applies to treating that 100% as a stable ranking?
Answer: The estimate is based on very few eligible cases.
Reason: One additional case can change the percentage substantially.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Applying published measure specifications before comparing clinicians
Prompt: What should a practice verify when a reported quality score changes sharply at a reporting-year boundary?
Answer: Whether measure definitions, data capture or patient eligibility changed.
Reason: Inspect underlying cases before attributing the change to care.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Applying published measure specifications before comparing clinicians
Prompt: The new measure version changes the follow-up window from 30 to 60 days. Can the new score be directly interpreted against the old 30-day trend?
Answer: No. Recompute using a common window or clearly mark a new series.
Reason: The outcome has more time in which to occur.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Applying published measure specifications before comparing clinicians
Prompt: The measure specification is unchanged, but completed services disappeared after an EHR code migration. What should be validated before redesigning the clinical service?
Answer: The mapping from the new codes to the measure numerator.
Reason: The apparent decline may reflect corrupted measurement.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Using incident reports as learning signals
Prompt: What does a voluntary incident reporting system directly count?
Answer: Events that someone recognized and submitted.
Reason: Many events go unrecognized or unreported.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Measurement of patient safety · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/measurement-patient-safety

Topic: Using incident reports as learning signals
Prompt: A ward staff member reports a near miss from yesterday. What does the single report reliably establish for improvement work?
Answer: A specific hazard or event is available for investigation.
Reason: It does not indicate how often comparable events occur.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Measurement of patient safety · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/measurement-patient-safety

Topic: Using incident reports as learning signals
Prompt: After anonymous online reporting begins, near-miss submissions triple. What measurement change could explain the increase without a change in actual hazards?
Answer: Staff may now report a greater fraction of events.
Reason: The reporting channel changed ascertainment.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Measurement of patient safety · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/measurement-patient-safety

Topic: Using incident reports as learning signals
Prompt: Why is a denominator alone insufficient to estimate true harm incidence from voluntary reports?
Answer: The numerator can miss an unknown fraction of harms.
Reason: Ascertain events systematically as well as defining the population.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Measurement of patient safety · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/measurement-patient-safety

Topic: Using incident reports as learning signals
Prompt: A unit needs an estimate of medication harm per 100 admissions and suspects severe underreporting. Which additional approach could improve ascertainment?
Answer: Systematic review of a defined sample of admissions using a consistent injury definition.
Reason: This supplies an independent source of potential events and a denominator.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Measurement of patient safety · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/measurement-patient-safety

Topic: Using incident reports as learning signals
Prompt: Which two processes can change the number of incident reports?
Answer: How often events occur and how often they are recognized and reported.
Reason: Consider both before drawing conclusions.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Measurement of patient safety · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/measurement-patient-safety

Topic: Identifying implementation barriers with the people doing the work
Prompt: Why include frontline staff on an improvement team?
Answer: They know how the process actually operates and where failures occur.
Reason: Patients may identify additional burdens or barriers.
Source: IHI · Forming the improvement team · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/forming-team

Topic: Identifying implementation barriers with the people doing the work
Prompt: A senior leader funds a new referral workflow, but no one consulted the people receiving referrals. Whose perspective is most immediately missing?
Answer: The staff who must receive, process and act on the referrals.
Reason: Include them in mapping and testing the workflow.
Source: IHI · Forming the improvement team · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/forming-team

Topic: Identifying implementation barriers with the people doing the work
Prompt: Frontline staff agree on a solution but cannot authorize needed cross-department access. What different role is required?
Answer: An accountable sponsor who can resolve the organizational barrier.
Reason: Expertise in the workflow and authority to remove barriers can belong to different people.
Source: IHI · Forming the improvement team · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/forming-team

Topic: Identifying implementation barriers with the people doing the work
Prompt: Before assuming teams are resistant to a new workflow, what should an improvement lead find out?
Answer: What prevents staff from carrying out the task in actual practice.
Reason: Observe work and invite feedback.
Source: IHI · Forming the improvement team · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/forming-team

Topic: Identifying implementation barriers with the people doing the work
Prompt: Night staff support a new interpreter-assisted discharge process but do not have access to the service number. What is the most direct change?
Answer: Provide reliable after-hours access at the point of discharge.
Reason: Additional persuasion does not supply the resource.
Source: IHI · Forming the improvement team · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/forming-team

Topic: Identifying implementation barriers with the people doing the work
Prompt: Staff have the service number and working equipment but disagree about who initiates the call. Which change addresses this barrier?
Answer: Assign the task to a defined role and confirm it in the workflow.
Reason: The barrier is ownership.
Source: IHI · Forming the improvement team · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/forming-team

Topic: Identifying implementation barriers with the people doing the work
Prompt: What information should a change leader seek before spreading a pilot across a hospital?
Answer: Evidence about its effects, feasibility and unintended consequences under representative conditions.
Reason: Include the people affected by the spread.
Source: IHI · Forming the improvement team · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/forming-team

Topic: Identifying implementation barriers with the people doing the work
Prompt: A new version works across shifts. Weeks after the original champion leaves, completion declines. What should leadership examine?
Answer: Whether ownership, training, feedback and resources were embedded in routine work.
Reason: A successful pilot may still lack a sustainable operating process.
Source: IHI · Forming the improvement team · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/forming-team

Topic: Choosing care whose likely benefit justifies its burdens
Prompt: What clinical question should you ask before repeating a laboratory test?
Answer: Would the new result change a decision for this patient?
Reason: A repeat test can add cost, discomfort and downstream investigation.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Choosing care whose likely benefit justifies its burdens
Prompt: A transfer patient has a verified potassium result from ten minutes ago, is stable and has had no intervening treatment. What should you check before redrawing it by routine?
Answer: Whether the existing result already answers the clinical question.
Reason: Use available reliable information when no new result would change care.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Choosing care whose likely benefit justifies its burdens
Prompt: Another transfer patient received emergency treatment for severe hyperkalemia after the last potassium measurement. Why does a repeat potassium now have value?
Answer: It shows the response to treatment and guides the next action.
Reason: The earlier result predates a clinically important intervention.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Choosing care whose likely benefit justifies its burdens
Prompt: When deciding whether to repeat an outside imaging study, what should the receiving team first establish?
Answer: Whether an accessible study of adequate quality already answers the current question.
Reason: A new institution alone is insufficient reason for a new exposure.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Choosing care whose likely benefit justifies its burdens
Prompt: A stable patient brings a recent readable CT answering the consultant's question. What is the least burdensome next step?
Answer: Have the existing images reviewed.
Reason: Review may provide the needed information without additional radiation.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Choosing care whose likely benefit justifies its burdens
Prompt: Another patient's outside images are unreadable, and an urgent treatment choice depends on the finding. What makes obtaining adequate imaging reasonable?
Answer: The previous study cannot answer the current decision.
Reason: Consider the safest timely way to obtain the required information.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Choosing care whose likely benefit justifies its burdens
Prompt: What patient-level benefit should a clinician identify before recommending an additional diagnostic service?
Answer: A plausible way the information will improve a decision or outcome.
Reason: Cost and potential harms also matter.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Choosing care whose likely benefit justifies its burdens
Prompt: A clinician discloses ownership of a facility. An indicated test will determine which of two treatments is appropriate. How should the clinician present the referral?
Answer: Explain the clinical indication, the financial interest and reasonable alternatives.
Reason: The patient can make an informed choice about where to obtain a clinically useful service.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Physician self-referral · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/physician-self-referral

Topic: Investigating differences in who benefits from a service
Prompt: A clinic changes its scheduling system. Which denominators allow a fair assessment of completion across language groups?
Answer: Eligible patients in each language group during each period.
Reason: Counting only people who completed the visit hides barriers to access.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Checking whether a decision reflects a patient's own priorities
Prompt: What information is necessary to judge whether a preference-sensitive decision fits the patient?
Answer: The patient's informed priorities for the relevant outcomes.
Reason: The same trade-off may be acceptable to one person and unacceptable to another.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Checking whether a decision reflects a patient's own priorities
Prompt: Two options offer similar survival. A patient prioritizes staying alert enough to care for a child. Which outcome deserves particular attention in comparing options?
Answer: The expected effect on alertness and daily function.
Reason: The patient's goal identifies which trade-off needs discussion.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Checking whether a decision reflects a patient's own priorities
Prompt: Another patient facing the same options prioritizes relief of otherwise intolerable symptoms and accepts drowsiness. Which outcome should guide this comparison?
Answer: Expected symptom relief, with the accepted sedation trade-off.
Reason: The patient's priorities changed even though the treatment options did not.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Checking whether a decision reflects a patient's own priorities
Prompt: A patient asks you to recommend one of two reasonable treatments. What should you elicit before making a tailored recommendation?
Answer: Which outcomes and burdens matter most to them.
Reason: A clinician can recommend a plan after understanding the patient's priorities.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Checking whether a decision reflects a patient's own priorities
Prompt: A patient wants to keep working during cancer treatment. What practical question helps compare two similarly effective regimens?
Answer: How would each regimen's visits and adverse effects affect the patient's work?
Reason: Clarify the impact the patient wants to minimize.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Checking whether a decision reflects a patient's own priorities
Prompt: A patient says both preserving hand function and having the shortest recovery matter. The options favor different goals. What should the clinician clarify next?
Answer: Which trade-off the patient would accept if both goals cannot be achieved together.
Reason: A preference list alone leaves the decision unresolved.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Checking whether a decision reflects a patient's own priorities
Prompt: Which comparison directly assesses whether delivered care matches a patient's goals?
Answer: Compare the actual care with the patient's informed goals at the time of the decision.
Reason: A completed preferences form alone does not establish concordance.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Checking whether a decision reflects a patient's own priorities
Prompt: A patient consistently requested home support, but a planning meeting presumed nursing-home placement without discussing alternatives. What should be reviewed?
Answer: Whether the team explored a feasible plan consistent with the patient's stated goal.
Reason: Review the assumptions and available support with the patient.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Checking whether a decision reflects a patient's own priorities
Prompt: After learning what home care would require, the same capable patient expressly chooses residential care. How should the team interpret the change?
Answer: Assess the plan against the patient's updated informed preference.
Reason: Record why the goal changed and share it with the care team.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Locating delays in a patient's path through care
Prompt: How do you locate a bottleneck when a total wait contains several steps?
Answer: Measure the elapsed time in each step.
Reason: A total duration alone cannot identify where the time was spent.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Locating delays in a patient's path through care
Prompt: In the urgent-clinic record, which interval accounts for most of the time before the result?
Answer: Arrival to assessment, 70 minutes.
Reason: The second interval takes 20 minutes.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Locating delays in a patient's path through care
Prompt: In this second clinic, which interval accounts for most of the same total wait?
Answer: Assessment to result, 75 minutes.
Reason: The first interval takes 15 minutes.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Locating delays in a patient's path through care
Prompt: For a project to reduce the time until a patient receives an indicated medicine, what event should end the measured interval?
Answer: Actual administration to the patient.
Reason: Time of ordering measures an earlier part of the process.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Locating delays in a patient's path through care
Prompt: On an audit, orders are usually signed promptly but doses arrive late. Which interval should the team examine next?
Answer: Order signing to administration.
Reason: Timing the later stages can locate an actionable delay.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Locating delays in a patient's path through care
Prompt: After bedside delivery is introduced, doses follow signed orders promptly, but patients still wait before anyone recognizes the need. Which interval now deserves review?
Answer: First qualifying finding to clinical recognition or order.
Reason: The remaining delay happens upstream of delivery.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Locating delays in a patient's path through care
Prompt: Which percentile helps assess delays among the longest-waiting patients when the median looks acceptable?
Answer: An upper percentile, such as the 90th percentile.
Reason: Report it alongside the median and denominator.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Locating delays in a patient's path through care
Prompt: After a pilot, the median wait falls from 40 to 30 minutes but the 90th percentile rises from 95 to 130 minutes. Which patients warrant closer review?
Answer: Patients with the longest waits.
Reason: The typical wait improved while the upper end worsened.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Locating delays in a patient's path through care
Prompt: After a second pilot, both median and 90th-percentile waits fall, but patients who left before being seen were excluded. Which group must be counted to assess timely access?
Answer: Patients who left before receiving care.
Reason: The recorded waits describe only those who stayed.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Interpreting a localization study for a missing surgical item
Prompt: What feature of a surgical sponge is designed to make it visible on an x-ray?
Answer: Its radiopaque marker.
Reason: Ordinary cloth by itself can be difficult to distinguish from soft tissue.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Interpreting a localization study for a missing surgical item
Prompt: A postoperative film shows an unexpected folded radiopaque strip in the operative area. Which feature makes a retained sponge a consideration?
Answer: The strip may represent a sponge marker.
Reason: Alert the surgical team and correlate with intended devices and packing.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Interpreting a localization study for a missing surgical item
Prompt: An unmarked nonradiopaque dressing is missing and a plain film appears clear. Can the clear film exclude retention of that dressing?
Answer: No. The item may be radiographically invisible.
Reason: The imaging method must be capable of detecting the missing material.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Interpreting a localization study for a missing surgical item
Prompt: Before relying on a negative localization image for a missing radiopaque item, what should the team check about the field of view?
Answer: That it includes the entire area where the item could remain.
Reason: Even a conspicuous marker can lie outside the image.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Interpreting a localization study for a missing surgical item
Prompt: A sponge is missing after a pelvic procedure. A negative film ends above the operative pelvis. What does the image establish about the pelvis?
Answer: It does not evaluate the operative pelvis.
Reason: Tell the team about the incomplete coverage and obtain the indicated evaluation.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Interpreting a localization study for a missing surgical item
Prompt: Another patient has a film covering the whole operative field. The radiologist identifies an unexplained sponge marker in it. What should the clinician do with this finding?
Answer: Notify the operating team promptly to localize and address the suspected retained item.
Reason: A positive finding warrants action regardless of the earlier count.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Interpreting a localization study for a missing surgical item
Prompt: When might an operating team need to defer a standard surgical-item check?
Answer: When completing it immediately would obstruct lifesaving care.
Reason: The team must keep track of the unresolved check.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Interpreting a localization study for a missing surgical item
Prompt: A patient is exsanguinating, and immediate hemorrhage control cannot safely wait for a count discrepancy to be investigated. What takes priority at that moment?
Answer: Control the life-threatening hemorrhage.
Reason: Communicate the outstanding discrepancy during resuscitation.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Interpreting a localization study for a missing surgical item
Prompt: Hemorrhage is controlled. A count skipped during the emergency remains unresolved. What should the team do now?
Answer: Resume reconciliation and arrange indicated examination or localization.
Reason: Record the unresolved count, actions taken and who will follow up.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Updating the handoff when the patient's acuity changes
Prompt: What does the illness-severity statement at clinical handoff communicate?
Answer: How stable the patient is now and how worried the sender is about deterioration.
Reason: The admission diagnosis alone cannot convey current risk.
Source: AHRQ · TeamSTEPPS I-PASS · https://www.ahrq.gov/teamstepps-program/curriculum/communication/tools/ipass.html

Topic: Updating the handoff when the patient's acuity changes
Prompt: A patient admitted with pneumonia has a rapidly rising oxygen requirement just before handoff. Which fact should lead the verbal update?
Answer: The acute respiratory deterioration.
Reason: The receiver needs the change in acuity before routine tasks.
Source: AHRQ · TeamSTEPPS I-PASS · https://www.ahrq.gov/teamstepps-program/curriculum/communication/tools/ipass.html

Topic: Updating the handoff when the patient's acuity changes
Prompt: A second patient with pneumonia has been off oxygen all day and is preparing for discharge. Which finding supports communicating lower immediate acuity?
Answer: Sustained stability off supplemental oxygen.
Reason: Report the actual trend and any residual concerns.
Source: AHRQ · TeamSTEPPS I-PASS · https://www.ahrq.gov/teamstepps-program/curriculum/communication/tools/ipass.html

Topic: Updating the handoff when the patient's acuity changes
Prompt: When should you verify the stability description in a handoff drafted earlier in the day?
Answer: Immediately before transfer, using the latest assessment.
Reason: A stale label can change how the receiving clinician prioritizes care.
Source: AHRQ · TeamSTEPPS I-PASS · https://www.ahrq.gov/teamstepps-program/curriculum/communication/tools/ipass.html

Topic: Updating the handoff when the patient's acuity changes
Prompt: A copied handoff says stable. At bedside the patient is newly hypotensive and confused. What should happen before routine sign-out proceeds?
Answer: Assess and escalate the deterioration now, and tell the receiver directly.
Reason: Routine documentation cannot substitute for an urgent clinical response.
Source: AHRQ · TeamSTEPPS I-PASS · https://www.ahrq.gov/teamstepps-program/curriculum/communication/tools/ipass.html

Topic: Updating the handoff when the patient's acuity changes
Prompt: The same symptoms occurred hours ago, resolved after treatment, and the patient is stable on reassessment. How should the handoff describe the episode?
Answer: Report the earlier deterioration, response and current reassessment.
Reason: The incoming team needs the history and what recurrence would look like.
Source: AHRQ · TeamSTEPPS I-PASS · https://www.ahrq.gov/teamstepps-program/curriculum/communication/tools/ipass.html

Topic: Updating the handoff when the patient's acuity changes
Prompt: An urgent deterioration occurs during a transfer between units. Who needs immediate notification?
Answer: The clinicians able to act where the patient is now, with direct coordination across the transfer.
Reason: A future bed assignment does not identify who is physically caring for the patient.
Source: AHRQ · TeamSTEPPS I-PASS · https://www.ahrq.gov/teamstepps-program/curriculum/communication/tools/ipass.html

Topic: Updating the handoff when the patient's acuity changes
Prompt: A ward patient assigned an ICU bed develops severe respiratory distress while still on the ward. Where must the immediate response be activated?
Answer: At the patient's current ward location.
Reason: Notify the ICU as well and arrange an appropriately supported transfer.
Source: AHRQ · TeamSTEPPS I-PASS · https://www.ahrq.gov/teamstepps-program/curriculum/communication/tools/ipass.html

Topic: Updating the handoff when the patient's acuity changes
Prompt: The patient has arrived in the ICU. The sending team then learns of a critical lab result requiring immediate review. Who should it contact directly?
Answer: The receiving ICU clinician now responsible for the patient.
Reason: Confirm receipt so the new result reaches someone who can act.
Source: AHRQ · TeamSTEPPS I-PASS · https://www.ahrq.gov/teamstepps-program/curriculum/communication/tools/ipass.html

Topic: Acting on evolving symptoms and ECG findings in suspected ACS
Prompt: At unchanged cardiac workload, sudden loss of coronary blood flow changes which side of myocardial oxygen balance first?
Answer: Oxygen supply falls.
Reason: Coronary flow delivers oxygenated blood to the myocardium.
Source: AHA/ACC · Evaluation and diagnosis of chest pain · https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001029

Topic: Acting on evolving symptoms and ECG findings in suspected ACS
Prompt: New chest pressure at rest starts as a platelet-rich thrombus forms on a disrupted coronary plaque. Which change most directly caused ischemia?
Answer: A sudden fall in blood flow beyond the thrombus.
Reason: There need be no increase in exertion.
Source: AHA/ACC · Evaluation and diagnosis of chest pain · https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001029

Topic: Acting on evolving symptoms and ECG findings in suspected ACS
Prompt: An adult with fixed coronary narrowing develops predictable chest pressure only when climbing a steep hill. Which change triggers ischemia during the climb?
Answer: The heart's oxygen requirement rises beyond its available supply.
Reason: The fixed lesion limits flow reserve as cardiac work increases.
Source: AHA/ACC et al. · Management of chronic coronary disease · https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001168

Topic: Acting on evolving symptoms and ECG findings in suspected ACS
Prompt: Which change during observation for possible ACS should prompt an immediate repeat 12-lead ECG?
Answer: Recurrent or worsening symptoms suggesting ischemia.
Reason: A pain-free tracing can miss transient changes.
Source: AHA/ACC · Evaluation and diagnosis of chest pain · https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001029

Topic: Acting on evolving symptoms and ECG findings in suspected ACS
Prompt: During observation for rest pain, chest pressure recurs despite initial medical therapy and new ST depression appears. Which evaluation must be escalated?
Answer: Urgent cardiology assessment for an immediate invasive strategy.
Reason: Refractory ischemia is a high-risk feature even before all scheduled biomarkers return.
Source: ACC/AHA et al. · 2025 acute coronary syndromes guideline · https://professional.heart.org/en/science-news/2025-guideline-for-the-management-of-patients-with-acute-coronary-syndromes

Topic: Acting on evolving symptoms and ECG findings in suspected ACS
Prompt: A separate patient is pain-free, has nonischemic serial ECGs and meets all criteria of a validated low-risk acute chest pain pathway. Is urgent inpatient ischemia testing routinely required?
Answer: No. Discharge with appropriate follow-up is reasonable.
Reason: The low-risk disposition depends on the entire pathway and assessment.
Source: AHA/ACC · Evaluation and diagnosis of chest pain · https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001029

Topic: Identifying infarction and its cause with biomarker and imaging evidence
Prompt: What imbalance makes myocardial tissue ischemic?
Answer: Its oxygen supply is inadequate for the prevailing oxygen demand.
Reason: A change in either supply or demand can produce this mismatch.
Source: ESC/ACC/AHA/WHF · Fifth universal definition of myocardial infarction · https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001477

Topic: Identifying infarction and its cause with biomarker and imaging evidence
Prompt: Under the 2026 definition, what makes a spontaneous infarction primary?
Answer: An acute coronary pathology causes the infarction.
Reason: Examples include plaque disruption, dissection and coronary embolism.
Source: ESC/ACC/AHA/WHF · Fifth universal definition of myocardial infarction · https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001477

Topic: Locating an early beat by the timing of atrial activation

Answer: Timing of the symptom marker relative to the ectopic beat.

Answer: Symptomatic atrial ectopy.

Prompt: A patient's usual hour-long pounding is recorded during sinus rhythm. Two PACs occurred while the patient was asymptomatic overnight. Do those PACs explain the recorded episode?

Topic: Interpreting the origin and burden of ventricular ectopy
Prompt: What determines whether a premature complex is classified as atrial or ventricular?
Answer: Where the early electrical impulse originates.
Reason: QRS width helps, but an atrial beat can also conduct aberrantly.
Source: ESC · Ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehac262

Topic: Interpreting the origin and burden of ventricular ectopy
Prompt: An early abnormal P wave is followed by a narrow QRS identical to the usual beats. Where did the premature impulse most likely arise?
Answer: In the atrium.
Reason: The normal QRS suggests conduction through the usual ventricular pathway.
Source: ESC · Ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehac262

Topic: Interpreting the origin and burden of ventricular ectopy
Prompt: How is PVC burden calculated on an ambulatory recording?
Answer: PVC count divided by total ventricular beats during the analyzed recording.
Reason: Report the time sampled because the fraction can vary over the day.
Source: ESC · Ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehac262

Topic: Interpreting the origin and burden of ventricular ectopy
Prompt: In a run of twelve ventricular complexes, every second complex is a PVC. What fraction are PVCs?
Answer: One half, or 50%.
Reason: Six of twelve beats are ectopic.

Topic: Interpreting the origin and burden of ventricular ectopy
Prompt: Another recording has one PVC after every two sinus beats for the entire sampled interval. What is the PVC burden in that interval?
Answer: One third, about 33%.
Reason: One of every three ventricular complexes is a PVC.
Source: ESC · Ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehac262

Topic: Interpreting the origin and burden of ventricular ectopy
Prompt: What reversible cause should be considered when unexplained LV dysfunction accompanies frequent predominantly monomorphic PVCs?
Answer: PVC-induced or PVC-aggravated cardiomyopathy.
Reason: Quantify the burden, assess structural disease and seek specialist evaluation.
Source: ESC · Ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehac262

Topic: Interpreting the origin and burden of ventricular ectopy
Prompt: A monitor shows a 24% PVC burden. EF has fallen without another clear cause. What cardiac function should be reassessed after successful PVC suppression?
Answer: LV systolic function by repeat imaging.
Reason: Improvement supports a causal contribution from the ectopy.
Source: ESC · Ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehac262

Topic: Interpreting the origin and burden of ventricular ectopy
Prompt: An asymptomatic patient has isolated PVCs comprising 0.2% of beats, a normal echocardiogram and no concerning history. Does the finding alone establish PVC-induced cardiomyopathy?
Answer: No.
Reason: There is no documented ventricular dysfunction and the measured burden is low.
Source: ESC · Ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehac262

Topic: Distinguishing atrial flutter waves from their ventricular response
Prompt: In typical atrial flutter, what sustains the rapid atrial rhythm?
Answer: A large reentrant circuit in the right atrium involving the cavotricuspid isthmus.
Reason: The AV node determines how many impulses reach the ventricles.
Source: ESC · Supraventricular tachycardia guideline · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Topic: Distinguishing atrial flutter waves from their ventricular response
Prompt: The atrial circuit runs at 300/min with fixed 2:1 AV conduction. What is the ventricular rate?
Reason: One of each two atrial impulses conducts.
Source: ESC · Supraventricular tachycardia guideline · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Topic: Distinguishing atrial flutter waves from their ventricular response
Prompt: The same atrial circuit continues at 300/min, but conduction becomes fixed 4:1. What is the ventricular rate now?
Answer: 75/min.
Reason: The ventricular rate changes without requiring a change in the atrial circuit.
Source: ESC · Supraventricular tachycardia guideline · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Topic: Distinguishing atrial flutter waves from their ventricular response
Prompt: What atrial feature favors flutter over fibrillation during an irregular ventricular response?
Answer: Repetitive organized flutter activity at a regular atrial cycle length.
Reason: Variable AV conduction can make the ventricular rhythm irregular.
Source: ESC · Supraventricular tachycardia guideline · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Topic: Distinguishing atrial flutter waves from their ventricular response
Prompt: In a regular narrow tachycardia, transient AV nodal block instead terminates the tachycardia and sinus P waves reappear. What mechanism does that support?
Answer: An AV-node-dependent reentrant tachycardia.
Reason: Termination supports that mechanism, although drug response alone is not definitive.
Source: ESC · Supraventricular tachycardia guideline · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Topic: Distinguishing atrial flutter waves from their ventricular response
Prompt: What immediate rhythm treatment is indicated when atrial flutter with a rapid response is causing hemodynamic instability?
Answer: Synchronized cardioversion.
Reason: Assess and support the circulation without delaying required treatment.
Source: AHA · 2025 adult advanced life support · https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-advanced-life-support

Topic: Distinguishing atrial flutter waves from their ventricular response
Prompt: A patient with known typical flutter has repeated symptomatic recurrences despite rate-control therapy and is stable at follow-up. Which definitive circuit-directed intervention should be discussed?
Answer: Catheter ablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus.
Reason: It targets the critical portion of the usual flutter circuit.
Source: ESC · Supraventricular tachycardia guideline · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Topic: Distinguishing atrial flutter waves from their ventricular response
Prompt: Another patient develops shock attributable to rapid flutter while awaiting elective ablation. What is the immediate rhythm intervention?
Answer: Synchronized cardioversion.
Reason: Elective circuit ablation is not the immediate stabilization strategy.
Source: AHA · 2025 adult advanced life support · https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-advanced-life-support

Topic: Separating atrial rhythm, ventricular response and embolic risk
Prompt: Why do the R–R intervals generally vary during untreated AF with intact AV conduction?
Answer: Disorganized atrial impulses reach an AV node with changing refractoriness.
Reason: An irregular subset of impulses conducts.

Topic: Separating atrial rhythm, ventricular response and embolic risk
Prompt: A patient remains in AF but develops complete AV block and a steady ventricular escape rhythm. Must the R–R intervals remain irregular?
Answer: No. An independent escape pacemaker can produce regular intervals.
Reason: Ventricular regularity alone cannot exclude fibrillating atria.
Source: ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS · Diagnosis and management of atrial fibrillation · https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001193

Topic: Separating atrial rhythm, ventricular response and embolic risk
Prompt: What atrial feature accompanies the irregularly irregular ventricular response in ordinary AF?
Answer: No consistent discrete repeating P waves.
Reason: Look at atrial activity as well as beat spacing.
Source: ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS · Diagnosis and management of atrial fibrillation · https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001193

Topic: Separating atrial rhythm, ventricular response and embolic risk
Prompt: An irregular narrow tachycardia has at least three distinct P-wave shapes in one lead, varying PR intervals and an isoelectric baseline between P waves. Which diagnosis is favored?
Answer: Multifocal atrial tachycardia.
Reason: Discrete organized atrial depolarizations distinguish this pattern from AF.
Source: ESC · Supraventricular tachycardia guideline · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Topic: Separating atrial rhythm, ventricular response and embolic risk
Prompt: A patient with documented paroxysmal AF and prior ischemic stroke is in sinus rhythm today. Does normal rhythm at this visit remove the need to assess long-term anticoagulation?
Answer: No. Base prevention on thromboembolic risk and contraindications.
Reason: A normal tracing today does not erase the prior AF or stroke.
Source: ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS · Diagnosis and management of atrial fibrillation · https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001193

Topic: Separating atrial rhythm, ventricular response and embolic risk
Prompt: A 35-year-old with AF has no nonsex stroke risk factors or separate anticoagulation indication. Does recurrent palpitation intensity alone justify indefinite oral anticoagulation?
Answer: No.
Reason: Symptom severity guides symptom management, while estimated embolic risk guides long-term stroke prevention.
Source: ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS · Diagnosis and management of atrial fibrillation · https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001193

Topic: Recognizing multifocal atrial activity in acute pulmonary illness
Prompt: Why do P waves have different shapes during multifocal atrial tachycardia?
Answer: Atrial depolarization begins at different sites.
Reason: Changing activation directions project differently onto the same ECG lead.
Source: ESC · Supraventricular tachycardia guideline · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Topic: Recognizing multifocal atrial activity in acute pulmonary illness
Prompt: A single continuous lead records three recurring P shapes before narrow QRS complexes. Which chamber's activation pathway is demonstrably changing?
Answer: The atria.
Reason: P waves represent atrial depolarization.
Source: ESC · Supraventricular tachycardia guideline · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Topic: Recognizing multifocal atrial activity in acute pulmonary illness
Prompt: Another tracing has identical sinus P waves but alternating narrow and aberrantly wide QRS complexes. Does QRS variation alone show multifocal atrial activation?
Answer: No. The variation is in ventricular activation.
Reason: Determine the atrial origin from the atrial deflections.
Source: ESC · Supraventricular tachycardia guideline · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Topic: Recognizing multifocal atrial activity in acute pulmonary illness
Prompt: In an irregular atrial rhythm, how many distinct P-wave morphologies in a single lead support a multifocal origin?
Answer: At least three.
Reason: MAT also has an atrial rate above 100/min and intervening isoelectric intervals.
Source: ESC · Supraventricular tachycardia guideline · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Topic: Recognizing multifocal atrial activity in acute pulmonary illness
Prompt: Read the atrial measurements from one continuous lead. Which rhythm accounts for this pattern?
Answer: Multifocal atrial tachycardia.
Reason: The atrial rate is 126/min and three distinct P morphologies are present.
Source: ESC · Supraventricular tachycardia guideline · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Topic: Recognizing multifocal atrial activity in acute pulmonary illness
Prompt: Read the second atrial record. What is the usual name for this slower multifocal rhythm?
Answer: Wandering atrial pacemaker.
Reason: The same multifocal pattern occurs at 78/min, below the tachycardia threshold.
Source: ESC · Supraventricular tachycardia guideline · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Topic: Recognizing multifocal atrial activity in acute pulmonary illness
Prompt: In stable multifocal atrial tachycardia during an acute COPD exacerbation, what is the first treatment priority?
Answer: Correct the underlying pulmonary or metabolic disturbance.
Reason: Address hypoxemia and relevant electrolyte abnormalities.
Source: ESC · Supraventricular tachycardia guideline · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Topic: Recognizing multifocal atrial activity in acute pulmonary illness
Prompt: A patient with MAT remains stable but is hypoxemic during pneumonia. Why is elective electrical cardioversion unlikely to solve the rhythm problem?
Answer: Multiple active atrial foci persist while the underlying trigger continues.
Reason: Treat the illness and reassess the ventricular response.
Source: ESC · Supraventricular tachycardia guideline · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Topic: Recognizing multifocal atrial activity in acute pulmonary illness
Prompt: A different patient has organized atrial flutter with shock attributable to the rhythm. Does the stable MAT approach suffice?
Answer: No. Perform urgent synchronized cardioversion while supporting the patient.
Reason: The rhythm mechanism and hemodynamic urgency have changed.

Topic: Recognizing and terminating AV-node-dependent reentry
Prompt: An AV nodal reentry circuit stops when conduction through one limb of the circuit is transiently blocked. Why does the rapid rhythm stop?

Topic: Recognizing and terminating AV-node-dependent reentry
Prompt: A separate rapid atrial flutter circuit continues during transient AV block. What happens to its ventricular response during that block?
Answer: It slows or pauses transiently.
Reason: The atrial rhythm can continue independently of the AV node.

Topic: Recognizing and terminating AV-node-dependent reentry
Prompt: In a stable adult with abrupt-onset regular narrow-complex tachycardia consistent with reentry, what is a reasonable initial bedside maneuver?
Answer: A vagal maneuver such as a modified Valsalva.
Reason: AV nodal slowing can interrupt the circuit.
Source: ESC · Supraventricular tachycardia guideline · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Topic: Recognizing and terminating AV-node-dependent reentry
Prompt: The patient remains stable, has a regular narrow tachycardia after vagal maneuvers and has no contraindication. Which short-acting IV agent can terminate AV-node-dependent reentry?
Answer: Adenosine.
Reason: Use appropriate monitoring and readiness to manage the rhythm.
Source: ESC · Supraventricular tachycardia guideline · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Topic: Recognizing and terminating AV-node-dependent reentry
Prompt: A different patient with the same regular narrow tachycardia becomes hypotensive and confused due to the rhythm. What is the urgent treatment?
Answer: Synchronized cardioversion.
Reason: Do not delay indicated electrical treatment in an unstable patient.
Source: AHA · 2025 adult advanced life support · https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-advanced-life-support

Topic: Recognizing and terminating AV-node-dependent reentry
Prompt: What procedure can definitively treat recurrent symptomatic AV nodal reentrant tachycardia?
Answer: Catheter ablation targeting the slow pathway.
Reason: Discuss the benefits and procedural risks.
Source: ESC · Supraventricular tachycardia guideline · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Topic: Recognizing and terminating AV-node-dependent reentry
Prompt: A patient with confirmed AVNRT needs repeated emergency visits and wants definitive treatment. What referral is appropriate?
Answer: Electrophysiology referral for catheter ablation.
Reason: The recurrent burden and preference support a definitive strategy.
Source: ESC · Supraventricular tachycardia guideline · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Topic: Recognizing and terminating AV-node-dependent reentry
Prompt: A patient with rare, brief, minimally symptomatic confirmed AVNRT prefers to avoid a procedure. Is immediate ablation required solely by the diagnosis?
Answer: No. Observation with follow-up can be reasonable.
Reason: Discuss symptom management and when to seek reassessment.
Source: ESC · Supraventricular tachycardia guideline · https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Topic: Assessing ventricular tachycardia by morphology and perfusion

Answer: Diastole.
Reason: Rapid rates can curtail filling and coronary perfusion.

Topic: Assessing ventricular tachycardia by morphology and perfusion
Prompt: At the same stroke volume, slowing the ventricular rate lowers cardiac output. If output instead rises after a poorly tolerated VT ends, what must have increased enough to compensate?

Topic: Assessing ventricular tachycardia by morphology and perfusion
Prompt: In sustained monomorphic VT, what bedside assessment distinguishes the arrest pathway from treatment of tachycardia with a pulse?
Answer: Whether there is a definite pulse.
Reason: Assess immediately when there are signs of collapse.

Topic: Assessing ventricular tachycardia by morphology and perfusion
Prompt: Sustained monomorphic VT is causing the deterioration in this bedside record. Which electrical intervention is indicated?

Topic: Assessing ventricular tachycardia by morphology and perfusion
Prompt: The organized wide tachycardia persists in this second bedside record. Which shock mode is indicated?

Topic: Assessing ventricular tachycardia by morphology and perfusion
Prompt: A monitored adult has a regular monomorphic wide tachycardia, preserved mentation, adequate blood pressure and a definite pulse. Should the team initiate chest compressions solely for the ECG appearance?
Answer: No. Evaluate and treat perfusing wide-complex tachycardia with monitoring and expert support.
Reason: Be ready to cardiovert if instability develops.
Source: AHA · 2025 adult advanced life support · https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-advanced-life-support

Topic: Assessing ventricular tachycardia by morphology and perfusion
Prompt: During that assessment the patient loses consciousness, stops breathing normally and has no definite pulse within ten seconds. What pathway should start immediately?
Answer: The shockable cardiac arrest pathway with CPR and defibrillation as soon as available.
Reason: The change in perfusion overrides the earlier stable presentation.
Source: AHA · 2025 adult advanced life support · https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-advanced-life-support

Topic: Recognizing disorganized ventricular activity in context
Prompt: An arrest rhythm has chaotic electrical deflections without recognizable QRS complexes. Why is coordinated systolic ejection lost?
Answer: The ventricles are activated in a disorganized manner.
Reason: Different regions are excited at different times.

Topic: Recognizing disorganized ventricular activity in context
Prompt: An equally pulseless patient has regular discrete QRS complexes. Is disorganized electrical activation required to explain this arrest?
Answer: No. Organized electrical activity can occur without effective mechanical output.

Topic: Recognizing disorganized ventricular activity in context
Prompt: What ECG feature distinguishes VF from an organized electrical rhythm in an adult arrest?
Answer: Chaotic activity without recurring organized ventricular complexes.
Reason: Confirm signal quality during the brief rhythm assessment.
Source: AHA · 2025 adult advanced life support · https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-advanced-life-support

Topic: Selecting a safe approach to an undifferentiated wide rhythm
Prompt: What ventricular electrical event lasts longer when a QRS complex is wide?
Answer: Depolarization of the ventricles.
Reason: The ventricles are not fully activated within the usual time.
Source: AHA · 2025 adult advanced life support · https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-advanced-life-support

Topic: Selecting a safe approach to an undifferentiated wide rhythm
Prompt: A ventricular focus activates the myocardium partly by slower cell-to-cell conduction. What change in QRS duration is expected?
Answer: QRS widening.

Topic: Selecting a safe approach to an undifferentiated wide rhythm
Prompt: An atrial rhythm conducts with preexisting complete bundle branch block and has a wide QRS. Does the width alone prove that the atrial rhythm has become VT?
