Reason: The trial selected for these EGFR alterations. Histology and stage alone do not establish the same treatment benefit.
Source: Tsuboi et al. · Overall survival in ADAURA · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2304594

Topic: Independent defenses against error
Prompt: Why does checking a dose against an independent source add protection?
Answer: The second check need not reproduce the first error.
Reason: Two displays fed by the same faulty entry can agree while both are wrong.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Systems approach · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/systems-approach

Topic: Independent defenses against error
Prompt: A vial is picked from the wrong bin, but a bedside scan compares its actual code with the patient-specific order and stops administration. Which layer intercepted the error?
Answer: The independent product-to-order check.
Reason: The storage defense failed but the administration defense still worked.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Systems approach · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/systems-approach

Topic: Independent defenses against error
Prompt: Two screens show the same incorrect concentration copied from one erroneous order field. Why did agreement between the screens fail to protect the patient?
Answer: The checks shared the same source of error.
Reason: Agreement was not independent verification.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Systems approach · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/systems-approach

Topic: Independent defenses against error
Prompt: What distinguishes a latent hazard from the clinician's active selection error?
Answer: A latent hazard is an underlying system condition that makes failure more likely.
Reason: An active failure is the action or omission at the point of work.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Systems approach · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/systems-approach

Topic: Independent defenses against error
Prompt: Look-alike vials are still stored together. A nurse selects the wrong one but an independent identity scan stops it. Which latent hazard remains after the interception?
Answer: Confusable shared storage.
Reason: The scanner prevented exposure on this occasion without removing the upstream hazard.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Systems approach · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/systems-approach

Topic: Independent defenses against error
Prompt: What should investigators trace when a verified dose later appears incorrectly in the administration record?
Answer: Each interface or manual step between verification and administration.
Reason: A downstream step can undo an upstream safeguard.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Systems approach · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/systems-approach

Topic: Independent defenses against error
Prompt: The verified value transfers electronically without transcription, but the receiving screen labels milligrams as micrograms. Which process now needs redesign and end-to-end testing?
Answer: The unit mapping at the receiving interface.
Reason: Another check of the prescriber's arithmetic would miss the demonstrated failure.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Systems approach · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/systems-approach

Topic: Classifying safety events and reporting signals
Prompt: What extra judgment is needed after identifying an adverse event to call it preventable?
Answer: Whether an accepted safeguard or appropriate care could reasonably have prevented the injury.
Reason: Harm alone does not establish an error.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Responding to patient safety events · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/responding-patient-safety-events

Topic: Classifying safety events and reporting signals
Prompt: An indicated drug is given correctly to a patient without a known contraindication. An unpredictable first allergic reaction causes injury. How should preventability be judged from these facts?
Answer: This is an adverse event without demonstrated preventable error.
Reason: A reaction can occur despite appropriate care.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Responding to patient safety events · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/responding-patient-safety-events

Topic: Classifying safety events and reporting signals
Prompt: Another patient receives the same drug despite a clear prior anaphylaxis warning and develops anaphylaxis. Which finding supports preventability?
Answer: The known contraindication was available before administration.
Reason: Acting on that information could have avoided this exposure.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Responding to patient safety events · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/responding-patient-safety-events

Topic: Classifying safety events and reporting signals
Prompt: What fact separates a near miss from a preventable adverse event in an intercepted medication order?
Answer: Whether the error caused patient injury.
Reason: Trace what happened to the patient before classifying the outcome.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Responding to patient safety events · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/responding-patient-safety-events

Topic: Classifying safety events and reporting signals
Prompt: An order contradicts a documented severe allergy. Pharmacy catches it before any drug is dispensed. What type of event should the team report?
Answer: A near miss.
Reason: The error was intercepted before exposure.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Responding to patient safety events · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/responding-patient-safety-events

Topic: Classifying safety events and reporting signals
Prompt: A separate allergy warning is overlooked and the administered drug causes a documented allergic injury. How should this event be classified?
Answer: A preventable adverse drug event.
Reason: A usable warning existed and the patient was harmed.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Responding to patient safety events · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/responding-patient-safety-events

Topic: Classifying safety events and reporting signals
Prompt: During a walk-through, staff find two look-alike concentrations in the same bin. No order has been selected or prepared. What should be reported?
Answer: An unsafe condition or safety hazard.
Reason: There is something to fix before a specific error occurs.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Responding to patient safety events · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/responding-patient-safety-events

Topic: Classifying safety events and reporting signals
Prompt: Before deciding whether harm was preventable, what causal distinction should a review make?
Answer: Whether the injury arose from care or from the underlying illness.
Reason: Timing alone cannot establish causation.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Responding to patient safety events · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/responding-patient-safety-events

Topic: Classifying safety events and reporting signals
Prompt: A patient is injured after a pump is programmed at ten times the ordered rate, confirmed by the device log and clinical review. What supports classifying this as preventable harm?
Answer: A verified delivery error caused the injury.
Reason: The review can investigate which defenses should have intercepted it.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Responding to patient safety events · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/responding-patient-safety-events

Topic: Classifying safety events and reporting signals
Prompt: A patient deteriorates before the planned infusion begins. Review attributes the decline to progression of the underlying disease. What does this imply about an alleged adverse event from that infusion?
Answer: The infusion did not cause this deterioration.
Reason: Evaluate the illness and other possible care issues on their own evidence.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Responding to patient safety events · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/responding-patient-safety-events

Topic: Identifying barriers to treatment access
Prompt: What question can reveal an access barrier after a patient accurately explains a medication plan?
Answer: Ask what might make obtaining or taking it difficult at home.
Reason: Correct teach-back shows understanding of the plan, not access to the treatment.
Source: AHRQ · Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit · https://www.ahrq.gov/health-literacy/improve/precautions/toolkit.html

Topic: Identifying barriers to treatment access
Prompt: A patient explains the dose correctly but leaves the pharmacy after hearing the price. What most directly prevented treatment?
Answer: The out-of-pocket cost.
Reason: More dose instruction alone would leave that barrier intact.
Source: AHRQ · Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit · https://www.ahrq.gov/health-literacy/improve/precautions/toolkit.html

Topic: Identifying barriers to treatment access
Prompt: A patient fills an affordable prescription but believes it is needed only on painful days, contrary to its scheduled use. Which problem should the clinician explore first?
Answer: The patient's understanding and beliefs about the schedule.
Reason: The medication was obtained, so purchase cost does not explain this pattern.
Source: AHRQ · Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit · https://www.ahrq.gov/health-literacy/improve/precautions/toolkit.html

Topic: Identifying barriers to treatment access
Prompt: What should a clinician clarify before interpreting missed refills as unwillingness to take treatment?
Answer: Whether the patient can actually obtain and afford it.
Reason: Ask about access in a way that permits an honest answer.
Source: AHRQ · Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit · https://www.ahrq.gov/health-literacy/improve/precautions/toolkit.html

Topic: Identifying barriers to treatment access
Prompt: A patient can pay for a medicine but has no way to reach the only dispensing pharmacy. What part of the plan needs changing?
Answer: The route of access, such as an accessible pharmacy or delivery option.
Reason: Find an option that the patient can actually use.
Source: AHRQ · Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit · https://www.ahrq.gov/health-literacy/improve/precautions/toolkit.html

Topic: Identifying barriers to treatment access
Prompt: Another patient can reach the pharmacy but the copay exceeds their food budget. What should the team address first?
Answer: Find an affordable, clinically appropriate option with the patient and pharmacist.
Reason: Travel assistance would leave the stated barrier unresolved.
Source: AHRQ · Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit · https://www.ahrq.gov/health-literacy/improve/precautions/toolkit.html

Topic: Identifying barriers to treatment access
Prompt: What outcome confirms that a medication-access intervention worked for an individual patient?
Answer: The patient actually obtains the intended treatment on a feasible plan.
Reason: An electronic order or referral alone cannot confirm access.
Source: AHRQ · Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit · https://www.ahrq.gov/health-literacy/improve/precautions/toolkit.html

Topic: Identifying barriers to treatment access
Prompt: A clinician switches to a covered medicine. The patient reports that the only local pharmacy cannot stock it before the current supply runs out. What is the next coordination task?
Answer: Arrange and confirm timely supply or an appropriate alternative.
Reason: Insurance approval solved only the price barrier.
Source: AHRQ · Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit · https://www.ahrq.gov/health-literacy/improve/precautions/toolkit.html

Topic: Responding to missed appointments
Prompt: After a missed visit, what opening question best identifies the reason without assuming the patient declined care?
Answer: Ask what made attending difficult or unnecessary from their perspective.
Reason: A missed visit alone cannot distinguish beliefs, logistics or illness.
Source: AHRQ · Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit · https://www.ahrq.gov/health-literacy/improve/precautions/toolkit.html

Topic: Responding to missed appointments
Prompt: A patient says, “I felt fine, so I didn't think follow-up mattered.” What belief should the clinician explore?
Answer: That symptoms are needed for follow-up to be worthwhile.
Reason: Explain the visit's purpose in terms relevant to the patient.
Source: AHRQ · Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit · https://www.ahrq.gov/health-literacy/improve/precautions/toolkit.html

Topic: Responding to missed appointments
Prompt: A patient understands the purpose of follow-up but cannot leave work at the assigned hour. What need does that explanation identify?
Answer: A feasible appointment time or format.
Reason: Repeating the rationale alone does not change the scheduling constraint.
Source: AHRQ · Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit · https://www.ahrq.gov/health-literacy/improve/precautions/toolkit.html

Topic: Responding to missed appointments
Prompt: What is the first communication step after learning that a patient repeatedly missed a recommended test?
Answer: Ask privately about their concerns and practical barriers.
Reason: Understand the patient's own reason before choosing an intervention.
Source: AHRQ · Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit · https://www.ahrq.gov/health-literacy/improve/precautions/toolkit.html

Topic: Responding to missed appointments
Prompt: A patient says they missed a biopsy because they fear that taking tissue will spread cancer. What should the clinician do first?
Answer: Explore the concern and explain the purpose and risks of this particular biopsy.
Reason: An additional automated reminder would not address the stated belief.
Source: AHRQ · Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit · https://www.ahrq.gov/health-literacy/improve/precautions/toolkit.html

Topic: Responding to missed appointments
Prompt: A different patient wants the biopsy but cannot use the scheduling phone menu in their preferred language. What specific service should be arranged?
Answer: Interpretation or language-accessible scheduling assistance.
Reason: Confirm that contact and scheduling actually occur.
Source: AHRQ · Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit · https://www.ahrq.gov/health-literacy/improve/precautions/toolkit.html

Topic: Responding to missed appointments
Prompt: What information determines how urgently the team should act after a missed diagnostic appointment?
Answer: The clinical risk and time sensitivity of the unresolved finding.
Reason: Routine scheduling rules alone are insufficient for a potentially serious result.
Source: ONC · SAFER Guide to Test Results Reporting and Follow-Up · https://healthit.gov/resources/2025-safer-guide-test-results-reporting-and-follow-up/ · AHRQ · TeamSTEPPS · https://www.ahrq.gov/teamstepps-program/curriculum/situation/tools/index.html

Topic: Responding to missed appointments
Prompt: A patient misses evaluation of a suspicious mass and cannot initially be reached. What should the responsible team do?
Answer: Continue timely outreach through appropriate channels and track the unresolved evaluation.
Reason: Assign ownership and document attempts so the result does not disappear from follow-up.
Source: ONC · SAFER Guide to Test Results Reporting and Follow-Up · https://healthit.gov/resources/2025-safer-guide-test-results-reporting-and-follow-up/ · AHRQ · TeamSTEPPS · https://www.ahrq.gov/teamstepps-program/curriculum/situation/tools/index.html

Topic: Responding to missed appointments
Prompt: A patient is reached, understands the potentially serious result and alternatives, has capacity, and declines the proposed visit. How should the team close today's discussion?
Answer: Document the informed decision and agree on acceptable follow-up and return precautions.
Reason: Respect the decision while leaving a clear route back to care.
Source: ONC · SAFER Guide to Test Results Reporting and Follow-Up · https://healthit.gov/resources/2025-safer-guide-test-results-reporting-and-follow-up/ · AHRQ · TeamSTEPPS · https://www.ahrq.gov/teamstepps-program/curriculum/situation/tools/index.html

Topic: Fatigue, duty schedules and patient safety
Prompt: How can sleep loss increase error during familiar work?
Answer: It impairs sustained attention and can produce lapses.
Reason: Knowing the correct procedure does not ensure it will be executed reliably while fatigued.
Source: Landrigan et al. · Intern duty schedules and serious errors · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa041406 · ACGME · Common program requirements · https://www.acgme.org/what-we-do/accreditation/common-program-requirements/

Topic: Fatigue, duty schedules and patient safety
Prompt: After prolonged wakefulness a clinician repeatedly loses their place during familiar checks but can explain each step correctly. Which contributor best fits?
Answer: Fatigue-related lapses of attention.
Reason: The observed execution problem differs from lack of knowledge.
Source: Landrigan et al. · Intern duty schedules and serious errors · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa041406 · ACGME · Common program requirements · https://www.acgme.org/what-we-do/accreditation/common-program-requirements/

Topic: Fatigue, duty schedules and patient safety
Prompt: A rested clinician consistently selects the wrong interval because they learned an outdated rule and can explain that incorrect rule. Which contributor better fits?
Answer: A knowledge gap.
Reason: The evidence supports correcting the rule and its decision support.
Source: Landrigan et al. · Intern duty schedules and serious errors · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa041406 · ACGME · Common program requirements · https://www.acgme.org/what-we-do/accreditation/common-program-requirements/

Topic: Fatigue, duty schedules and patient safety
Prompt: What should a clinician do when fatigue is interfering with safe patient care?
Answer: Notify the responsible supervisor and obtain safe coverage or assistance.
Reason: Fitness for duty and continuity both need attention.
Source: Landrigan et al. · Intern duty schedules and serious errors · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa041406 · ACGME · Common program requirements · https://www.acgme.org/what-we-do/accreditation/common-program-requirements/

Topic: Fatigue, duty schedules and patient safety
Prompt: A trainee is repeatedly nodding off while reconciling routine orders. A qualified covering clinician is available. What should happen before the trainee steps away?
Answer: An explicit handoff of active tasks to the covering clinician.
Reason: Quietly leaving a queue creates a new hazard.
Source: Landrigan et al. · Intern duty schedules and serious errors · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa041406 · ACGME · Common program requirements · https://www.acgme.org/what-we-do/accreditation/common-program-requirements/

Topic: Fatigue, duty schedules and patient safety
Prompt: A fatigued clinician is caring for an unstable patient and the relief team is still en route. What is the immediate response?
Answer: Call for bedside assistance now and maintain coverage until responsibility is accepted.
Reason: The patient cannot safely be left while awaiting routine relief.
Source: Landrigan et al. · Intern duty schedules and serious errors · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa041406 · ACGME · Common program requirements · https://www.acgme.org/what-we-do/accreditation/common-program-requirements/

Topic: Fatigue, duty schedules and patient safety
Prompt: Which denominator permits comparison of serious error rates between schedules with different observation time and census?
Answer: Patient-days under each schedule.
Reason: Use the same definition and ascertainment of errors.
Source: Landrigan et al. · Intern ICU schedules · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa041406 · ROSTERS pediatric ICU study · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1900669

Topic: Fatigue, duty schedules and patient safety
Prompt: Read the intern ICU study. How many fewer serious errors per 1,000 patient-days occurred under the intervention schedule?
Answer: 35.9 fewer.
Reason: The rates were 136.0 and 100.1 per 1,000 patient-days. This compares the studied schedules.
Source: Landrigan et al. · Intern ICU schedules · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa041406 · ROSTERS pediatric ICU study · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1900669

Topic: Fatigue, duty schedules and patient safety
Prompt: In the later pediatric ICU trial, serious resident errors were higher under the schedule without 24-hour shifts. What concurrent staffing difference complicates attribution to shift length alone?
Answer: Residents cared for more patients per resident under the intervention schedule.
Reason: Workload and implementation differed. The studies evaluated schedule packages in different settings.
Source: Landrigan et al. · Intern ICU schedules · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa041406 · ROSTERS pediatric ICU study · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1900669

Topic: Recognizing cognitive contributors to diagnosis
Prompt: What distinguishes a clinical knowledge deficit from premature closure?
Answer: Lack of the necessary clinical knowledge versus stopping consideration of alternatives too early.
Reason: The distinction helps target a corrective intervention.
Source: AHRQ · Measure Dx · https://www.ahrq.gov/sites/default/files/publications2/files/MeasureDx-guide.pdf

Topic: Recognizing cognitive contributors to diagnosis
Prompt: A clinician misses an interaction because they do not know the two drugs interact and no information source is consulted. Which deficit is demonstrated?
Answer: Missing clinical knowledge about the interaction.
Reason: Provide access to reliable information and build a check where the decision is made.
Source: AHRQ · Measure Dx · https://www.ahrq.gov/sites/default/files/publications2/files/MeasureDx-guide.pdf

Topic: Recognizing cognitive contributors to diagnosis
Prompt: A clinician accurately describes a dangerous alternative but dismisses supporting findings once the first diagnosis is proposed. Which reasoning fault is more likely?
Answer: Premature closure or anchoring.
Reason: The alternative was known, but conflicting evidence was not integrated.
Source: AHRQ · Measure Dx · https://www.ahrq.gov/sites/default/files/publications2/files/MeasureDx-guide.pdf

Topic: Recognizing cognitive contributors to diagnosis
Prompt: What is availability bias in diagnosis?
Answer: Overweighting a diagnosis because an example comes readily to mind.
Reason: A recent vivid event can distort the estimate of likelihood.
Source: AHRQ · Measure Dx · https://www.ahrq.gov/sites/default/files/publications2/files/MeasureDx-guide.pdf

Topic: Recognizing cognitive contributors to diagnosis
Prompt: A chart labels symptoms as anxiety. New focal weakness appears, but the clinician keeps the label without reassessment. Which bias does this illustrate?
Answer: Anchoring on the earlier explanation.
Reason: A new objective finding warrants reconsideration.
Source: AHRQ · Measure Dx · https://www.ahrq.gov/sites/default/files/publications2/files/MeasureDx-guide.pdf

Topic: Recognizing cognitive contributors to diagnosis
Prompt: An initial working diagnosis is revised when a new test specifically supports a competing explanation. Is revision itself evidence of anchoring?
Answer: No. It is updating the assessment from new evidence.
Reason: Anchoring is undue persistence despite information that should change the judgment.
Source: AHRQ · Measure Dx · https://www.ahrq.gov/sites/default/files/publications2/files/MeasureDx-guide.pdf

Topic: Recognizing cognitive contributors to diagnosis
Prompt: What should trigger a diagnostic pause during an otherwise familiar clinical pathway?
Answer: A new finding that the working diagnosis cannot adequately explain.
Reason: Reassess the patient, the reliability of the evidence and competing explanations.
Source: AHRQ · Measure Dx · https://www.ahrq.gov/sites/default/files/publications2/files/MeasureDx-guide.pdf

Topic: Recognizing cognitive contributors to diagnosis
Prompt: An unexpected result initially conflicts with the patient's course. The laboratory confirms it belongs to a different patient. What should determine the next diagnostic decision?
Answer: The patient's own verified findings and a valid specimen or result.
Reason: Correct and communicate the misassignment before treating it as evidence about this patient.
Source: AHRQ · Measure Dx · https://www.ahrq.gov/sites/default/files/publications2/files/MeasureDx-guide.pdf

Topic: Recognizing differences in risk framing
Prompt: What must be held constant to identify a framing effect when comparing survival and mortality descriptions?
Answer: The underlying outcome probability, population and time horizon.
Reason: Only the presentation should change.
Source: NICE · Shared decision making, communicating risks, benefits and consequences · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng197/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Recognizing differences in risk framing
Prompt: Why put benefit and harm estimates on the same time horizon and denominator during counseling?
Answer: To make the absolute outcomes directly comparable.
Reason: Different denominators or durations can make equivalent risks appear different.
Source: NICE · Shared decision making, communicating risks, benefits and consequences · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng197/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Recognizing differences in risk framing
Prompt: A patient hears “risk falls by half” for one treatment and asks how many events per 100 people it prevents. What additional quantity is needed?
Answer: The untreated risk over the same time horizon in a comparable population.
Reason: A relative reduction alone cannot establish the absolute difference.
Source: NICE · Shared decision making, communicating risks, benefits and consequences · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng197/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Recognizing differences in risk framing
Prompt: What should a clinician verify before saying two numerical presentations give equivalent information?
Answer: That they describe the same endpoint in comparable people over the same period.
Reason: Complementary wording alone does not guarantee equivalence.
Source: NICE · Shared decision making, communicating risks, benefits and consequences · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng197/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Recognizing differences in risk framing
Prompt: One leaflet gives one-year risk of any bleeding and another gives one-year risk of bleeding requiring hospitalization. What must be aligned before comparing their figures?
Answer: The outcome definition.
Reason: An identical follow-up duration cannot make a broader endpoint interchangeable with a narrower one.
Source: NICE · Shared decision making, communicating risks, benefits and consequences · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng197/chapter/Recommendations

Topic: Choosing safeguards that prevent an unsafe action
Prompt: Two routes use physically incompatible connectors. What makes this a forcing function for that mismatch?
Answer: The wrong connection cannot be completed through the intended interface.
Reason: The protection does not rely on noticing or remembering a warning.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Systems approach · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/systems-approach

Topic: Choosing safeguards that prevent an unsafe action
Prompt: A redesigned connector has a prominent colored stripe but still fits both ports. What type of defense was added?
Answer: A visual cue.
Reason: The user can still make the incorrect connection.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Systems approach · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/systems-approach

Topic: Choosing safeguards that prevent an unsafe action
Prompt: What question tests whether a proposed redesign prevents the specified error?
Answer: Can the unsafe action still be completed through the redesigned pathway?
Reason: Check the real workflow, including common workarounds.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Systems approach · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/systems-approach

Topic: Choosing safeguards that prevent an unsafe action
Prompt: A prescription field should accept only a weight in kilograms. A different unit can still be saved if the user ignores a banner. What stronger input design targets that error?
Answer: Constrain the permitted unit and require a verified kilogram value.
Reason: A banner alone permits the unsafe entry to continue.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Systems approach · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/systems-approach

Topic: Choosing safeguards that prevent an unsafe action
Prompt: How should a unit evaluate a hard stop in addition to checking its effect on the target error?
Answer: Measure unintended consequences, including delays and workarounds.
Reason: A barrier can shift risk elsewhere in the care pathway.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Systems approach · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/systems-approach

Topic: Applying high reliability principles
Prompt: What is preoccupation with failure in a high-reliability organization?
Answer: Attention to weak warning signals and small failures even during apparently successful operations.
Reason: Near misses can reveal where a defense is fragile.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · High reliability · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/high-reliability

Topic: Applying high reliability principles
Prompt: A unit has had no harmful pump events but examines three programming near misses to learn why a final check was needed. Which principle is illustrated?
Answer: Preoccupation with failure.
Reason: Staff are investigating a weak signal before harm occurs.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · High reliability · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/high-reliability

Topic: Applying high reliability principles
Prompt: During an unfamiliar equipment failure, the team invites the respiratory therapist who knows this device to guide that part of the response. Which principle is illustrated?
Answer: Deference to expertise.
Reason: Relevant knowledge guides the task while the team coordinates patient care.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · High reliability · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/high-reliability

Topic: Applying high reliability principles
Prompt: What does reluctance to simplify mean when analyzing a recurring patient-safety event?
Answer: Look beyond the first convenient explanation and examine how the work actually occurs.
Reason: Different workflows can produce superficially similar events.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · High reliability · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/high-reliability

Topic: Applying high reliability principles
Prompt: A dashboard calls every delayed antibiotic “late nursing administration.” What timestamps would test that explanation?
Answer: Order, verification, availability at the bedside and administration times.
Reason: Locate the delay before assigning its cause.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · High reliability · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/high-reliability

Topic: Applying high reliability principles
Prompt: Review now shows orders and verification were prompt, but doses repeatedly arrived on the ward after the due time. Which interval should the team investigate first?
Answer: Distribution from pharmacy to bedside availability.
Reason: The observed sequence locates the bottleneck upstream of administration.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · High reliability · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/high-reliability

Topic: Applying high reliability principles
Prompt: What does resilience mean for a clinical team during a system disruption?
Answer: Maintaining safe care and recovering when normal processes fail.
Reason: Plans need roles, backup communication and recovery checks.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · High reliability · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/high-reliability

Topic: Applying high reliability principles
Prompt: The electronic order system fails during a busy shift. What should the lead activate to preserve continuity?
Answer: The rehearsed downtime process with explicit responsibilities and communication routes.
Reason: Reliable backup work limits competing unofficial lists.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · High reliability · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/high-reliability

Topic: Applying high reliability principles
Prompt: The system returns while paper orders are still active. Which recovery step prevents duplicate or missed treatment?
Answer: Reconcile downtime orders and actions with the restored electronic record.
Reason: System availability alone does not account for work completed offline.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · High reliability · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/high-reliability

Topic: Interpreting voluntary event reports
Prompt: Why is the number of voluntary incident reports an unreliable direct measure of the number of actual adverse events?
Answer: Detection and willingness to report vary.
Reason: A report is an observation through a particular reporting process.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Responding to patient safety events · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/responding-patient-safety-events

Topic: Interpreting voluntary event reports
Prompt: A hospital makes reporting easier and receives twice as many near-miss forms. Does this alone show that near misses became twice as frequent?
Answer: No. Easier reporting could explain the rise.
Reason: An independent surveillance measure would help distinguish the explanations.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Responding to patient safety events · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/responding-patient-safety-events

Topic: Interpreting voluntary event reports
Prompt: A separate audit consistently reviews all 500 eligible administrations and confirms 5 wrong-time events by the same definition. What proportion of audited administrations had such an event?
Reason: This denominator and case ascertainment support an estimate for the audited administrations.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Responding to patient safety events · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/responding-patient-safety-events

Topic: Interpreting voluntary event reports
Prompt: What inputs does a medication-error incidence estimate require?
Answer: Consistently identified errors and the corresponding population of opportunities or observation time.
Reason: Voluntary reports can supply leads but usually miss events.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Responding to patient safety events · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/responding-patient-safety-events

Topic: Interpreting voluntary event reports
Prompt: The ward wants examples of pump workarounds staff have encountered so it can investigate their causes. What can a reporting system contribute?
Answer: Descriptions of hazards and events to investigate.
Reason: For learning about mechanisms, a report can be valuable even without a population denominator.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Responding to patient safety events · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/responding-patient-safety-events

Topic: Interpreting voluntary event reports
Prompt: What additional evidence helps distinguish safer care from changed reporting behavior?
Answer: Independent measurements of harm or error using comparable surveillance and denominators.
Reason: Reporting volume alone cannot distinguish the two.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Responding to patient safety events · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/responding-patient-safety-events

Topic: Recognizing injury during a pleural procedure
Prompt: Why does ultrasound assessment before elective pleural fluid aspiration include identifying the diaphragm?
Answer: To distinguish the pleural target from underlying abdominal organs.
Reason: The target and diaphragm may move with position and respiration.
Source: British Thoracic Society · Clinical Statement on pleural procedures · https://thorax.bmj.com/content/78/Suppl_3/s43

Topic: Recognizing injury during a pleural procedure
Prompt: After a pleural aspiration a patient becomes dyspneic and imaging shows new pleural air. What complication should the team assess?
Answer: Procedure-associated pneumothorax.
Reason: Assess breathing and circulatory status immediately and manage according to clinical severity.
Source: British Thoracic Society · Clinical Statement on pleural procedures · https://thorax.bmj.com/content/78/Suppl_3/s43

Topic: Recognizing injury during a pleural procedure
Prompt: After a low left-sided attempted pleural aspiration, a different patient develops left upper abdominal pain, peritoneal signs and falling hemoglobin. Which adjacent organ injury is particularly concerning?
Answer: Splenic injury with bleeding.
Reason: The spleen lies below the left hemidiaphragm. This deterioration needs urgent assessment.
Source: British Thoracic Society · Clinical Statement on pleural procedures · https://thorax.bmj.com/content/78/Suppl_3/s43

Topic: Recognizing injury during a pleural procedure
Prompt: Before a nonemergency pleural aspiration, when should the target be confirmed with ultrasound?
Answer: With the patient in the procedural position immediately before the procedure.
Reason: A remote mark can become misleading after movement.
Source: British Thoracic Society · Clinical Statement on pleural procedures · https://thorax.bmj.com/content/78/Suppl_3/s43

Topic: Recognizing injury during a pleural procedure
Prompt: A recent chest film suggests a sizable effusion, but bedside ultrasound finds no safe accessible pocket. What should the operator do?
Answer: Defer that attempt and seek an alternative plan or expert imaging.
Reason: A film alone cannot justify a blind attempt at an unsafe site.
Source: British Thoracic Society · Clinical Statement on pleural procedures · https://thorax.bmj.com/content/78/Suppl_3/s43

Topic: Recognizing injury during a pleural procedure
Prompt: A safe pocket was marked while the patient sat upright. The patient must now lie on their side. What should happen before proceeding?
Answer: Repeat ultrasound localization in the new position.
Reason: The fluid and nearby organs may have shifted relative to the skin mark.
Source: British Thoracic Society · Clinical Statement on pleural procedures · https://thorax.bmj.com/content/78/Suppl_3/s43

Topic: Recognizing injury during a pleural procedure
Prompt: What should guide the urgency of review when a patient develops symptoms after a pleural procedure?
Answer: The new symptoms, trajectory and physiologic stability.
Reason: Reassess the patient and consider complications related to the procedure.
Source: British Thoracic Society · Clinical Statement on pleural procedures · https://thorax.bmj.com/content/78/Suppl_3/s43

Topic: Recognizing injury during a pleural procedure
Prompt: A patient has mild improving puncture-site soreness, normal breathing and stable vital signs after uncomplicated aspiration. What follow-up is appropriate?
Answer: Continue clinical observation and explain when to report worsening symptoms.
Reason: Mild improving local discomfort has a different urgency from deterioration.
Source: British Thoracic Society · Clinical Statement on pleural procedures · https://thorax.bmj.com/content/78/Suppl_3/s43

Topic: Recognizing injury during a pleural procedure
Prompt: Another patient develops worsening pain, tachycardia, hypotension and falling hemoglobin after pleural sampling. What action takes priority over routine incident documentation?
Answer: Urgent stabilization and assessment for procedure-related hemorrhage with appropriate specialist support.
Reason: Reporting follows immediate care of the injured patient.
Source: British Thoracic Society · Clinical Statement on pleural procedures · https://thorax.bmj.com/content/78/Suppl_3/s43

Topic: Checking the anesthesia monitoring pathway
Prompt: What process does the ongoing exhaled carbon dioxide waveform monitor during general anesthesia?
Answer: Ventilation and delivery of exhaled gas to the sensor.
Reason: It complements oxygenation monitoring.

Topic: Checking the anesthesia monitoring pathway
Prompt: In an anesthetized patient on supplemental oxygen, carbon dioxide waveforms abruptly disappear while pulse oximetry still reads 99%. Which problem needs immediate evaluation?
Answer: Loss of effective ventilation, airway continuity or the monitoring signal.

Topic: Checking the anesthesia monitoring pathway
Prompt: A second patient has a consistent exhaled carbon dioxide waveform but a confirmed falling arterial oxygen saturation. Which physiologic variable is deteriorating?
Answer: Oxygenation.
Reason: Detection of exhaled carbon dioxide alone does not guarantee satisfactory arterial oxygenation.
Source: ASA · Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring · https://www.asahq.org/standards-and-practice-parameters/standards-for-basic-anesthetic-monitoring · WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/patient-safety/9789241598590-eng.pdf

Topic: Checking the anesthesia monitoring pathway
Prompt: When should the anesthesia safety check confirm that a functioning pulse oximeter is on the patient?
Answer: Before induction of anesthesia.
Reason: The sign-in also reviews relevant allergies and airway risks.
Source: ASA · Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring · https://www.asahq.org/standards-and-practice-parameters/standards-for-basic-anesthetic-monitoring · WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/patient-safety/9789241598590-eng.pdf

Topic: Checking the anesthesia monitoring pathway
Prompt: The elective team is ready, but the pulse oximeter has no usable signal and nobody has verified a working replacement. What should happen before induction?
Answer: Pause and establish reliable oxygenation monitoring.
Reason: A checked box cannot substitute for an actual patient signal.
Source: ASA · Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring · https://www.asahq.org/standards-and-practice-parameters/standards-for-basic-anesthetic-monitoring · WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/patient-safety/9789241598590-eng.pdf

Topic: Checking the anesthesia monitoring pathway
Prompt: A working monitor is now in place. During sign-in the patient reports a prior life-threatening reaction to an anesthetic that the chart omits. What should happen before elective induction?
Answer: Pause for anesthesia review and reconciliation of the history and plan.
Reason: Resolve the new patient-specific risk before exposing the patient.
Source: ASA · Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring · https://www.asahq.org/standards-and-practice-parameters/standards-for-basic-anesthetic-monitoring · WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/patient-safety/9789241598590-eng.pdf

Topic: Checking the anesthesia monitoring pathway
Prompt: What does a failed pre-use anesthesia workstation check require before an elective case?
Answer: Resolution of the defect or a verified safe alternative.
Reason: The safety check is a decision point.
Source: ASA · Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring · https://www.asahq.org/standards-and-practice-parameters/standards-for-basic-anesthetic-monitoring · WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/patient-safety/9789241598590-eng.pdf

Topic: Checking the anesthesia monitoring pathway
Prompt: The only anesthesia workstation fails its pre-use check for reliable ventilation and no verified backup is available. How should the elective induction proceed?
Answer: Defer induction until safe equipment and support are available.
Reason: Scheduling pressure does not correct a failed ventilation system.
Source: ASA · Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring · https://www.asahq.org/standards-and-practice-parameters/standards-for-basic-anesthetic-monitoring · WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/patient-safety/9789241598590-eng.pdf

Topic: Checking the anesthesia monitoring pathway
Prompt: A different fully checked workstation is brought in and the team verifies readiness. What should happen to the original defective workstation?
Answer: Remove it from service and refer it for investigation and repair.
Reason: Substitution protects this patient, but the defective unit remains a risk to others.
Source: ASA · Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring · https://www.asahq.org/standards-and-practice-parameters/standards-for-basic-anesthetic-monitoring · WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/patient-safety/9789241598590-eng.pdf

Topic: Interpreting and following up diagnostic studies

Answer: Could collection, identification, timing or interpretation have affected the result?

Topic: Interpreting and following up diagnostic studies
Prompt: A stable patient has a very high potassium reported from a visibly hemolyzed specimen. Which preanalytic effect can falsely elevate that value?
Answer: Potassium released from damaged blood cells.
Reason: Promptly assess the patient and obtain a valid measurement. A spurious result cannot be assumed in an unstable patient.
Source: AHRQ · Measure Dx · https://www.ahrq.gov/sites/default/files/publications2/files/MeasureDx-guide.pdf · AHRQ PSNet · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/web-mm/fatal-twist-pseudohyperkalemia

Topic: Interpreting and following up diagnostic studies
Prompt: A second high potassium is obtained promptly on a nonhemolyzed specimen, with compatible ECG changes. What does that do to the hemolysis explanation?
Answer: It makes isolated specimen artifact insufficient to explain the abnormality.

Topic: Interpreting and following up diagnostic studies
Prompt: Why does a technically nondiagnostic test differ from a negative test?
Answer: It did not adequately assess the target finding.

Topic: Interpreting and following up diagnostic studies
Prompt: Ultrasound for suspected venous thrombosis cannot visualize the symptomatic segment. Can the report establish absence of thrombosis in that segment?
Answer: No. The symptomatic segment was not assessed.

Topic: Interpreting and following up diagnostic studies
Prompt: A repeat high-quality study now finds that the symptomatic proximal vein does not compress and contains thrombus. How should the earlier unvisualized segment affect interpretation?
Answer: It does not contradict the positive repeat study.

Topic: Interpreting and following up diagnostic studies
Prompt: What should a responsible team determine when a final radiology interpretation differs from the preliminary reading?
Answer: Whether the change affects the patient's current care or follow-up.

Topic: Interpreting and following up diagnostic studies
Prompt: A discharged patient was told a film was normal. The final read identifies a fracture requiring prompt reassessment. What must the responsible service ensure?
Answer: Direct patient contact and a timely plan for reevaluation and treatment.

Topic: Interpreting and following up diagnostic studies
Prompt: A radiologist corrects an old comparison date but confirms the final diagnosis and follow-up recommendation are unchanged. What should determine the urgency of outreach?
Answer: Whether the correction changes care or information previously communicated.

Topic: Prospective and retrospective error analysis
Prompt: What distinguishes retrospective systems analysis from prospective hazard analysis?
Answer: Retrospective analysis reconstructs an actual event.
Reason: The case can be a near miss or an event that caused harm.
Source: IHI/NPSF · RCA² · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/rca2-improving-root-cause-analyses-and-actions-prevent-harm

Topic: Prospective and retrospective error analysis
Prompt: A unit wants to learn how a specific wrong-dose order passed two checks yesterday. Which approach fits?
Answer: Reconstruct the event and its contributing system conditions through a retrospective review.
Reason: Examine the sequence, people, information and safeguards as they functioned at the time.
Source: IHI/NPSF · RCA² · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/rca2-improving-root-cause-analyses-and-actions-prevent-harm

Topic: Prospective and retrospective error analysis
Prompt: A unit has never used its proposed dispensing pathway. It wants to find likely failure points before rollout. Which approach now fits?
Answer: Prospective failure modes and effects analysis.
Reason: There is no observed event sequence to reconstruct.
Source: IHI/NPSF · RCA² · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/rca2-improving-root-cause-analyses-and-actions-prevent-harm

Topic: Prospective and retrospective error analysis
Prompt: Why should an event reviewer ask what information was available at the time of a decision?
Answer: To avoid hindsight bias and identify the conditions under which the decision was made.
Reason: The eventual diagnosis may not have been evident to the original team.
Source: IHI/NPSF · RCA² · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/rca2-improving-root-cause-analyses-and-actions-prevent-harm

Topic: Prospective and retrospective error analysis
Prompt: An investigator writes “the nurse should have known” without examining the screen used at the time. Which evidence is missing?
Answer: What the clinician could actually see and how the workflow presented it.
Reason: An outcome does not establish the cause of the error.
Source: IHI/NPSF · RCA² · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/rca2-improving-root-cause-analyses-and-actions-prevent-harm

Topic: Prospective and retrospective error analysis
Prompt: A reconstruction shows critical units were hidden on every affected screen and two users independently misread the value. What can reasonably be concluded?
Answer: The display is a supported contributing hazard to address and test.
Reason: Evidence for this mechanism does not justify declaring it the only cause.
Source: IHI/NPSF · RCA² · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/rca2-improving-root-cause-analyses-and-actions-prevent-harm

Topic: Prospective and retrospective error analysis
Prompt: What makes an action plan from an event review testable?
Answer: A specific change, a responsible owner and a measure with a review date.
Reason: A completed report by itself changes no patient care.
Source: IHI/NPSF · RCA² · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/rca2-improving-root-cause-analyses-and-actions-prevent-harm

Topic: Prospective and retrospective error analysis
Prompt: A review led to a redesign of a hazardous ordering screen. What evidence is still needed before calling the action effective?
Answer: Postimplementation measurement of the target failure and possible unintended consequences.
Reason: Implementation is a milestone. It does not establish prevention.
Source: IHI/NPSF · RCA² · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/rca2-improving-root-cause-analyses-and-actions-prevent-harm

Topic: Prospective and retrospective error analysis
Prompt: A new referral platform will go live next month. The team maps where urgent referrals could be lost and what each loss would cause. Which method is being used?
Answer: Failure modes and effects analysis.
Reason: The team anticipates failures in a proposed process.

Topic: Prospective and retrospective error analysis
Prompt: A patient was already harmed after a referral disappeared. The team reconstructs that patient's timestamps and interviews the involved staff. Which method is illustrated?
Answer: A retrospective event analysis.
Reason: The subject is an actual pathway failure even if its lessons later inform prospective analysis.

Topic: Prospective and retrospective error analysis
Prompt: What should lead a team to prioritize a failure mode identified before rollout?
Answer: Its potential severity, likelihood and the ability of existing controls to detect or prevent it.
Reason: Use local evidence and judgment when ranking hazards.
Source: IHI · Failure Modes and Effects Analysis Tool · https://www.ihi.org/library/tools/failure-modes-and-effects-analysis-fmea-tool

Topic: Prospective and retrospective error analysis
Prompt: A pilot blocks the highest-priority mismatch, but staff begin using a free-text route that bypasses the check. What should happen before wider rollout?
Answer: Analyze the workaround and retest the revised workflow.
Reason: The formal screen can succeed while the end-to-end risk persists.

Topic: Learning from morbidity and mortality review
Prompt: What is the learning purpose of a systems-oriented morbidity and mortality conference?
Answer: Understand a case's contributing factors and identify opportunities for safer care.
Reason: It can also clarify why an adverse outcome occurred despite appropriate management.

Topic: Learning from morbidity and mortality review
Prompt: A case presentation ends with “the result was missed.” What question would make the discussion actionable?
Answer: How was the result routed, received, acknowledged and acted on?
Reason: This identifies specific steps and defenses that can be examined.

Topic: Learning from morbidity and mortality review
Prompt: A patient dies despite timely recognition and appropriate treatment of severe illness. Does selection for a mortality conference establish preventable error?
Answer: No. A poor outcome alone cannot establish preventability.
Reason: The conference reviews evidence before judging causation and preventability.
Source: AHRQ · Learning From Defects Through Sensemaking · https://www.ahrq.gov/hai/tools/surgery/modules/implementation/learn-from-defects-fac-notes.html

Topic: Learning from morbidity and mortality review
Prompt: When discussing a delayed diagnosis at conference, what timeline helps separate hindsight from a missed opportunity?
Answer: When each finding was first available to the treating team.
Reason: A later finding cannot guide a decision that preceded it.
Source: AHRQ · Learning From Defects Through Sensemaking · https://www.ahrq.gov/hai/tools/surgery/modules/implementation/learn-from-defects-fac-notes.html

Topic: Learning from morbidity and mortality review
Prompt: A conference slide faults an initial clinician for ignoring a culture that finalized the following day. What correction is needed?
Answer: Remove that later result from the information available at the initial decision.
Reason: Review separately who was responsible for acting when it finalized.

Topic: Learning from morbidity and mortality review
Prompt: Another timeline shows a critical result was available and acknowledged before discharge, but no one acted. Which specific transition needs review?
Answer: The step from acknowledgment to a clinical decision and follow-up.
Reason: Having seen a result is different from having acted on it.
Source: AHRQ · Learning From Defects Through Sensemaking · https://www.ahrq.gov/hai/tools/surgery/modules/implementation/learn-from-defects-fac-notes.html

Topic: Learning from morbidity and mortality review
Prompt: What should the conference assign before closing an agreed safety action?
Answer: An owner, a due date and a plan to evaluate its effect.
Reason: Return the findings to the clinical team.
Source: AHRQ · Learning From Defects Through Sensemaking · https://www.ahrq.gov/hai/tools/surgery/modules/implementation/learn-from-defects-fac-notes.html

Topic: Learning from morbidity and mortality review
Prompt: A conference recommends “improve follow-up” after a missed pathology result. What concrete action could a service owner test?
Answer: Assign pending results to a named queue with an overdue escalation and audit timely action.
Reason: This changes how responsibility and failure detection work.

Topic: Learning from morbidity and mortality review
Prompt: An audit now finds every discharge checklist signed, but the same fraction of critical results still lack timely action. What does the audit establish?
Answer: Checklist completion improved without demonstrated improvement in the target outcome.
Reason: Reexamine the mechanism linking a signature to actual follow-up.

Topic: Raising an unresolved concern
Prompt: What does psychological safety allow a team member to do?
Answer: Raise a question, uncertainty or safety concern without fear of humiliation or retaliation.

Topic: Raising an unresolved concern
Prompt: A student questions a mismatched identifier. The attending thanks them, pauses and checks it with the team. What feature encourages future speaking up?

Topic: Raising an unresolved concern

Topic: Raising an unresolved concern

Answer: State the concrete concern, its clinical risk and the response needed.
Reason: Give the recipient a clear opportunity to check and act.
Source: AHRQ · TeamSTEPPS curriculum · https://www.ahrq.gov/teamstepps-program/curriculum/team/teach/two-day.html

Topic: Raising an unresolved concern

Topic: Raising an unresolved concern

Topic: Raising an unresolved concern

Topic: Coordinating a response across professions

Topic: Assigning responsibility between clinical teams

Topic: CARS · Humanities · Reviving a dance
Prompt:
At the first rehearsal of a dance that had gone unperformed for thirty years, two dancers reached the far corner of the stage on different feet. The video from the original production was quite clear. In it the leading dancer arrived on her left. The rehearsal director let the difference pass. Ten minutes later he stopped the music because the following dancer had looked up a fraction too soon. An observer might reasonably have wondered how the director could be so generous about a whole step and so exacting about a glance.

The director later offered an explanation. In that passage the follower was to change direction only after noticing that the leader had turned. If she lifted her eyes early, she appeared to know what was coming. Her subsequent turn would then look like obedience to a count. When she looked up later, the same turn could look like a discovery. As for the foot, the new leader had a longer stride than the original one. Insisting on the left would have made him shorten the last step so conspicuously that the audience might have taken the adjustment for a hesitation.

It would be easy to say that the director preserved the spirit of the dance by departing from its letter. But this formula is too hospitable. Almost any departure can find lodging in a word as spacious as spirit. The delayed glance was a small, observable requirement, as much a part of the letter as the foot in the recording. What the director supplied was a reason for insisting on one visible detail while allowing another to vary. That reason could be challenged. Someone might watch both versions and find that the earlier glance made no perceptible difference, or that an arrival on the right turned the leader's shoulders away from the follower and made the encounter unreadable.

A former member of the company objected that the glance had never been discussed when the dance was new. This is important testimony about what the original dancers were told. It is less decisive about what their performances accomplished. Two dancers who have worked together for years may arrive at a timing neither has ever needed to name. Conversely, a director who speaks at length about discovery may be unable to produce anything onstage beyond two people turning on cue. An explanation acquires no authority merely by being eloquent, any more than it loses all authority because it came late.

A rehearsal is unusually well equipped to settle the narrower dispute. The dancers can alter the glance while leaving the approach substantially intact. They can also let the leader arrive on either foot and ask watchers what, if anything, becomes harder to see. Such trials will not retrieve everything an audience saw thirty years ago. They can establish whether the director's distinctions do any work in the production being made today. That is a modest claim for a revival. It is also more demanding than tracing a sequence of footprints.

Which claim best captures the author’s position on reviving the dance?
Choices:
Every observable difference from the recording requires the same justification.
A choice about which details to preserve should be answerable to what spectators can perceive.
Original performers alone can distinguish a choreographic requirement from an accident.
The most faithful revival is the one that changes the fewest audience expectations.
Answer: A choice about which details to preserve should be answerable to what spectators can perceive.
Reason: The author wants reasons for differential treatment of details and proposes testing the perceptual consequences.
