Source: British Association of Dermatologists · Lichen sclerosus guideline · https://academic.oup.com/bjd/article/178/4/839/6602656 · ISSVD Practical Guide · https://www.issvd.org/application/files/4117/5691/7613/LichenSclerosusISSVDPracticalGuide.pdf

Topic: Evaluating recent sexual exposure
Prompt: Within what interval should HIV nPEP ordinarily begin after a substantial-risk sexual exposure?
Answer: As soon as possible, within 72 hours.
Reason: CDC favors initiation ideally within 24 hours. The usual course is 28 days.
Source: CDC · Nonoccupational postexposure prophylaxis recommendations, 2025 · https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/74/rr/rr7401a1.htm

Topic: Evaluating recent sexual exposure
Prompt: An adult presents 18 hours after condomless receptive anal sex with a partner known to have HIV without viral suppression. Baseline blood has been drawn but lab results are pending. What action is time-sensitive?
Answer: Offer and start indicated HIV nPEP promptly.
Reason: The first dose should not wait for pending laboratory results.
Source: CDC · Nonoccupational postexposure prophylaxis recommendations, 2025 · https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/74/rr/rr7401a1.htm

Topic: Evaluating recent sexual exposure
Prompt: The same substantial-risk exposure occurred five days ago with no subsequent exposure. What prevention plan is generally appropriate under CDC guidance?
Answer: HIV testing, follow-up and prevention counseling including assessment for PrEP.
Reason: Routine nPEP initiation is outside the recommended window. Assess other STI risks.
Source: CDC · Nonoccupational postexposure prophylaxis recommendations, 2025 · https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/74/rr/rr7401a1.htm

Topic: Localizing and assessing cervicitis
Prompt: Which factors influence the decision to treat chlamydia and gonorrhea presumptively in cervicitis?
Answer: STI risk, access to testing and the likelihood of follow-up.
Reason: Also assess for PID. Gonococcal coverage depends on individual and local risk.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/urethritis-and-cervicitis.htm

Topic: Localizing and assessing cervicitis
Prompt: A lower-risk stable adult has cervicitis without pelvic tenderness, same-day NAAT collection and reliable follow-up. Must antimicrobial treatment always start before results?
Answer: Treatment may be deferred while awaiting results.
Reason: Arrange follow-up and address the findings and identified pathogens.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/urethritis-and-cervicitis.htm

Topic: Localizing and assessing cervicitis
Prompt: A 19-year-old with mucopurulent cervicitis has a new partner with confirmed gonorrhea, no access to NAAT today and uncertain follow-up. Should treatment wait?
Answer: Give presumptive treatment covering gonorrhea and chlamydia.
Reason: The exposure and risk of loss to follow-up change the decision.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/urethritis-and-cervicitis.htm

Topic: Evaluating possible chancroid
Prompt: Why does examination alone have limited value for diagnosing chancroid in a patient with a painful genital ulcer?
Answer: Different genital infections can produce overlapping ulcer appearances.
Reason: Evaluate for syphilis and HSV even when the ulcer looks characteristic.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chancroid.htm · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/lgv.htm · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/genital-ulcers.htm

Topic: Evaluating possible chancroid
Prompt: In an outbreak, a painful typical ulcer has negative HSV lesion NAAT and properly timed negative syphilis evaluation. No H. ducreyi assay is available. What level of chancroid diagnosis can the clinical criteria support?
Answer: A probable clinical diagnosis.
Reason: Definitive confirmation needs organism-specific evidence.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chancroid.htm · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/lgv.htm · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/genital-ulcers.htm

Topic: Evaluating possible chancroid
Prompt: A second patient has the same painful ulcer, but syphilis serology was obtained only on the second day of ulceration. Why does the negative result leave early syphilis open?
Answer: Serologic reactivity may not yet have developed.
Reason: For probable chancroid, CDC specifies appropriate direct testing or serology at least 7–14 days after ulcer onset.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chancroid.htm · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/lgv.htm · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/genital-ulcers.htm

Topic: Selecting a diagnostic test for genital herpes
Prompt: Why is the presence of an active genital lesion important when choosing an HSV diagnostic test?
Answer: A lesion can be sampled directly for type-specific viral testing.
Reason: Random swabs between outbreaks have low sensitivity.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/herpes.htm

Topic: Recognizing and following gonococcal disease
Prompt: Which mucosal site requires a scheduled test of cure after treatment for uncomplicated gonorrhea under CDC guidance?
Answer: The pharynx.
Reason: Pharyngeal infection is more difficult to eradicate.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm

Topic: Recognizing and following gonococcal disease
Prompt: A nonpregnant patient completed recommended therapy for uncomplicated cervical gonorrhea, has no symptoms and reports no reexposure. What repeat testing should be scheduled routinely?
Answer: Retesting for reinfection at about three months.
Reason: An early test of cure is generally unnecessary for uncomplicated urogenital disease treated appropriately.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm

Topic: Recognizing and following gonococcal disease
Prompt: A second asymptomatic patient was treated for pharyngeal gonorrhea. When should the site be tested for cure?
Answer: At 7–14 days after initial treatment.
Reason: Retesting for reinfection is a separate later step. Early NAAT at seven days can yield false-positive results.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm

Topic: Assessing anogenital warts
Prompt: How are typical external anogenital warts usually diagnosed?
Answer: By visual inspection.
Reason: Routine HPV testing does not confirm the clinical diagnosis or guide wart management.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/anogenital-warts.htm

Topic: Assessing anogenital warts
Prompt: A patient has several classic soft pedunculated genital warts with no atypical features. What role does HPV typing have in selecting their treatment?
Answer: Routine HPV typing has no role in choosing wart treatment.
Reason: Management depends on clinical features, patient preference and available methods.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/anogenital-warts.htm

Topic: Assessing anogenital warts
Prompt: An immunocompromised patient has a wart-like lesion that bleeds, feels fixed and is ulcerated. Which diagnostic step is appropriate?
Answer: Biopsy the atypical lesion.
Reason: Histology can identify high-grade disease or invasive cancer.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/anogenital-warts.htm

Topic: Recognizing invasive chlamydial syndromes
Prompt: Which test on a symptomatic rectal site supports a diagnosis of chlamydial proctocolitis?
Answer: A rectal C. trachomatis NAAT.
Reason: Routine assays detect chlamydia but usually do not distinguish LGV genotypes.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/lgv.htm · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm

Topic: Recognizing invasive chlamydial syndromes
Prompt: A nonpregnant adult's screening rectal chlamydia NAAT is positive, with no rectal symptoms or other LGV features. What duration of doxycycline is standard for uncomplicated infection?
Answer: Seven days.
Reason: This clinically uncomplicated infection differs from an invasive proctocolitis syndrome.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/lgv.htm · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm

Topic: Recognizing invasive chlamydial syndromes
Prompt: A nonpregnant adult has bloody discharge, tenesmus, rectal ulcers and a positive rectal chlamydia NAAT. LGV genotyping is unavailable. What duration of doxycycline is recommended for symptomatic LGV?
Answer: Twenty-one days.
Reason: Do not delay treatment of the invasive syndrome for unavailable genotyping.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/lgv.htm · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm

Topic: Testing after chlamydia treatment
Prompt: What clinical question does a chlamydia test of cure answer?
Answer: Whether the infection was eradicated following treatment.
Reason: Retesting later looks for repeat infection.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm

Topic: Testing after chlamydia treatment
Prompt: A nonpregnant adult completed recommended chlamydia treatment with good adherence, symptom resolution and no reexposure. When is routine retesting appropriate?
Answer: At approximately three months.
Reason: Routine early proof of cure is unnecessary in this setting.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm

Topic: Choosing treatment setting and reassessment for PID
Prompt: What complication involving both tube and ovary is a criterion for hospitalization in PID?
Answer: A tubo-ovarian abscess.
Reason: It requires parenteral treatment and observation.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/pid.htm · CNGOF/SPILF guideline · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30880246/

Topic: Recognizing PID-associated perihepatitis
Prompt: When pleuritic right upper quadrant pain occurs with pelvic inflammatory disease, which associated condition belongs in the differential?
Answer: PID-associated perihepatitis, or Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome.
Reason: Also evaluate biliary and other urgent causes according to the presentation.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/pid.htm · Clinical series · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18617765/ · Capsular imaging findings · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12934547/

Topic: Recognizing PID-associated perihepatitis
Prompt: A young adult with confirmed cervicitis, pelvic tenderness and right upper quadrant pain has a normal gallbladder ultrasound. CT shows enhancement along the liver capsule. Which diagnosis unifies the findings?
Answer: Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome accompanying PID.
Reason: The enhancement is supportive in this clinical context.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/pid.htm · Clinical series · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18617765/ · Capsular imaging findings · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12934547/

Topic: Recognizing PID-associated perihepatitis
Prompt: A different patient with PID, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain has a dilated common bile duct and an obstructing stone. Which process needs attention in addition to PID?
Answer: Biliary obstruction from choledocholithiasis.
Reason: The stone and ductal dilation cannot be explained by isolated perihepatitis.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/pid.htm · Clinical series · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18617765/ · Capsular imaging findings · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12934547/

Topic: Recognizing and following syphilis
Prompt: Which test resolves a reactive screening treponemal immunoassay with a nonreactive RPR in the reverse algorithm?
Answer: A different treponemal assay, preferably TP-PA.
Reason: Use a test based on different antigens from the original screening assay.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/syphilis.htm

Topic: Recognizing and following syphilis
Prompt: A patient with no history of syphilis treatment has reactive EIA, negative RPR and reactive TP-PA. With no evidence of recent infection, what should be offered?
Answer: Treatment for syphilis of unknown duration or late latent syphilis.
Reason: Stage using history and exam before assigning duration.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/syphilis.htm

Topic: Recognizing and following syphilis
Prompt: In a low-risk asymptomatic patient, the initial EIA is reactive but RPR and the second treponemal assay are nonreactive. What further syphilis management is indicated if clinical probability is low?
Answer: No further evaluation or treatment is generally indicated.
Reason: The discordant initial result is most consistent with a false-positive screen in this setting.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/syphilis.htm

Topic: Evaluating urethral inflammation
Prompt: What finding on the first-void urine specimen supports urethral inflammation in symptomatic men?
Answer: Positive leukocyte esterase or elevated white cells in the sediment.
Reason: NAAT can identify gonorrhea or chlamydia.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/urethritis-and-cervicitis.htm

Topic: Evaluating urethral inflammation
Prompt: A man has dysuria but no discharge, negative first-void leukocyte esterase and no microscopic inflammation. He can return promptly. What testing still helps determine whether an STI is present?
Answer: Obtain NAAT for gonorrhea and chlamydia.
Reason: Symptoms without documented inflammation can still accompany infection. Empiric therapy is reserved for selected high-risk patients unlikely to return.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/urethritis-and-cervicitis.htm

Topic: Interpreting evidence for bacterial vaginosis
Prompt: Whose standard BV treatment continued in both groups of the StepUp partner-treatment trial?
Answer: The symptomatic woman's treatment.
Reason: The randomized difference was whether the ongoing male partner also received combined oral and topical treatment.
Source: StepUp trial · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2405404 · ACOG Clinical Practice Update, 2025 · https://doi.org/10.1097/AOG.0000000000006102

Topic: Interpreting evidence for bacterial vaginosis
Prompt: Using the rounded 12-week proportions from StepUp, how much lower was observed BV recurrence with concurrent male-partner treatment?
Answer: About 28 percentage points.
Reason: Subtract 35% from 63%. These are observed proportions over 12 weeks, not incidence rates per person-year.
Source: StepUp trial · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2405404 · ACOG Clinical Practice Update, 2025 · https://doi.org/10.1097/AOG.0000000000006102

Topic: Interpreting evidence for bacterial vaginosis
Prompt: A clinician proposes using the same 28-point reduction to promise a benefit from a different regimen for a female partner. What limits that projection?
Answer: That partner population and regimen were not studied in StepUp.
Reason: The open-label trial enrolled women with BV in monogamous relationships with male partners. Discuss management using evidence relevant to the patient's circumstances.
Source: StepUp trial · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2405404 · ACOG Clinical Practice Update, 2025 · https://doi.org/10.1097/AOG.0000000000006102

Topic: Interpreting patient outcomes after Bartholin procedures
Prompt: Why should a patient choosing between Word catheter and marsupialization consider early recovery and recurrence separately?
Answer: They are distinct outcomes measured over different intervals.
Reason: A procedure may differ in short-term burden without a demonstrated difference in long-term recurrence.
Source: WoMan randomized trial · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27640367/

Topic: Interpreting patient outcomes after Bartholin procedures
Prompt: The WoMan trial recorded use of analgesics during the first 24 hours. Which group used analgesics less often?
Answer: The Word catheter group.
Reason: About 33% used analgesics versus 74% after marsupialization. The endpoint measures use, not pain intensity directly.
Source: WoMan randomized trial · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27640367/

Topic: Interpreting patient outcomes after Bartholin procedures
Prompt: Using the one-year recurrence results, can a patient conclude that the two procedures have equivalent recurrence risks?
Answer: No. The interval allows meaningful differences in either direction.
Reason: The relative-risk interval of 0.64–1.91 crosses 1 and spans potentially important differences.
Source: WoMan randomized trial · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27640367/

Topic: Recognizing postoperative pelvic infection
Prompt: What should persistent fever despite appropriate antibiotics for postoperative pelvic cellulitis prompt?
Answer: Reassessment for an undrained focus, another diagnosis or inadequate antimicrobial coverage.
Reason: Source control may be needed if an abscess has developed.
Source: IDSA · Imaging and microbiological evaluation of complicated intra-abdominal infection · https://www.idsociety.org/practice-guideline/intra-abdominal-infections/ · ACOG Practice Bulletin 195 · https://doi.org/10.1097/AOG.0000000000002670 · Post-hysterectomy CT findings · https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5990996/

Topic: Recognizing postoperative pelvic infection
Prompt: A stable patient receiving antibiotics for postoperative pelvic cellulitis is improving. Imaging shows inflammatory changes but no collection. What should guide continued management?
Answer: Clinical response to antimicrobial therapy and ongoing reassessment.
Reason: There is no identified fluid cavity to drain.
Source: IDSA · Imaging and microbiological evaluation of complicated intra-abdominal infection · https://www.idsociety.org/practice-guideline/intra-abdominal-infections/ · ACOG Practice Bulletin 195 · https://doi.org/10.1097/AOG.0000000000002670 · Post-hysterectomy CT findings · https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5990996/

Topic: Recognizing postoperative pelvic infection
Prompt: After apparent improvement, fever returns, focal pelvic pain worsens and CT shows a new large rim-enhancing collection. What management issue now requires urgent attention?
Answer: Evaluate for drainage of a pelvic abscess in addition to antibiotics.
Reason: Discuss source control with surgery or interventional radiology according to stability and access.
Source: IDSA · Imaging and microbiological evaluation of complicated intra-abdominal infection · https://www.idsociety.org/practice-guideline/intra-abdominal-infections/ · ACOG Practice Bulletin 195 · https://doi.org/10.1097/AOG.0000000000002670 · Post-hysterectomy CT findings · https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5990996/

Topic: Diagnosing and treating vulvovaginal candidiasis
Prompt: What turns detection of vaginal Candida into a treatment indication in an otherwise healthy patient?
Answer: Compatible vulvovaginal symptoms and signs with evidence supporting candidiasis.
Reason: Candida can colonize the vagina without causing disease.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/candidiasis.htm

Topic: Evaluating persistent vulvar dermatoses
Prompt: When itching persists during topical treatment of lichen sclerosus, which practical factors should be checked before escalating therapy?
Answer: The site, amount and frequency of application and adherence.
Reason: Also reconsider diagnosis, infection and neoplasia.
Source: British Association of Dermatologists · Lichen sclerosus guideline · https://academic.oup.com/bjd/article/178/4/839/6602656 · ISSVD Practical Guide · https://www.issvd.org/application/files/4117/5691/7613/LichenSclerosusISSVDPracticalGuide.pdf

Topic: Evaluating persistent vulvar dermatoses
Prompt: A patient with diffuse persistent itching has been applying prescribed ointment only to the inner thighs. No suspicious focal lesion is present. What should be corrected first?
Answer: Demonstrate correct application to the affected vulvar skin and arrange reassessment.
Reason: Apparent treatment failure can reflect failure to expose the affected skin to treatment.
Source: British Association of Dermatologists · Lichen sclerosus guideline · https://academic.oup.com/bjd/article/178/4/839/6602656 · ISSVD Practical Guide · https://www.issvd.org/application/files/4117/5691/7613/LichenSclerosusISSVDPracticalGuide.pdf

Topic: Evaluating persistent vulvar dermatoses
Prompt: A patient applies treatment correctly and diffuse symptoms settle, but a new ulcer persists at one site. What should follow?
Answer: Prompt specialist assessment and biopsy of the persistent ulcer.
Reason: A focal refractory lesion warrants evaluation for neoplasia.
Source: British Association of Dermatologists · Lichen sclerosus guideline · https://academic.oup.com/bjd/article/178/4/839/6602656 · ISSVD Practical Guide · https://www.issvd.org/application/files/4117/5691/7613/LichenSclerosusISSVDPracticalGuide.pdf

Topic: Evaluating recent sexual exposure
Prompt: Why can a recently exposed partner of a person with early syphilis need treatment despite a negative blood test?
Answer: Antibodies may not yet be detectable during incubation.
Reason: A negative early result cannot rule out recent infection.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/syphilis.htm

Topic: Evaluating recent sexual exposure
Prompt: A partner had sexual contact 30 days before the index patient's diagnosis of secondary syphilis. Today the partner's serology is negative. How should the partner be managed?
Answer: Treat presumptively for early syphilis.
Reason: CDC recommends presumptive treatment for exposure within 90 days even with negative serology.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/syphilis.htm

Topic: Evaluating recent sexual exposure
Prompt: A different partner's only contact was five months before the index diagnosis. Serologic results are available immediately, both tests are negative and follow-up is reliable. Is presumptive therapy needed solely for this contact?
Answer: No. Negative serology is sufficient in this circumstance.
Reason: For exposure more than 90 days earlier, presumptive treatment is recommended when results are unavailable and follow-up is uncertain.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/syphilis.htm

Topic: Localizing and assessing cervicitis
Prompt: What history is especially important before attributing recurrent cervicitis to failure of an appropriate antibiotic?
Answer: Adherence and possible reexposure to an untreated partner.
Reason: Also confirm persistent cervicitis and review the initial tests.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/urethritis-and-cervicitis.htm

Topic: Localizing and assessing cervicitis
Prompt: Cervicitis recurs after sex with an untreated partner known to have chlamydia. Which explanation should management address immediately?
Answer: Reinfection from the untreated partner.
Reason: Reevaluate and treat the patient and arrange partner management.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/urethritis-and-cervicitis.htm

Topic: Localizing and assessing cervicitis
Prompt: Cervicitis objectively persists despite adherence, partner treatment and no reexposure. GC, chlamydia, trichomoniasis and BV evaluations are negative. Which additional infectious cause merits testing?
Answer: Mycoplasma genitalium.
Reason: Consider NAAT for M. genitalium and gynecologic review for noninfectious causes.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/urethritis-and-cervicitis.htm

Topic: Evaluating possible chancroid
Prompt: When should a patient treated for chancroid generally return for early reassessment?
Answer: In three to seven days.
Reason: Symptoms often begin improving before the ulcer has fully healed.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chancroid.htm

Topic: Evaluating possible chancroid
Prompt: Several days after treatment, pain is much less and the deep genital ulcer is shrinking, although it remains open. Does incomplete closure alone establish treatment failure?
Answer: No. Larger ulcers can take more than two weeks to heal.
Reason: The early symptomatic and examination trends are favorable.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chancroid.htm

Topic: Evaluating possible chancroid
Prompt: At the planned early follow-up a different patient's ulcer has worsened despite completing treatment and avoiding reexposure. What should be reconsidered before repeating the same regimen?
Answer: The diagnosis, coinfections including HIV, and potential antimicrobial failure.
Reason: A persistently worsening ulcer needs renewed clinical and laboratory evaluation.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chancroid.htm

Topic: Selecting a diagnostic test for genital herpes
Prompt: Can successful treatment of a genital HSV outbreak eradicate latent infection?
Answer: No. Latent infection persists.
Reason: Antiviral therapy can reduce recurrences and shedding.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/herpes.htm

Topic: Selecting a diagnostic test for genital herpes
Prompt: A patient using daily suppressive therapy develops the familiar prodromal tingling preceding genital lesions. What advice applies to sexual contact during the prodrome?
Answer: Avoid sexual contact during prodromal symptoms and active lesions.
Reason: Suppressive therapy lowers risk but cannot guarantee absence of transmission.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/herpes.htm

Topic: Recognizing and following gonococcal disease
Prompt: In suspected gonococcal treatment failure, what can culture add beyond a routine diagnostic NAAT?
Answer: An isolate for antimicrobial susceptibility testing.
Reason: Interpret the finding alongside adherence, prior treatment and subsequent exposures.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm

Topic: Recognizing and following gonococcal disease
Prompt: An adult improved after gonorrhea treatment, then had sex with an untreated infected partner and has recurrent symptoms. Which possibility should guide the first reassessment?
Answer: Reinfection is likely.
Reason: Evaluate and manage the patient and partner. Many apparent failures reflect repeat exposure.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm

Topic: Recognizing and following gonococcal disease
Prompt: Five days after directly observed recommended treatment, purulent discharge has not improved and the patient reports no sexual contact. Which specimens should be sought before retreatment when failure is suspected?
Answer: Obtain cultures from relevant sites for susceptibility testing, preferably with simultaneous NAAT.
Reason: Consult an STI expert and notify public health promptly about suspected treatment failure.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/gonorrhea-adults.htm

Topic: Assessing anogenital warts
Prompt: What is the immediate target of treatment for ordinary anogenital warts?
Answer: Removal or reduction of visible warts and associated symptoms.
Reason: Local treatment may not eliminate HPV from surrounding tissue.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/anogenital-warts.htm

Topic: Assessing anogenital warts
Prompt: A small group of warts reappears two months after complete visible clearance. Does recurrence by itself prove that a new partner transmitted HPV?
Answer: No. Warts can recur after treatment of the original infection.
Reason: The timing of visible lesions cannot date acquisition.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/anogenital-warts.htm

Topic: Assessing anogenital warts
Prompt: All visible warts have been removed. Can the clinician assure a patient that transmission is now impossible?
Answer: No. HPV can be present and transmissible after lesions resolve.
Reason: Discuss prevention and routine recommended vaccination and screening.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/anogenital-warts.htm

Topic: Testing after chlamydia treatment
Prompt: Why can a chlamydia NAAT remain positive briefly after effective treatment?
Answer: It can detect residual nucleic acid from nonviable organisms.
Reason: A positive result at that time need not indicate ongoing infection.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm

Topic: Testing after chlamydia treatment
Prompt: An asymptomatic nonpregnant adult completed recommended therapy, has had no sexual contact since, and obtained a repeat NAAT eight days later. What limits interpretation of a positive result?
Answer: Testing was too early to establish persistence of viable infection.
Reason: Review adherence and exposures. CDC discourages routine NAAT within four weeks after therapy.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm

Topic: Testing after chlamydia treatment
Prompt: A different patient has a positive NAAT three months after completing treatment and reports sex with an untreated partner. Which explanation is particularly important now?
Answer: Reinfection.
Reason: Manage the repeat infection and address partner treatment.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm

Topic: Choosing treatment setting and reassessment for PID
Prompt: What change in a patient with a known tubo-ovarian abscess suggests possible rupture?
Answer: Abrupt deterioration with peritoneal signs or hemodynamic instability.
Reason: Rupture can release infected material into the peritoneal cavity.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/pid.htm · CNGOF/SPILF guideline · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30880246/

Topic: Choosing treatment setting and reassessment for PID
Prompt: A hospitalized patient with a tubo-ovarian abscess has sustained clinical improvement after initial parenteral therapy. What antimicrobial spectrum must be preserved when completing the course?
Answer: Effective anaerobic coverage as part of the full PID regimen.
Reason: CDC recommends completing 14 days of therapy with appropriate coverage when an abscess is present.
Source: CDC · STI Treatment Guidelines · https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/pid.htm · CNGOF/SPILF guideline · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30880246/

Topic: Choosing treatment setting and reassessment for PID
Prompt: A different patient being treated for a tubo-ovarian abscess suddenly becomes hypotensive with diffuse guarding. What needs to happen immediately?

Topic: CARS · Social sciences · A place at the wheel
Prompt:
When the city opened its ceramics workshop, the first places went to people who could spend a Tuesday morning outside the door. Nobody proposed this as a principle of selection. The building opened on a Tuesday, the applications were on a table inside, and when the last place was taken the clerk put the table away. Within a year, however, people had begun to speak of a long wait in the rain as evidence that a potter deserved a wheel. A consequence of the opening hours had acquired the dignity of a qualification.

The city replaced the queue with a lottery. This seemed an admirably literal answer to the complaint that a night worker could not spend the morning on the steps. It also produced a surprise. Applicants who won a place sometimes failed to appear. The old queue had seldom produced an empty wheel. At the next meeting, advocates of the queue took these vacancies as proof that waiting had measured commitment after all.

There is something in their observation. An applicant who has already arranged leave and traveled to the workshop has overcome two obstacles that might otherwise prevent attendance. But to predict that someone will arrive is a narrower achievement than to discover who most wants to learn. The night worker who cannot ask for another morning off might rearrange an entire season of evenings for a weekly class. A visitor with a free morning might happily queue for a novelty and never touch clay again. The queue obtains evidence about one occasion at the cost of making other kinds of evidence invisible.

A member of the workshop committee suggested asking successful applicants to confirm by telephone two days before the first class, and offering released places to alternates. The proposal drew an objection from each side. A defender of the queue thought that a telephone call was too slight a sacrifice to establish seriousness. A defender of the lottery objected that some people could not answer a call at work. Both objections make sense if confirmation is another examination of merit. Its proponent had something less ambitious in mind. The workshop simply needed enough information to put a person in front of each wheel. A message left in the evening, or a reply by post, would serve that purpose if it reached the clerk in time.

The distinction matters because a modest administrative improvement can quietly change the question an institution thinks it has answered. If confirmations reduce the number of empty wheels, the clerk has learned something about arranging attendance. It would be a considerable leap to announce that the workshop now admits more deserving potters. Conversely, a comparison of the pots made by the two groups would tell us little about applicants whom both procedures excluded. Before the city sets another ingenious task for people who want to use a wheel, it might decide which uncertainty it really needs to remove. Some uncertainties, including what a person will come to love after trying it, are part of the point of opening a workshop.

Which distinction is central to the author’s argument?
Choices:
A public program should select applicants whose work will attract private buyers.
Evidence that predicts attendance can have a different meaning from evidence of deserving a place.
Random allocation becomes fair only if each applicant receives an identical class schedule.
The quality of the finished pots provides the best available evidence about the former queue.
Answer: Evidence that predicts attendance can have a different meaning from evidence of deserving a place.
Reason: The author grants the queue some predictive value and questions the larger judgment people attach to it.

Topic: CARS · Humanities · Marks in the playing parts
Prompt:
When the town orchestra decided to restore its oldest set of performance parts, the librarian expected the players to welcome her proposal. She would give each musician a clean copy of the printed score and put the worn originals in the archive. The first violinist held up a page on which someone had drawn a pair of spectacles over a bar of rests. The notes themselves were easy, she said. The spectacles meant to look up and catch the conductor's cue. A clean part would tell her exactly how long to wait, provided everybody else waited exactly that long too.

In a sense the mark belonged to a performance that had already ended. The conductor who needed watching had retired, and a later player had crossed out several of his instructions. Yet the violinist used the spectacles under the new conductor. She watched for a cue and, on finding none, listened to the oboes. What she had inherited was a question about the entry, together with a convenient place to ask it. An instruction can outlive the circumstances that made it correct by teaching its next reader where to exercise judgment.

It would be easy to turn this observation into a defense of saving every pencil mark. Consider the cellist who had written the name of a street beside a change of tempo. Nobody could remember whose address it was. A volunteer proposed copying the name in red so that future players would appreciate its age. That would have given the inscription a prominence it had never enjoyed while it meant something. The street name might interest a historian, but age offered a poor reason for placing it on the stand of a working musician.

The librarian eventually offered the orchestra two services. The archive would photograph every page before it was repaired. For the playing copies she invited musicians to bring an old part to rehearsal and report which marks they had actually consulted. One violist objected that this favored the experienced. A beginner might pass over a mark precisely because nobody had explained it. The librarian agreed and asked the musicians to exchange desks for one rehearsal. Each player was to lend a stranger a part and listen to the questions it provoked.

The resulting copies were neither clean nor crowded. Some familiar instructions disappeared when their owners found that they could give no account of using them. An inconspicuous line connecting two notes survived when a novice asked whether the second should answer the first. The former owner had never named the relationship, but the two players could demonstrate it by playing the phrase in different ways. They could also disagree about which way sounded better. The archive preserved the line as a fact about an earlier page. The playing copy preserved it as an invitation to hear a difference. Those are two distinct reasons for keeping the same stroke of pencil, and a library serving both purposes can afford to be exacting about each.

Choices:
Historical evidence and a working prompt serve different purposes.
Accurate photographs preserve every feature that affects musical expression.
The best playing copy reproduces the oldest surviving performance.
A disagreement between players prevents the archive from authenticating a mark.
Answer: Historical evidence and a working prompt serve different purposes.
Reason: The archive records what was on the page. The playing copy retains markings that can inform a present decision.

The archive preserved the line as a fact about an earlier page. The playing copy preserved it as an invitation to hear a difference. Those are two distinct reasons for keeping the same stroke of pencil, and a library serving both purposes can afford to be exacting about each.

The musician who drew it cannot be identified.
Performers prefer different versions of the phrase after trying them.
In repeated desk exchanges the line causes a persistent, unintended misreading even after discussion.
A photograph in the archive shows the same line clearly.

Reason: A persistent misleading effect challenges the line's usefulness in performance. Uncertain authorship and differing preferences are compatible with its proposed role.

Topic: CARS · Humanities · A vowel at the landing
Prompt:
A lexicographer who made a dictionary of island speech once invited the ferry workers to her office to hear their voices. She played a recording of one worker telling another where to leave a coil of rope. On hearing it, the speaker insisted that the word for the covered landing had a vowel quite different from the one on the tape. To prove the point, he repeated the word slowly, several times. The dictionary now had two pronunciations from a single speaker and the problem of deciding which one to print.

An easy solution would be to treat the recording as the truth and the demonstration as a mistake. Nobody on the ferry had stopped work to consider a vowel. The recording had captured what people said when they were concerned with something else. But the demonstration, too, occurred during a recognizable activity. Asked to teach a stranger a word, the worker distinguished sounds he routinely allowed to run together when he spoke to his crew. If a visitor learned only the version on the tape, the worker might well correct her in precisely the way he had corrected himself.

One might instead print the deliberate version and call the other a matter of speed. Yet many exchanges on the ferry were slow, and the shortened vowel could be heard in those as well. What united them was a shared destination for the rope, the parcels, or the passengers. Nobody in such an exchange had to distinguish the landing from another place with a similar name. Attention to a contrast, the lexicographer suspected, mattered at least as much as the number of syllables per minute.

This suspicion was quite practical. A dictionary large enough to record every occasion on which a sound changed would be a collection of transcriptions, difficult to consult and likely to be obsolete by the time it was bound. A dictionary that printed just one sound without explanation would be convenient until the reader took it to the docks. The lexicographer printed both vowels with short descriptions of the circumstances in which she had heard each. She wanted the descriptions to be vulnerable to correction. A worker who used the longer vowel with his usual crew could now tell her exactly which part of her account needed attention.

At the launch, a teacher complained that the entry had left her pupils without an answer to a fairly simple question. Which vowel should they use at the examination? The complaint was reasonable, though the dictionary by itself could hardly settle it. A school could announce which form it expected in a formal reading, just as the ferry company could require its workers to give place names distinctly over the radio. Neither instruction would invalidate the conversation about the rope. Each would establish a reason to speak one way on a particular occasion. The dictionary's achievement was to make room for such a reason without quietly turning it into a rule for every occasion.

Which claim best expresses the author’s view of pronunciation in this dictionary?
Choices:
A speaker’s most frequent pronunciation should govern formal instruction.
A useful entry can document alternatives and specify conditions under which each was observed.
A pronunciation produced for a stranger reveals how the speaker wishes to sound in all settings.
Dictionary entries should confine themselves to recorded spontaneous speech.
Answer: A useful entry can document alternatives and specify conditions under which each was observed.
Reason: The lexicographer makes the observed variation usable by describing its contexts and leaving those descriptions open to correction.

Topic: CARS · Humanities · The train in three panels
Prompt:
A critic reviewing a comic strip about a man catching a train praised the artist for drawing an entire afternoon in three seconds. In the first panel the man was buying a ticket. In the second he stood on the platform looking at the clock. In the third he was seated by a window, holding a half-finished crossword. The critic meant that it took three seconds to look across the page. But it is doubtful whether anybody who had actually read those panels could say how much of the man's afternoon they contained.

The crossword is what makes the question interesting. We may imagine that the man began it after boarding and has been riding for some time. He may equally well have taken the paper from his coat with half the squares filled in from yesterday. A film director could withhold the same information. What is peculiar to the strip is that the reader who has reached the crossword can look back at the platform without leaving the last panel behind. The man's coat is there to be inspected. Its pockets bulge, though not in a way that settles the matter.

Some enthusiasts have suggested that the empty band between panels is where readers do the real work of imagining events. I doubt the band deserves quite so much credit. Cut the strip into separate cards and hand them over one by one. Readers will still infer that the man passed through a door to board the train, though no white band now separates two pictures. What the altered arrangement makes difficult is a different activity. To check the coat pockets a reader must ask for an earlier card, putting aside the view that gave the pockets their sudden interest.

This distinction would matter little if the artist's job were simply to reward alert readers with clues. The pockets, however, have no solution. Their usefulness lies in the brief possibility of revising what the crossword first seemed to mean. A page that permits such revision can feel unhurried even when its subject is a dash for a train. Another page can feel breathless while showing a man sitting perfectly still. The number of actions depicted will predict neither effect without some account of what it costs the eye to compare them.

For an exhibition the artist mounted the three drawings in separate rooms, with a bench in the room containing the crossword. Visitors spent longer there than they had spent reading the whole strip on paper. It is tempting to say that the exhibition had slowed the story down. It had unquestionably slowed the visitors down. But their added minutes might have been spent resting their feet, remembering the coat, or regretting that they had not looked at it more closely. The change in arrangement altered what kinds of attention were convenient. A stopwatch could report a consequence of that change without identifying the kind of attention responsible for it.

Which claim best captures the author's account of pacing in the strip?
Choices:
The elapsed time inside a story can be calculated from how long readers inspect it.
Ambiguous details mainly reward readers who discover the artist's solution.
The arrangement of panels shapes how easily readers can compare and revise impressions.
The band between images prevents readers from imagining events that were omitted.
Answer: The arrangement of panels shapes how easily readers can compare and revise impressions.
Reason: The author emphasizes returning from the crossword to the coat and distinguishes this activity from elapsed viewing time.
Source: Original passage and item · AAMC CARS framework · https://students-residents.aamc.org/whats-mcat-exam/critical-analysis-and-reasoning-skills-section-overview

In the second he stood on the platform looking at the clock. In the third he was seated by a window, holding a half-finished crossword. The critic meant that it took three seconds to look across the page. But it is doubtful whether anybody who had actually read those panels could say how much of the man's afternoon they contained.

The crossword is what makes the question interesting. We may imagine that the man began it after boarding and has been riding for some time. He may equally well have taken the paper from his coat with half the squares filled in from yesterday. A film director could withhold the same information. What is peculiar to the strip is that the reader who has reached the crossword can look back at the platform without leaving the last panel behind. The man's coat is there to be inspected. Its pockets bulge, though not in a way that settles the matter.

Some enthusiasts have suggested that the empty band between panels is where readers do the real work of imagining events. I doubt the band deserves quite so much credit. Cut the strip into separate cards and hand them over one by one. Readers will still infer that the man passed through a door to board the train, though no white band now separates two pictures. What the altered arrangement makes difficult is a different activity. To check the coat pockets a reader must ask for an earlier card, putting aside the view that gave the pockets their sudden interest.

This distinction would matter little if the artist's job were simply to reward alert readers with clues. The pockets, however, have no solution. Their usefulness lies in the brief possibility of revising what the crossword first seemed to mean. A page that permits such revision can feel unhurried even when its subject is a dash for a train. Another page can feel breathless while showing a man sitting perfectly still. The number of actions depicted will predict neither effect without some account of what it costs the eye to compare them.

For an exhibition the artist mounted the three drawings in separate rooms, with a bench in the room containing the crossword. Visitors spent longer there than they had spent reading the whole strip on paper. It is tempting to say that the exhibition had slowed the story down. It had unquestionably slowed the visitors down. But their added minutes might have been spent resting their feet, remembering the coat, or regretting that they had not looked at it more closely. The change in arrangement altered what kinds of attention were convenient. A stopwatch could report a consequence of that change without identifying the kind of attention responsible for it.

Why does the author mention that there was a bench in the final room?
Choices:
To show that the artist expected the crossword to be solved there
To establish that the room was larger than the other rooms
To suggest that the exhibition improved the drawings' legibility
To illustrate another possible reason for a longer visit
Answer: To illustrate another possible reason for a longer visit
Reason: Visitors may simply have rested. The timing measurement cannot identify what occupied their attention.

Topic: CARS · Humanities · The reverse of the festival quilt
Prompt:
When a harbor town lent its festival quilt to a museum, the museum proposed hanging it so that visitors could walk around it. The reverse was a confusion of stitches, knots, and faded names. On the front, each household that contributed a square had embroidered its name in blue. The museum called the reverse a record of the anonymous work that the attractive face concealed. The town’s sewing circle objected to that description. They had no objection to showing the back. They objected to the claim that turning a thing over necessarily told you who had made it.

The objection arose from a custom older than the present quilt. At the end of a festival, the quilt spent the winter with whichever household had most recently joined the circle. Its keeper was expected to mend loose squares before the spring procession. A keeper might sew several repairs in a single evening, or none for years. Sometimes a keeper asked a neighbor to make a difficult repair. The names on the front recorded the gift of cloth, not the hand that performed the embroidery. The stitches on the reverse recorded acts of maintenance, but no convention required a keeper to sign them. A viewer who credited every repair to the keeper of its year would be inventing a fairly plausible history.

The museum revised its label. It now said that the front documented membership while the reverse documented labor. This was closer, yet a woman from the circle pointed to an untouched square of thin green cotton. It was still sound because three successive keepers had protected it with a removable lining during the procession. The lining did not go into the display case. On the reverse, the best visible evidence of their particular care was precisely the absence of a repair. Even that absence would have meant little without someone’s account of the lining.

A historian suggested recording such accounts and playing them beside the quilt. Some members welcomed the proposal. Others recalled arguments over who had supplied a particular lining. To exhibit one recollection in a recorded voice, they said, might give it a finality that it had never possessed at the sewing table. Still, disagreement need not turn every account into mere decoration. Two neighbors could disagree about the maker of a lining while agreeing that it had been used, when it had been attached, and why the green cloth mattered. Their disagreement set limits on one claim without discrediting all the others.

The most informative exhibit would allow the visitor to handle different degrees of certainty. A seam can establish that a repair was made. A pair of recollections can explain the survival of an unbroken square. Neither must yield a name. The trouble with the original label was not its generosity toward forgotten hands. It was the assumption that fairness requires distributing credit with greater precision than the available traces allow.

Which claim best expresses the author’s position?
Choices:
A museum can honor maintenance while distinguishing what the surviving evidence establishes about it.
The identities of contributors can be recovered by combining every repair with its keeper’s dates.
Unrecorded care should be excluded from museum interpretation because it cannot be demonstrated.
The quilt should be displayed only by the community that owns it.
Answer: A museum can honor maintenance while distinguishing what the surviving evidence establishes about it.
Reason: The author supports interpreting care, including care without a visible repair, while limiting claims about individual credit.
